items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You have built RAG systems and tuned them by feel. This week you replace feel with numbers. You build a RAG evaluation CLI: point it at a config file (which pipeline, which chunking, which model, which top-k) and a golden test set, and it runs the whole pipeline over every test question and outputs a structured report, retrieval precision and recall, answer faithfulness and relevance and correctness. By Sunday you can answer "is this RAG change an improvement or a regression?" with evidence, run it on every code change, and tune your pipeline the way you would tune any system you can measure. This is the week RAG stops being art and becomes engineering.

## Why "the answers seem reasonable" is a trap
The default way people evaluate RAG, ask it a few questions, eyeball the answers, conclude it works, fails for reasons that compound. You test on a handful of questions you happen to think of, which are not representative; you judge "reasonable" subjectively and inconsistently; and crucially, you have no baseline to compare a change against, so you cannot tell whether your new reranker helped, hurt, or did nothing. Worse, an answer that sounds fluent and confident can be completely wrong (a hallucination reads exactly like a correct answer), so "seems reasonable" actively misleads you. Measurement replaces all of that with a fixed test set, defined metrics, and comparable numbers, the only way to know if RAG works that survives contact with reality.

## The two halves: retrieval metrics and answer metrics
RAG eval mirrors the two failure stages from last week, and you measure each. Retrieval metrics ask "did we find the right documents?", recall (did the relevant chunks make it into the top-k?), precision (are the top-k actually relevant?), and rank-aware versions (does the best chunk come first?). Answer metrics ask "given what we retrieved, is the final answer good?", faithfulness (are the answer's claims supported by the context, i.e. is it hallucinating?), answer relevance (does it address the question?), and correctness (does it match the known right answer?). Splitting eval this way is what makes it actionable: a bad retrieval score and a bad answer score point you at completely different fixes, so the report does not just grade your RAG, it tells you which stage to work on.

## Where this fits
You build the eval CLI this week, the measurement discipline that the entire production phase rests on. It closes the RAG phase: you can now build production RAG (W11) and prove whether it works (W12). And the skill generalises immediately, evals are how you ship any AI feature with confidence (W17 makes them a deployment gate), because the lesson is universal: an AI system you cannot measure is one you cannot trust, improve, or responsibly put in front of users. RAG was the concrete case; eval is the discipline.

items.title: Building a golden test set
items.body:
## Ground truth is the foundation, and it's manual work
Every metric this week is measured against something, and that something is a golden test set: a fixed set of questions, each paired with the known-correct answer and the known source document(s) that contain it. Without ground truth you literally cannot compute the metrics, recall asks "did we retrieve the relevant docs?", which is meaningless unless you have defined which docs are relevant. Building this set is hand work, you read your corpus, write real questions, and record the right answer and the supporting sources for each, and there is no shortcut around the fact that it is the single most valuable and most skipped investment in RAG quality. A mediocre pipeline with a great test set beats a great pipeline with no test set, because the first you can improve and the second you can only hope about.

## Cover the cases that actually stress the system
A good golden set is not just easy questions; it is deliberately built to exercise the ways RAG fails. Include at least three kinds:
- **Single-chunk questions** where the answer sits in one obvious passage, the easy baseline.
- **Multi-chunk questions** whose answer requires combining information from two or more passages, which stress retrieval recall and the model's synthesis.
- **Unanswerable questions** whose answer is NOT in the corpus at all, which test whether your system abstains (says "not in the sources") instead of hallucinating, the grounding behaviour from W11.
A test set of only easy single-chunk questions will tell you your RAG is great right up until it faceplants on the hard cases in production; including the hard and the unanswerable cases is what makes the score predict real behaviour.

## What retrieval metrics the golden set unlocks
With known-relevant source documents per question, you can now compute the retrieval metrics that grade the finding stage:
- **Recall@k:** of the documents that are relevant, what fraction appear in your top-k? (Did you find the right stuff?)
- **Precision@k:** of your top-k results, what fraction are actually relevant? (Is your top-k full of junk?)
- **MRR** (Mean Reciprocal Rank): how high up is the first relevant result, averaged across questions? (Does the good stuff come early?)
- **NDCG:** like recall but position-aware, a relevant doc at rank 1 counts more than one at rank 5.
These turn "retrieval seems okay" into "recall@5 is 0.82, MRR is 0.74", numbers you can compare across pipeline variants. The golden set's known-relevant labels are exactly what makes them computable.

## Where this fits
Hand-build a golden test set for your paper assistant, twenty or so questions spanning single-chunk, multi-chunk, and unanswerable, each with its correct answer and source docs, and compute recall@k and MRR for your current retrieval. You now have the ground truth everything else this week measures against, and your first hard retrieval numbers, which is the foundation the answer metrics and the eval CLI build on.

items.title: Answer metrics
items.body:
## Grading the answer, not just the retrieval
Retrieval metrics tell you whether the right chunks were found; answer metrics tell you whether the final answer is any good given those chunks. Three matter, and they catch different failures:
- **Faithfulness** (groundedness): are the answer's claims actually supported by the retrieved context? This is the hallucination detector, an unfaithful answer asserts things the sources do not say. It is measured independently of whether the answer is "correct", a faithful answer sticks to the context even if the context was wrong.
- **Answer relevance:** does the answer actually address the question asked, or does it wander? A relevant answer is on-topic and responsive.
- **Correctness:** does the answer match the known correct answer from your golden set? This needs ground truth and is the closest thing to "is it right".
Three lenses, because an answer can be faithful but irrelevant, or relevant but wrong, and you want to know which.

## LLM-as-judge: how these get scored at scale
You cannot hand-grade faithfulness on hundreds of answers, so the standard technique is LLM-as-judge: you use a model to score the output. For faithfulness, you give a judge model the answer and the retrieved context and ask it to check whether each claim in the answer is supported, returning a structured verdict (the structured-output skill from W6 doing real work). Frameworks like RAGAS package exactly these metrics, faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall, on top of an LLM judge, so you do not hand-roll the prompts. LLM-as-judge is powerful and has a known caveat: the judge is itself a fallible model, so you validate it (spot-check its verdicts against your own judgement on a sample) rather than trusting it blindly. But for scoring hundreds of answers consistently, a validated LLM judge is far better than no measurement.

## Read the two halves together to find the fix
The payoff of having both retrieval and answer metrics is diagnosis, the report tells you not just that RAG is bad but where. The combinations are diagnostic:
- **Low retrieval recall, low correctness:** the right chunk was not found, fix retrieval (chunking, reranker, query rewrite).
- **High retrieval recall, low faithfulness:** the right chunk was found and the model hallucinated anyway, fix generation (the grounding prompt, the model).
- **High faithfulness, low relevance:** the answer is grounded but not answering the question, fix the prompt or the question handling.
This is why you measure both halves separately: a single "RAG quality: 6/10" number tells you nothing actionable, but "recall is fine, faithfulness is low" points straight at the broken stage. That diagnostic power is the whole reason eval is worth building.

## Where this fits
Add answer metrics, faithfulness, relevance, and correctness via an LLM judge (or RAGAS), to your eval over the golden set, and read them alongside the retrieval metrics to diagnose where your paper assistant is weakest. You can now grade the full RAG pipeline end to end and, crucially, tell which stage a problem lives in, which is what turns evaluation from a grade into a to-do list.

items.title: Test set sizing
items.body:
## How many test questions is enough?
A natural question once you are hand-building golden sets: how big does the test set need to be? Too few questions and your metrics are noisy, recall@5 measured on 5 questions can swing wildly with one lucky or unlucky retrieval, so a "0.80 vs 0.60" difference between two pipelines might be pure chance. Too many and you have spent weeks hand-labelling when a fraction would have done. The answer is not a magic number; it is a tradeoff between the confidence you need and the effort you can spend, and understanding that tradeoff keeps you from both over-investing and from trusting a meaningless three-question eval.

## Enough to detect the difference you care about
The principled way to think about size: you need enough questions that a real quality difference shows up above the noise. A handful (5-10) is fine for catching gross regressions (your change dropped recall from 0.8 to 0.3, obvious even on 10 questions) but useless for distinguishing a 0.78 from a 0.81 pipeline (that gap is smaller than the noise on a small set). Detecting small improvements needs more questions, often 50-200 for a development RAG eval, because the smaller the difference you want to detect reliably, the more samples you need to see it through the noise. So size to your decision: a quick "did I break it" gate can be small; a careful "is variant A genuinely better than variant B" comparison needs to be bigger.

## Coverage matters as much as count
Raw count is not the whole story, what the questions cover matters as much as how many. A 200-question set that is all easy single-chunk lookups tells you a lot about easy lookups and nothing about the hard multi-chunk or unanswerable cases where RAG actually breaks. A smaller set that deliberately spans the failure modes (easy, multi-hop, unanswerable, different topics) is more informative than a larger uniform one, because the score reflects the full range of real queries. So size and composition together: enough questions to beat the noise on the decision you are making, distributed across the cases that actually stress the system, so the aggregate metric predicts production behaviour rather than just measuring the easy path. Growing the set over time, every real failure you discover becomes a new test case, is how a golden set gets genuinely representative.

## Where this fits
Decide a defensible size for your paper-assistant golden set based on what you are using it for (a quick regression gate vs a careful variant comparison), and make sure it covers the failure modes, not just easy questions. You understand that eval confidence depends on both the size and the coverage of the test set, which keeps you from drawing big conclusions from a tiny eval, and motivates the next lesson: if hand-labelling 200 questions is the bottleneck, can you generate some of them?

items.title: Synthetic test generation
items.body:
## The bottleneck is making test data; let a model help
Hand-building a 200-question golden set is slow, and that effort is the main reason teams skip RAG eval. Synthetic test generation eases it: you use an LLM to generate candidate test questions from your corpus. The method is neat, point a model at a chunk (or a document) and ask it to produce a question that the chunk answers, plus the answer, and you have created a (question, answer, source) triple, exactly the golden-set format, with the source already known because you generated the question from that source. Do this across your corpus and you bootstrap a large test set in minutes instead of days.
```text
chunk -> "Generate a question this passage answers, and the answer."
      -> { question, answer, source_chunk_id }   # a golden-set entry
```

## The catch: synthetic data needs human review
Synthetic generation is a force multiplier, not a free lunch, and the discipline is to treat generated questions as a draft you review, not ground truth you trust. The model produces some questions that are trivial (answerable from the chunk verbatim, testing nothing), some that are ambiguous, and occasionally some whose "answer" the model got wrong, and if you feed those straight into your eval, you are measuring against a flawed yardstick. So the workflow is generate-then-curate: the LLM proposes candidates fast, and you read, filter, and fix them, keeping the good ones, deleting the trivial, correcting the wrong. That human pass is much faster than writing every question from scratch, but it is not optional, an unreviewed synthetic test set can make a worse pipeline look better, the exact opposite of what eval is for.

## Use synthetics to scale coverage, keep a hand-built core
The mature pattern combines both: a small, carefully hand-built core of high-value questions (especially the tricky multi-hop and unanswerable cases the model struggles to generate well), plus a larger synthetic layer for breadth and coverage across the corpus. The hand-built core anchors quality; the synthetic layer cheaply expands the count and topic coverage so your metrics beat the noise (D4). You also use synthetics to target gaps, if your eval is thin on a particular document or question type, generate more there. The judgement, as always, is to use the LLM where it is a genuine accelerant (drafting many candidate questions) while keeping the human in the loop where correctness matters (curating the ones you will actually measure against), which is the same human-plus-model division that good AI engineering keeps coming back to.

## Where this fits
Generate synthetic test questions from your paper corpus, then curate them, deleting the trivial and fixing the wrong, and fold the good ones into your golden set alongside your hand-built questions. You can now build a substantial, well-covered test set far faster than hand-writing every question, while keeping the quality that makes the eval trustworthy, which removes the main excuse for not evaluating RAG at all.

items.title: Cost of evals
items.body:
## Evals cost money, and naive eval is expensive
Running a RAG eval is not free: every test question triggers a full pipeline run (retrieval plus a generation call), and every metric that uses an LLM judge is another model call. So evaluating 200 questions with three LLM-judged metrics can be 200 pipeline calls plus 600 judge calls, and if you run that on every code change, the eval bill can rival or exceed your production bill. This is a real and often-overlooked cost, and the W7 cost discipline now applies to your evaluation as much as your product: an eval so expensive you avoid running it is an eval that does not protect you.

## The levers, all familiar
Fortunately the cost levers are exactly the ones from W7, applied to eval:
- **Cheaper judge models:** the LLM judge does not need your most expensive model, a smaller, cheaper model often judges faithfulness and relevance perfectly well, and you can validate that it agrees with the expensive one on a sample before trusting it.
- **Batch the eval run:** an eval is the canonical non-interactive batch job, nobody is waiting on it, so run it through the Batch API at half price.
- **Cache shared prefixes:** if every judge call shares the same long rubric prompt, prompt-cache that prefix so you pay for it once.
- **Right-size the test set:** D4's lesson, do not run 500 questions when 100 gives you the confidence you need.
None of this is new, it is the cost toolkit you already built, pointed at the eval pipeline.

## Tier your evals: fast-and-cheap often, slow-and-thorough rarely
The production pattern that resolves the cost-vs-rigour tension is tiered evaluation, matching eval cost to how often you run it. A small, fast, cheap eval (a few dozen questions, maybe cheaper metrics) runs on every change as a quick regression gate, catching obvious breakage in seconds for cents. A large, thorough, expensive eval (the full golden set, all metrics, the better judge) runs rarely, before a release, on a schedule, when you need a confident quality read. This mirrors the W17 deployment-gating idea and the SRE alerting philosophy: cheap-and-frequent for fast feedback, expensive-and-rare for the high-stakes decision. Tiering is what makes evaluation sustainable, you get fast feedback on every change without paying full-eval cost every time, and a rigorous read exactly when the decision warrants it.

## Where this fits
Estimate what your RAG eval costs per run, apply the levers (a cheaper validated judge, batch the run, cache the rubric), and design a tiered setup, a small cheap eval per change, the full eval before a release. You have made evaluation affordable enough to actually run continuously, which is the whole point, an eval you cannot afford to run is an eval that does not protect your quality, and you have connected the cost discipline to the eval discipline, both of which the production phase depends on.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A repeatable RAG evaluation CLI that turns "seems fine" into numbers. By tonight:
- a golden test set (hand-built core plus curated synthetic), spanning easy, multi-chunk, and unanswerable questions, each with answer and sources.
- the CLI runs a pipeline (defined in a config file) over the set and reports retrieval metrics (recall@k, precision@k, MRR) and answer metrics (faithfulness, relevance, correctness).
- swapping the config (different chunking, top-k, model) produces a comparable report, so you can A/B pipeline variants on numbers.
- the eval is cost-aware: tiered (cheap per-change, full per-release) and affordable to run.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a measured pipeline comparison that changes a decision. Take two variants of your paper assistant, say with and without the reranker from W11, run both through the CLI on the same golden set, and report the difference: "the reranker raised recall@5 from 0.71 to 0.86 and answer correctness from 0.64 to 0.79; faithfulness was unchanged at 0.91." That sentence, a quality change quantified across the metrics that matter, is the entire payoff of evaluation: you now know the reranker helped (and by how much, and on which metric) instead of believing it did. Being able to run that comparison, and act on it, is the deliverable, and it is the exact workflow that makes the rest of AI engineering rigorous.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the eval CLI with its golden test set, config files for the variants, and a README showing a real before/after comparison. This is one of the strongest portfolio pieces on the whole track, because evaluation is where most AI engineers are weakest, plenty of people can build a RAG pipeline; very few can prove whether it works or whether a change improved it. Demonstrating a golden set, a full set of retrieval and answer metrics, and a repeatable, cost-aware eval that gates decisions shows the rigour that separates someone who builds AI features from someone who can be trusted to ship them.

## Where this fits in the track
You can now build production RAG (W11) and rigorously measure it (W12), which completes the RAG phase. More importantly, you have built the discipline the entire rest of the track runs on: evaluation. The Agents phase (W13-16) needs it (how do you know an agent's trajectory is good?), and Production AI (W17-20) makes evals a literal deployment gate, the test suite that blocks a release if quality regresses. The lesson generalises far past RAG: every AI feature you ship should be measured, because an AI system you cannot evaluate is one you cannot trust, improve, or responsibly put in front of users. Next week you give the model autonomy, agents, and the first thing you will ask is the question you can now answer: how do we know it's working?

weeks.title: Agent Architectures, ReAct, Planning, and the Loop That Runs The World
weeks.context:
An LLM that thinks step by step and can call tools is an agent. The basic loop is simple: observe the situation, reason about what to do next, take an action, observe the result, repeat until done. ReAct (Reason + Act) formalises this: the model explicitly alternates between reasoning tokens ("I need to find the cost comparison between GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet") and action tokens ("search: GPT-4o vs Claude Sonnet cost 2025"). The interleaved structure keeps the model's reasoning grounded in the actions it has taken.

This week you build a researcher agent. Given a research question, it searches, reads, synthesises, and produces a structured report. The agent loops, each tool call results inform the next, until it has enough information to write the final report. Building it forces you to confront every practical challenge in agent development: loop control, context management, tool failure handling, and knowing when the agent has enough information to stop.

Plan-then-execute is the alternative architecture. Instead of interleaving reasoning and action, the agent first produces a complete plan (a sequence of steps), then executes the plan deterministically. This architecture is more predictable but less adaptive, if step 3 fails, the plan breaks. ReAct is more adaptive but harder to observe and debug. Understanding when to use each is an architectural judgment call.

Reflection adds a self-critique step. After completing a draft answer, the agent sends it to itself (or a separate model instance) with the prompt "what is wrong or missing in this response?" The critic's feedback is incorporated into a second pass. This consistently improves output quality at the cost of additional tokens and latency. For research and writing tasks, the improvement is usually worth it.

Context management is the hard engineering problem in agents. Each tool call adds to the conversation history. A 10-step agent on a large research question can accumulate 30k tokens of context. You need a strategy: summarise old tool results, drop low-relevance results, enforce a maximum context budget.

concept_check.q: Your researcher agent is on step 8 of a research task. The context window has 45k tokens of conversation history. The model starts hallucinating details from its training data instead of from the retr?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: The agent calls a search tool and receives 10 results. It reads all 10 in full and includes them in its next reasoning step. The context grows by 8000 tokens on this one step. What should you have don?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You want to implement reflection: after the agent drafts its report, it critiques its own draft. How do you structure this as code without a separate model instance? Add a final step to the agent loop?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
This is the week the model stops answering and starts acting. You build a researcher agent: give it a question it cannot answer from memory ("how do GPT-4o and Claude Haiku compare on cost and latency for a high-volume classification job?") and it searches, reads what it finds, decides what to search next based on what it learned, and keeps going until it can write a grounded, structured report. The difference from everything you have built so far is the loop: previous projects called the model once and used the answer; this one lets the model call tools, see the results, and decide its own next move, over and over, until it judges itself done. That loop is the whole idea of an agent, and building one forces you to confront every hard part of agent engineering at once.

## An agent is a loop, not a model
The word "agent" sounds like a special kind of model, and it is not. An agent is an ordinary LLM placed inside a loop you write: the model proposes an action (call this tool with these arguments), your code executes the action and feeds the result back, and the model proposes the next action in light of that result. ReAct (Reason + Act) is the pattern that makes this work: the model interleaves reasoning ("I still do not have latency numbers, I should search for benchmarks") with actions ("search: claude haiku latency benchmark"), so each action is grounded in the reasoning that led to it and each new observation updates the reasoning. The model is the same `messages.create` call you already know; the agent is the orchestration around it, observe, reason, act, observe, repeat, and that orchestration is the thing you are learning to build this week.

## The four problems every agent forces you to solve
The reason a researcher agent is the right first project is that it surfaces all four of the engineering problems that make agents hard, and you will hit each one this week:
- **Loop control:** what makes the loop run, and what makes it stop? An agent with no stopping condition runs forever or until it bankrupts you.
- **Context management:** every tool result is appended to the conversation, so a ten-step research task can balloon to tens of thousands of tokens, slowing the model, raising cost, and eventually crowding out the original question.
- **Tool failure handling:** a search returns nothing, an API times out, a page is junk, and the agent has to cope rather than crash.
- **Knowing when it is done:** the agent has to judge that it has enough to answer, the single hardest call, because stopping too early gives a thin answer and stopping too late wastes tokens.
Every later week in the Agents phase is, in some sense, a deeper treatment of one of these, so meeting all four in one concrete project is the orientation.

## Where this fits
You spend this week building the researcher agent and, through it, internalising the agent loop and its four hard problems. It opens the Agents phase (W13-16): this week is the single agent and its loop, then W14 gives agents memory across turns, W15 standardises their tools with MCP, and W16 composes many agents into a system. And it rests directly on the eval discipline you just built, because the first honest question to ask about an agent that takes its own multi-step path is exactly the one W12 taught you to answer: how do you know its trajectory was any good? Today, get the loop running end to end on one real question, even crudely, the rest of the week makes it good.

items.title: The basic agent loop
items.body:
## The loop, concretely
Strip an agent to its core and it is a `while` loop around one model call. You send the model the conversation so far plus the list of tools it may use. The model replies either with a final answer (stop) or with a request to call a tool, a structured block naming the tool and its arguments. Your code executes that tool, appends the result to the conversation as a tool-result message, and loops back to call the model again with the now-longer conversation. The model sees its own previous request and the result it produced, reasons about what that tells it, and either answers or calls another tool. That is the entire engine:
```text
loop:
  reply = model(conversation, tools)
  if reply is final answer: return it
  result = run_tool(reply.tool_name, reply.tool_args)
  conversation += [reply, result]   # the model sees both next time
```
Everything else in agent engineering is making this loop robust, bounded, and observable.

## How the model actually requests a tool
The mechanism is the tool-use protocol you met in the structured-outputs phase, now running in a loop. You pass `tools=[{name, description, input_schema}]` on the model call. When the model decides to act, its response contains a tool-use block, a structured object with the tool's `name` and a validated `input` matching the schema (not free text you have to parse). Your code reads `block.name` and `block.input`, runs the real function, and sends the output back as a tool-result block tied to that call's id. On the next call, the model sees the result and continues. The skill's source-of-truth detail matters here: the Anthropic Messages API returns `stop_reason: "tool_use"` when the model wants a tool, and you keep looping while that is the stop reason, so the stop reason itself is your loop condition. This is why structured outputs came first: tool use is structured output with the schema being the tool's signature, and the agent loop is just that, repeated.

## Why ReAct (reasoning between actions) matters
You could let the model emit tool calls back to back with nothing in between, and it would work poorly. ReAct's insight is that the model should reason in text before each action and after each observation: "the search gave me pricing but no latency, so next I will search benchmarks." That visible reasoning does real work, it keeps each action grounded in what has been learned, and it is your window into why the agent did what it did. When an agent goes wrong (searches the same thing twice, ignores a result, stops early), the reasoning trace is where you see the mistake, which is why you log it. An agent with no reasoning between actions is both worse at the task and nearly impossible to debug, so you prompt the model to think out loud and you keep that thinking in the trace.

## Where this fits
Build the bare loop today: a model call with one tool (web search), a `while` that runs while the model keeps requesting tools, and a trace that logs every reasoning step, tool call, and result. Run it on one real research question and watch it take three or four steps to an answer. You now have a working agent, the loop that, as the week's title says, runs the world, and the rest of the week hardens it: alternative architectures, self-checking, decomposition, and the all-important question of when it should stop.

items.title: Plan-then-execute
items.body:
## A different shape: plan first, then execute
The ReAct loop decides its next action one step at a time, in the moment. Plan-then-execute inverts that: the agent first produces a complete plan, an ordered list of steps, before doing anything, and then executes those steps in order. For a research question the plan might be "1) find pricing for both models, 2) find latency benchmarks, 3) find context-window limits, 4) synthesise into a comparison table." The planning model writes all four up front; an executor then carries them out. The two architectures answer the same question, "what should the agent do?", at opposite times: ReAct answers continuously as it goes, plan-then-execute answers once at the start. That timing difference is the whole trade-off, and knowing which to reach for is an architectural judgement, not a default.

## The trade-off: predictable versus adaptive
Plan-then-execute is more predictable and more inspectable. You can read the plan before any tokens are spent on execution, you can show it to a user for approval, and the run is easy to follow because it just walks the list. Its weakness is rigidity: if step 3 fails or step 2 reveals that the plan was wrong, a naive executor ploughs ahead anyway, because the plan was fixed before the agent knew what it would find. ReAct is the mirror image: it adapts beautifully (a surprising search result immediately reshapes the next action) but it is harder to predict and harder to debug, because the trajectory only exists after the fact. So the honest framing is a spectrum, not a winner: predictable-but-rigid at one end, adaptive-but-unruly at the other, and most real agents live somewhere between.

## Choosing, and combining
The judgement is about the task. Use plan-then-execute when the steps are knowable in advance and predictability matters, a data-export pipeline, a multi-step form, anything where you want to show the plan before running it or where steps are independent. Use ReAct when each step genuinely depends on what the last one returned, open-ended research, debugging, exploration, where you cannot know step 3 until you have seen step 2. And the mature pattern often blends them: plan at a high level for structure, then run each step with a small adaptive loop that can react to failure, or let the agent re-plan when execution reveals the original plan was wrong. The point of learning both is not to pick a side but to recognise, for a given task, how much you can decide up front versus how much you must discover by doing, which is exactly the call a senior engineer makes when designing any agent.

## Where this fits
Reimplement your researcher with a plan-then-execute architecture: have the model produce the research plan first, print it, then execute the steps, and compare its behaviour to yesterday's ReAct loop on the same questions. You will feel the trade-off directly, the planned version is easier to follow and the ReAct version handles surprises better, which is the intuition that lets you choose architecture deliberately instead of always reaching for the same loop. Tomorrow you add a different lever for quality: running the agent more than once and reconciling the results.

items.title: Self-consistency
items.body:
## One run is a sample, not the truth
An agent's trajectory has randomness in it, the model's choices depend on sampling, so the same question run twice can take different paths and reach slightly different answers. Self-consistency turns that variability from a bug into a tool: instead of trusting one run, you run the agent (or the reasoning step) several times and reconcile the results. The classic version, run the chain of reasoning N times and take the majority answer, comes from the observation that a model is more likely to reach the right conclusion than any particular wrong one, so the most common answer across several independent attempts is more reliable than a single attempt. You are spending extra compute to buy reliability, the same trade every redundant system makes.

## Why agreement signals confidence
The deeper value of running multiple times is not just the majority vote, it is what the spread tells you. If five runs of your researcher all converge on "Haiku is roughly 5x cheaper and somewhat faster for this workload," that agreement is evidence the answer is stable and well-supported. If five runs scatter, one says cheaper, one says more expensive, one cannot find latency data, that disagreement is itself the finding: the question is underdetermined by the available sources, or your tools are not returning consistent information. So self-consistency gives you two things, a more reliable answer (the consensus) and a confidence signal (how much the runs agreed), and the second is often as useful as the first, because an agent that can say "I am uncertain, my attempts disagreed" is far safer than one that confidently returns whichever single answer it happened to land on.

## Spend the compute where it pays
Self-consistency is not free, N runs cost roughly N times the tokens and latency, so you apply it where reliability is worth the multiple and skip it where it is not. The judgement mirrors the tiered-eval thinking from last week: reserve the expensive, multi-run path for high-stakes or ambiguous questions (a final report a user will act on) and run a single pass for cheap, low-stakes ones. You can also apply it surgically, run only the critical reasoning step several times rather than the whole agent, getting most of the reliability for a fraction of the cost. And it composes with the cost levers you already know: cheaper model for the redundant runs, batch them since they are independent. The skill is recognising that more reliability has a price and choosing to pay it exactly where a wrong answer would cost more than the extra runs, not reflexively everywhere.

## Where this fits
Add self-consistency to your researcher for the questions that matter: run the agent several times, reconcile to a consensus answer, and surface how much the runs agreed as a confidence signal. You have added a reliability lever that trades compute for trustworthiness, and, just as importantly, a way for the agent to know and say when it is unsure, which is one of the most valuable properties a production agent can have. Next you scale the agent the other way, not by repeating it but by splitting it into a manager and workers.

items.title: Hierarchical agents
items.body:
## When one agent's context gets too crowded
A single agent doing a big task accumulates everything in one conversation: every search, every page, every reasoning step, all in one growing context. Past a point this hurts, the context is huge and expensive, and the model juggling pricing research, latency research, and report-writing all at once does each less well, the same generalisation limit that makes a single person worse at a job than a focused team. Hierarchical agents address this by decomposition: a manager (or orchestrator) agent breaks the task into subtasks and delegates each to a worker agent with its own fresh, narrow context. The manager does not do the research; it decides what research is needed and hands each piece to a worker, then collects the results.

## How delegation keeps each context clean
The key engineering benefit is context isolation. The manager assigns "find latency benchmarks for both models" to a worker; that worker runs its own little agent loop, accumulates its own search results in its own context, and returns only a clean summary, not its 8000 tokens of raw pages. The manager's context stays small because it holds plans and summaries, not raw tool output, and each worker's context stays focused on one subtask. This is the same pattern as breaking a monolith into services: each piece has a bounded responsibility and a clean interface (the summary it returns), and the whole stays comprehensible because no single context holds everything. It directly attacks the context-management problem from D1, the manager never sees the firehose, only the distilled results, so a ten-source research task does not blow up one giant conversation.

## The cost of coordination
Hierarchy is not free, and the failure mode is over-decomposition. Every worker is its own set of model calls, so a manager that spawns a worker for each trivial step multiplies cost and latency, and the manager-worker handoffs add their own overhead and their own chances to lose information (a worker summary that drops the detail the manager needed). So you decompose where subtasks are genuinely separable and each is substantial enough to justify its own agent, find-pricing and find-latency are good workers; "search one query" is not, that is just a tool call. The judgement is the same one a tech lead makes deciding how to split work across a team: split along real seams where the pieces are independent and each is worth a person's focus, not so finely that coordination costs more than the work. A flat single agent is often the right answer; reach for hierarchy when the task is genuinely too big or too varied for one context to hold well.

## Where this fits
Refactor your researcher into a manager that decomposes the question into research subtasks, delegates each to a worker agent with its own context, and synthesises the workers' summaries into the final report. You have learned the primary way agents scale to large tasks, decomposition with context isolation, and felt where it helps (big, separable tasks) versus where it just adds overhead (small ones). This manager-worker shape returns in W16 as full multi-agent systems; today it is one agent commanding sub-agents, which leaves one problem before you ship: in all these architectures, how does the agent know when to stop?

items.title: Stopping conditions
items.body:
## The question every agent has to answer about itself
An agent loops, and a loop needs a reason to end. This is not a detail, it is the most important safety and quality property an agent has, because the failure modes are severe in both directions. An agent that does not know when to stop either runs forever (or until it burns your budget), looping on the same searches, or it stops too early and hands back a thin, half-researched answer. Knowing when it has enough to answer is, as D1 warned, the single hardest judgement in the loop, and it is hard precisely because it is the model judging its own sufficiency, which models do imperfectly. So you do not rely on the model's judgement alone; you engineer stopping conditions around it.

## The layers of stopping
Robust agents stack several stopping conditions, from hard outer limits to soft inner judgement:
- **A hard iteration cap:** never loop more than N times, full stop. This is the backstop that guarantees termination even if every other condition fails, the seatbelt you always wear.
- **A budget cap:** stop when token or dollar spend crosses a threshold, so a runaway agent fails at a known cost instead of an unbounded one.
- **A no-progress check:** if the last step added nothing new (a repeated search, a duplicate result, no new information), stop or change strategy rather than spinning.
- **The model's own sufficiency judgement:** prompt the agent to ask, each iteration, "do I now have enough to answer well?" and to stop when the answer is yes.
The hard caps are non-negotiable infrastructure; the sufficiency judgement is the quality lever. Together they bound the worst case and aim for the right case.

## Tuning the stop is tuning quality and cost
Where you set these conditions is a direct quality-versus-cost dial, and it is exactly what your W12 evals let you tune honestly. Stop too eagerly and answers get thin (low correctness on your golden set); allow too many iterations and cost and latency climb for diminishing gains. Because you can now measure answer quality, you can find the iteration cap and sufficiency prompt that get most of the quality for a sane cost, instead of guessing. This is also where tool-failure handling lives: a search that errors should not crash the loop or count as progress, it should be caught, logged, maybe retried, and folded into the agent's view ("that source failed, I will try another"). An agent that stops cleanly on success, bounds its worst case on failure, and degrades gracefully when a tool breaks is the difference between a demo and something you would actually run unattended.

## Where this fits
Give your researcher real stopping conditions, a hard iteration cap, a budget cap, a no-progress check, and a model sufficiency judgement, plus graceful handling of tool failures, and use your evals to tune where it stops. You have closed the loop you opened on D1: it now starts, runs, adapts, and, crucially, ends, on purpose, at the right time, within a known cost. That makes it something you can trust to run on its own, which is precisely what tomorrow's ship step demands.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A researcher agent that takes a real question, runs its own multi-step investigation, and returns a grounded, structured report, safely and within bounds. By tonight it:
- runs the agent loop (ReAct) with a search-and-read tool, reasoning between actions and logging a full trace of what it did and why.
- offers an alternative plan-then-execute mode and uses self-consistency on high-stakes questions, surfacing a confidence signal from how much the runs agreed.
- decomposes large questions via a manager that delegates to worker agents with isolated context.
- always terminates: a hard iteration cap, a budget cap, a no-progress check, the model's own sufficiency judgement, and graceful handling of tool failures.

## The test that proves it
Point it at a question it cannot answer from memory and that needs several real sources, "compare GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku on cost, latency, and context window for a high-volume classification job, and recommend one", and read the trace. The proof is in the trajectory: you should see it search, read, reason about what it still lacks, search again to fill the gap, and then stop, on its own judgement, when it has enough, producing a report whose claims trace back to sources it actually retrieved. Run it twice and confirm the answer is stable (or that it honestly flags uncertainty when the runs disagree). An agent that investigates a genuine question end to end, grounds its answer, and stops itself at the right point, that visible, sensible trajectory, is the entire deliverable, because it demonstrates the loop working as engineering rather than luck.

## Ship the artifact, with the trace
Commit the agent with its tools, a README showing an example question and the resulting report, and, most importantly, a saved trace of a real run, the reasoning, the tool calls, the stopping decision. The trace is what makes this a portfolio piece: anyone can claim "I built an agent," but a readable trajectory that shows the agent reasoning, adapting to what it found, and deciding for itself when to stop demonstrates that you understand the loop and its hard problems, not just that you wired up a framework. If you ran a W12-style eval on its outputs, include those numbers too, an agent you can measure is worth far more than one you can only demo.

## Where this fits in the track
You have built the fundamental unit of the Agents phase: a single agent that loops, reasons, acts, and stops. Every remaining week in the phase extends it. W14 gives it memory so it can hold state across many turns and sessions instead of starting fresh each time. W15 standardises its tools with MCP so they live in a server any agent can connect to, not hard-coded in this one codebase. W16 composes several agents into a system, the manager-worker idea from D5, grown up. And the eval discipline from W12 rides along the whole way, because the question that opened this week is the one you will keep asking of every agent you build: how do you know its trajectory was good? You can now build the agent and answer that question, which is what separates an agent engineer from someone who got a demo to work once.

weeks.title: Memory and Multi-Step Agents, Holding State Across Time
weeks.context:
Single-turn agents answer one question and stop. Most useful agents need to remember: what the user asked yesterday, what topics have already been covered, who the user is and what they care about. Memory is the engineering problem that separates a demo agent from a daily-use one.

The conversation buffer is the simplest memory: append every turn to the history and pass it all to the model. It works until the context window fills, which happens faster than most people expect with verbose agents. Summarisation memory addresses this: periodically condense older turns into a compact summary. The model loses some detail but retains the arc of the conversation.

Vector-based long-term memory stores every turn as an embedding. When starting a new conversation, you retrieve the most relevant prior interactions based on the current topic. This gives the agent access to months of history without paying to include it all in the context. The technical challenge is retrieval quality, you want to retrieve the turns that are actually relevant, not just semantically adjacent ones.

Entity memory is a structured alternative: extract people, places, projects, and preferences from the conversation and maintain them as a structured record. When the conversation mentions "the project we discussed Tuesday," the entity memory lets you look up what project that was, when you last discussed it, and what conclusions were reached. Entity memory is expensive to build correctly but extremely powerful when it works.

The personal research librarian you build this week uses all of these. It helps you research multiple topics across sessions, remembers what you have already found, and avoids repeating research you have already done. That requires working memory (this session), long-term memory (across sessions), and entity memory (topics, sources, conclusions).

items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **LLM calls**, use **Ollama** (runs Llama 3 / Mistral locally, free, no API key): point the base URL at `http://localhost:11434`. The chat shape is identical; you just swap the endpoint. Hugging Face's free Inference API also needs no credit card.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

## Context
This applies specifically to week 14 ('Memory and Multi-Step Agents, Holding State Across Time'), day 0.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Last week's researcher agent had a kind of amnesia: every question started from nothing. This week you cure it. You build a personal research librarian, an agent that helps you research topics across many sessions and remembers: what you have already looked into, what it found, what conclusions you reached, who and what the conversations were about. Ask it about a topic you explored last Tuesday and it recalls the sources it found and does not waste tokens re-researching what it already knows. That continuity, remembering across turns and across sessions, is what separates an agent you demo once from one you actually use every day, and it is entirely an engineering problem: the model itself remembers nothing between calls, so memory is something you build around it.

## The model is stateless; memory is yours to build
The foundational fact, easy to forget because chat interfaces hide it, is that the LLM has no memory at all. Each `messages.create` call is independent; the only reason a chatbot "remembers" what you said three turns ago is that the entire conversation is resent on every call. The model is a pure function of the messages you hand it right now. So "giving an agent memory" always means the same thing mechanically: deciding what past information to put into the next call's context, and where to keep it between calls. Every memory technique this week, buffers, summaries, vector recall, structured records, is an answer to that one question, what goes in the context this turn, and where did it live until now. Internalising that the memory is your system's, not the model's, is what makes the rest of the week make sense.

## Four kinds of memory, each for a different horizon
The librarian needs memory at different timescales, and there is a distinct technique for each:
- **Working memory (this session):** the live conversation, what we are talking about right now. Simple to hold, but it grows and eventually overflows the context window.
- **Long-term memory (across sessions):** months of past interactions you cannot afford to resend in full, so you store them and retrieve only the relevant ones, vector recall, the RAG skill pointed inward at your own history.
- **Episodic memory (events):** what happened in past sessions as discrete episodes ("on Tuesday we researched embeddings and concluded Matryoshka was worth it"), so the agent can reason about its own past.
- **Entity/structured memory:** facts about people, projects, sources, and conclusions kept as a structured record, so "the project we discussed last week" resolves to a real lookup.
The week walks these from simplest to most powerful, and the librarian ends up using all of them together.

## Where this fits
This week is the second pillar of the Agents phase: W13 gave an agent the loop, W14 gives it persistence, the ability to hold state across time, which is what the phase title promises. It leans hard on the RAG phase you just finished, long-term memory is retrieval over your own conversation history, so embeddings, vector stores, and relevance ranking all return, now applied to remembering instead of researching. Today, get oriented and stand up the simplest memory, working memory, then build outward across the week toward a librarian that genuinely remembers, because an agent that cannot remember is an agent you have to re-explain everything to, every single time.

items.title: Conversation buffer
items.body:
## The simplest memory: keep the whole conversation
Working memory is the conversation buffer, and it is exactly as simple as it sounds: keep a list of every turn (user message, agent reply, tool result) and pass the whole list to the model on each call. Because the model is stateless, this list is the only reason the agent "remembers" anything within a session, the buffer is the session. It is the right default and you should always start here: for a short conversation it is perfect, lossless, trivial to implement, the model sees everything. Most memory engineering is about what to do when this simple approach stops working, so you begin by understanding why and when it does.

## Why the buffer eventually breaks
The buffer has one hard limit: the context window. Every turn you append makes the next call longer, and a verbose agent, especially one whose tool results dump search pages or documents into the history, fills the window far faster than people expect. A research session can hit tens of thousands of tokens in a handful of turns. When the buffer approaches the window limit, three bad things happen at once: cost climbs (you pay for the whole history every single turn), latency climbs (more tokens to process), and eventually the conversation simply will not fit and the oldest turns must be dropped, which means the agent forgets the start of its own conversation. So the naive buffer does not fail loudly; it gets slow and expensive and then silently loses the beginning, the classic demo-works-then-degrades trap.

## Summarisation: trading detail for room
The standard fix that keeps a session going past the window is summarisation memory: periodically take the older turns and condense them into a compact summary, then keep that summary plus the recent turns verbatim. The agent loses fine detail from early in the conversation but retains the arc, what was discussed, what was decided, so it stays coherent across a long session at a fraction of the tokens. The engineering judgement is where to draw the line: keep the last few turns in full (recent context matters most and you want it exact), summarise everything older, and choose how aggressively to compress, summarise too hard and you lose a detail you needed; too little and you have not solved the size problem. This recency-plus-summary shape, exact recent memory, compressed older memory, is how nearly every long-running chat agent manages its working memory, and it directly attacks the context-management problem you met in W13.

## Where this fits
Build your librarian's working memory: a conversation buffer that holds the session, plus summarisation that condenses older turns once the buffer grows past a threshold, keeping recent turns verbatim. Watch the token count stay bounded across a long session instead of climbing without limit. You have solved memory within a session, but a librarian's whole value is remembering across sessions, and a summary that lives only in this session's RAM is gone the moment the session ends. Tomorrow you make memory survive the session by storing it and retrieving it, the RAG skill turned inward.

items.title: Vector-based long-term memory
items.body:
## Across sessions, you cannot just keep everything
Working memory dies when the session ends, and even within a session you cannot hold months of history in the context. Long-term memory solves both by storing past interactions outside the context and pulling back only what is relevant to the current moment. The mechanism is exactly RAG, now aimed at your own conversation history: embed each past turn (or each meaningful exchange) and store the vectors; when a new session starts or a new question comes in, embed the current topic, retrieve the most relevant prior turns, and inject just those into the context. This gives the librarian access to everything it has ever discussed without paying to resend all of it, you carry months of history but spend tokens only on the slice that matters right now.

## Storing and retrieving turns as embeddings
Concretely, every turn worth remembering gets embedded and written to a vector store with metadata (when it happened, what session, who said it), the same pipeline from W9-W10, except the documents are conversation turns instead of papers. At recall time you embed the current query or topic and do a similarity search to find the past turns most related to it. So when you ask the librarian about "vector database trade-offs," it retrieves the turns from three weeks ago where you compared pgvector and Qdrant and brings that context forward, even though that conversation is long out of any buffer. The entire RAG toolkit transfers: chunking long turns, hybrid search if keywords matter (a project name, an exact title), reranking the retrieved turns, even citations, the librarian can say "you concluded this on May 3rd" because it retrieved the turn that proves it.

## The hard part is retrieval quality, again
The challenge is the same one that made RAG hard, and it bites harder here: you want to retrieve the turns that are actually relevant, not merely the ones that are semantically adjacent. Memory recall is full of near-misses, every past mention of "the model" is semantically close, but only one was about the cost comparison you are asking about now, so naive top-k similarity drags in a lot of related-but-useless history. The fixes are the ones you already know: filter by metadata (this user, this project, this time range) before ranking, rerank with a cross-encoder to push the truly relevant turns up, and tune k so you bring back enough to be useful without flooding the context with adjacent noise. Poor memory retrieval produces an agent that confidently "remembers" the wrong thing, worse than one that remembers nothing, so the W9-W12 discipline of measuring and tuning retrieval is exactly what makes memory trustworthy rather than just present.

## Where this fits
Give your librarian long-term memory: embed and store the turns worth keeping, and at the start of each session retrieve the past interactions relevant to the current topic. Now it remembers across sessions, ask about a topic from last week and it recalls what it found, the core of what makes a librarian useful. But raw retrieved turns are low-level; a librarian also wants to remember events ("we researched X and concluded Y") as coherent episodes, not just scattered relevant sentences. That is tomorrow.

items.title: Episodic memory
items.body:
## Remembering events, not just sentences
Vector recall brings back relevant turns, but turns are fragments: a few retrieved sentences from a past conversation, stripped of their arc. Episodic memory remembers at a higher level, as discrete episodes, coherent events with a beginning, middle, and conclusion. Instead of (or alongside) raw turns, you store records like "On Tuesday, researched embedding models; compared OpenAI text-embedding-3 and open Matryoshka models; concluded Matryoshka was worth the setup for the cost saving." That is one episode: what was investigated, what was found, what was decided. The librarian that remembers episodes can answer "what did we conclude about embeddings?" with the conclusion, not with five semantically-similar sentences you have to reread, which is far closer to how a human research assistant actually remembers your past work.

## Building episodes: summarise a session into a record
Episodic memory is constructed, not just collected. At the end of a session (or a research thread), you use the model to summarise what happened into a structured episode, the topic, the key sources found, the conclusion reached, the date, and store that record. This is the structured-outputs skill from W6 doing memory work: you prompt the model to extract a clean episode object from the raw conversation. Those episode records become their own retrievable memory, smaller and higher-signal than raw turns, so recall can pull back "the embeddings episode" as a unit. It connects to the entity memory the week's intro describes: from these episodes you also maintain structured facts, projects, sources, conclusions, so "the project we discussed Tuesday" resolves to a real lookup of a real record rather than a fuzzy similarity guess.

## Why episodes make an agent feel like it understands you
The payoff of episodic memory is qualitative: it is the difference between an agent that has searchable transcripts and one that has a memory of your shared work. Because episodes are conclusions and not just content, the librarian can avoid repeating research ("we already concluded this, here is what we found") instead of dutifully re-searching a topic it technically has turns about but no sense of having finished. Because episodes are dated and structured, it can reason about your history ("you have looked at three vector databases now; here is how they compared"). This is why the intro calls entity and episodic memory expensive to build but extremely powerful: extracting clean episodes and maintaining accurate structured records takes real engineering and can go wrong (a bad summary stores a wrong conclusion as fact), but when it works, the agent stops feeling like a tool you re-brief each time and starts feeling like a collaborator who remembers, the whole point of a librarian.

## Where this fits
Add episodic memory: at the end of a research thread, summarise it into a structured episode (topic, sources, conclusion, date) and store it, and let the librarian retrieve and reason over those episodes, not just raw turns. Maintain a small structured record of the entities that recur, projects, topics, sources. Your librarian now remembers events and conclusions, the layer that makes it genuinely useful across time. But memory that only ever grows becomes its own problem, stale, bloated, contradictory, so tomorrow you learn to forget on purpose.

items.title: Memory pruning
items.body:
## Memory that only grows becomes a liability
Every memory system you have built this week accumulates: the buffer grows, the vector store fills with turns, episodes pile up. Left unmanaged, that is a problem, and not just a storage one. A memory full of stale, redundant, or contradictory entries degrades recall, retrieving from a huge pile of near-duplicate turns brings back noise, old conclusions you have since revised resurface as if current, and the signal you actually want gets buried. So a real memory system needs the counterpart to remembering: pruning, deciding what to forget. This feels backwards (we worked all week to remember more) but it is exactly how useful memory works, the value is not in keeping everything, it is in keeping the right things and letting the rest go.

## What to keep, what to drop
Pruning is a relevance-and-recency judgement, and the levers are concrete:
- **Deduplicate:** the same fact learned five times should be one memory, not five, collapse near-duplicate turns and episodes so recall is not dominated by repetition.
- **Decay by recency and use:** memories that are old and never retrieved are candidates to drop or archive; memories that keep getting recalled are clearly valuable, keep them sharp. This mirrors how human memory fades what you never revisit.
- **Resolve contradictions:** when a new conclusion supersedes an old one ("we now think Qdrant, not pgvector"), the memory should reflect the update, not store both as equally true, which means writing memory is sometimes editing, not just appending.
- **Tier by importance:** keep high-value structured episodes long-term; let low-value chatter expire fast.
The aim is a memory whose size and quality stay bounded, so retrieval keeps returning the genuinely relevant, not whatever has accumulated.

## Forgetting is an engineering decision with stakes
Pruning has real risk in both directions, and that is why it is a deliberate design choice, not an afterthought. Prune too aggressively and the librarian forgets something you needed, the conclusion from a month ago that was actually still relevant, the failure mode of a system that throws away too much. Prune too little and recall quality rots and costs climb. So you make forgetting a policy you can reason about and tune, and, exactly as with retrieval and stopping conditions, your evals are how you tune it honestly: does pruning policy A still let the librarian recall the things a test set says it should? Measuring recall over a fixed set of "things it must remember" turns pruning from a guess into a tradeoff you can see. The mature view is that memory and forgetting are two halves of one system, an agent's intelligence about its own past is as much about what it sensibly drops as what it keeps.

## Where this fits
Add a pruning policy to your librarian: deduplicate memories, decay old and unused ones, resolve superseded conclusions, and tier by importance, then check against a small "must-remember" set that you have not broken recall. Your memory system is now sustainable, it stays useful and bounded over months instead of bloating into noise. One layer remains before you ship: a librarian is one agent, but in a multi-agent system several agents may need to share what they know, which is its own problem.

items.title: Multi-agent shared memory
items.body:
## When several agents need to remember together
So far the memory belongs to one agent. But the manager-worker structure from W13, and the full multi-agent systems coming in W16, raise a new question: when several agents collaborate, how do they share what they learn? If a worker researches latency and another researches cost, the manager and the other workers benefit from seeing those findings, and you do not want each agent siloed with its own private memory, re-discovering what a sibling already found. Multi-agent shared memory is a common store that multiple agents read from and write to, a shared blackboard where findings, conclusions, and state are posted so the whole system can build on them rather than each agent starting blind.

## The shared store as coordination
A shared memory is not just storage, it is how agents coordinate without talking directly to each other. One agent writes "found: Haiku latency is ~Xms (source: ...)" to the shared store; others read it and adjust their work, the researcher does not re-search what is already posted, the synthesis agent pulls all findings from one place. This is the classic blackboard pattern: agents contribute to and consume from a common workspace, and the workspace, not a tangle of direct messages, carries the collective state. It makes the system's knowledge inspectable too, you can read the shared memory and see everything the system currently knows, which is invaluable for debugging a multi-agent run, the same way W13's trace let you see one agent's reasoning.

## The hard parts: consistency and trust
Shared mutable memory introduces problems single-agent memory does not have, the same ones distributed systems always face. Two agents writing at once can conflict; one agent can write something wrong that every other agent then trusts and builds on, propagating a single error through the whole system; and without structure the shared store becomes a dumping ground no agent can use well. So shared memory needs discipline: a clear schema for what gets written (structured findings, not raw dumps), provenance so a reader knows which agent claimed what and from which source (the citation habit again), and a way to handle conflicting or superseding entries (the contradiction-resolution from D5, now across agents). The judgement is the same scaling caution as W13's hierarchy: shared memory is powerful when the agents genuinely need to build on each other's work, and pure overhead when they do not, so you add it where collaboration is real, not reflexively.

## Where this fits
Give a small multi-agent version of your librarian a shared memory: a common store where worker agents post structured, sourced findings and the others read them to avoid duplicate work and to synthesise, with provenance and conflict handling. You have learned how memory scales from one agent to many, the bridge into W16's multi-agent systems, where shared state is what lets a network of agents act as one coherent system instead of a crowd working past each other. Tomorrow you assemble the full librarian and ship it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A personal research librarian that remembers across turns, across sessions, and across topics, the agent that does not make you re-explain yourself. By tonight it has:
- working memory (a conversation buffer with summarisation) so a long session stays coherent and bounded.
- long-term memory (vector recall over past turns) so it remembers across sessions, with the retrieval quality tuned, not naive.
- episodic and structured memory so it recalls events and conclusions ("we concluded X about Y on this date"), not just fragments.
- a pruning policy so memory stays sharp and bounded over time instead of bloating.
- optionally, shared memory across a small set of collaborating agents.

## The test that proves it
The proof is a multi-session demonstration that the agent genuinely remembers. Research a topic with it today, latency benchmarks, say, and let it reach a conclusion. Start a fresh session tomorrow (or just a new session now) and ask a related question. The librarian should recall what it already found, reference the prior conclusion, and decline to re-research what it already knows, "we looked at this; here is what we found, do you want me to go deeper?", instead of starting from scratch as last week's amnesiac agent would. That single behaviour, continuity across a session boundary, with the right past brought back and the redundant work avoided, is the entire deliverable, because it is precisely the thing that separates a demo agent from one you would actually rely on day to day.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the librarian with its memory layers, a README explaining the four kinds of memory and which problem each solves, and, as the headline evidence, a transcript across two sessions showing it remember, recall the earlier conclusion, skip the redundant research, build on what it knew. That cross-session transcript is what makes this a standout portfolio piece: most agent demos are single-shot and forget everything the moment they end, so an agent that visibly carries knowledge from one session into the next demonstrates the engineering that turns a toy into a tool. If you tracked memory size and recall quality over the sessions (it stayed bounded; it recalled what a must-remember set required), include those numbers, they show you engineered the memory rather than just bolting on a store.

## Where this fits in the track
Your agent now has the two properties that make agents genuinely useful: a loop that lets it act (W13) and memory that lets it persist (W14). Together those are most of what "an agent" means in practice. Next, W15 standardises the tools your agents use, right now the librarian's tools are functions wired into its own codebase; MCP turns them into a server any agent can connect to, which is how tools are starting to be shared across the whole ecosystem. Then W16 composes multiple agents into a system, where this week's shared memory becomes the backbone. weeks.title: MCP and Tool Servers, The Protocol That's Standardising Agent Tools
weeks.context:
Every agent you build has tools. Right now those tools are Python functions in the same codebase as the agent. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the emerging standard for decoupling tool implementations from agent clients. Instead of writing tool code inside your agent, you run a separate MCP server process that exposes tools, and your agent client connects to it. This week you build your own MCP server with 8-10 tools over your personal data.

The protocol itself is JSON-RPC over either stdio (subprocess communication) or HTTP with Server-Sent Events. The client sends a tools/list request to discover what tools are available. When the agent calls a tool, the client sends a tools/call request with the tool name and arguments. The server executes the tool and returns the result. The protocol is simple. The value is in standardisation: any MCP-compatible client (Claude Code, Cursor, custom Python agent) can connect to any MCP server without modification.

Server primitives are three things: tools (callable functions with inputs and outputs), resources (readable data like files, database tables, or API endpoints), and prompts (parameterised prompt templates that the server exposes). Most practical MCP servers focus on tools, but resources and prompts become important when you want to expose structured data or reusable instructions.

Building your own MCP server forces you to design a clean tool interface. The tool schema, name, description, input schema, is what the client model reads to decide how to use the tool. A tool that is useful when called from the command line but hard to call correctly via MCP usually has a schema design problem: too many required parameters, parameters that depend on implicit context, or a description that does not tell the model when to use it.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Every agent you have built carries its tools inside its own codebase, Python functions sitting next to the agent loop. This week you cut that cord. You build your own MCP server: a separate process that exposes 8-10 tools over your personal data (your notes, files, a database, a calendar, whatever you actually use), and you connect agents to it over a standard protocol. The payoff is reuse and standardisation: once your tools live in an MCP server, any MCP-compatible client, Claude Code, Cursor, your own Python agent from W13, can use them without you rewriting anything. You are moving from "tools are part of this one agent" to "tools are a service that any agent can call," which is the shift the whole ecosystem is making right now.

## What MCP actually is, in one breath
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way for an AI client to discover and call tools that live in a separate server. Mechanically it is unglamorous and that is the point: the client asks the server "what tools do you have?" (a `tools/list` request), the server replies with each tool's name, description, and input schema, and when the model decides to use one, the client sends a `tools/call` with the name and arguments, the server runs it and returns the result. That is the same tool-use loop from W13, the model proposes a call, something executes it, the result comes back, except the "something" is now a separate process speaking a shared protocol instead of a function in your file. MCP did not invent tool use; it standardised where tools live and how clients reach them, so they stop being locked inside one app.

## Why decoupling tools from agents matters
The reason this is worth a week is the same reason APIs and standard protocols always win: decoupling. When tools are hard-coded into an agent, every agent that needs them re-implements them, and every tool is trapped in the app it was born in. When tools live behind MCP, one server exposes them once and every compatible client uses them, your file-search tool works in Claude Code and in Cursor and in your custom agent, written once. It is the same leap as going from copy-pasting database code into every app to running a database server everything connects to. This is also why building a server, not just consuming one, is the assignment: standing up your own forces you to design clean tool interfaces (the hard part, covered on D5), and that design skill is what makes tools genuinely reusable rather than technically shared.

## Where this fits
This is the third pillar of the Agents phase. W13 gave an agent a loop, W14 gave it memory, and W15 standardises its tools so they are not welded to one codebase. It sets up W16 directly: when you compose multiple agents into a system, shared MCP tool servers are how they all reach the same capabilities cleanly. And it reaches past the track, MCP is how Claude Code and other real agent products expose tools today, so building a server is building the actual interface modern AI tooling runs on. Today, get oriented and stand up the skeleton server; the week fills in the protocol, transport, auth, and, most importantly, the tool design that makes it good.
