items.title: What MCP is
items.body:
## The client-server split, and why it is the whole idea
MCP separates two roles that were previously fused. The MCP server owns the tools, the code that searches your files, queries your database, reads your calendar, and exposes them. The MCP client lives inside the AI application (Claude Code, Cursor, your agent) and connects to servers to use their tools. The model never talks to your tool code directly; it talks to its client, which talks to your server over the protocol. This split is exactly what makes tools portable: because the client and server agree on a standard contract, any client can talk to any server. Write a server once and every MCP client in the world can use it; that universality is the entire value proposition, and it only works because both sides speak the same protocol instead of bespoke glue.

## The three server primitives
An MCP server can expose three kinds of things, and knowing all three (even though most servers lean on the first) helps you design well:
- **Tools:** callable functions with inputs and outputs, the model invokes these to *do* something, search, write, query. This is the workhorse and where most servers focus.
- **Resources:** readable data the client can pull in as context, files, database rows, an API endpoint's output. Where tools are actions, resources are content the model can read.
- **Prompts:** parameterised prompt templates the server exposes, reusable instructions a client can fetch and fill in, so good prompting can be shipped alongside the tools it is meant to drive.
Most practical servers are mostly tools, but resources shine when you want to expose structured data for the model to read, and prompts when you want to ship reusable instructions, recognising which primitive a capability is keeps your server clean.

## Discovery is what makes it dynamic
The feature that makes MCP feel different from hard-coded tools is discovery. A client does not need to be told in advance what a server offers; it sends `tools/list` and the server describes its tools at runtime, names, descriptions, input schemas. The model then reads those descriptions to decide which tool fits the task. This is why the tool's schema and description are not paperwork but the actual interface: they are what the model reads, at connection time, to understand what it can do. Add a tool to your server and every connected client can use it immediately, no client change required, because discovery is dynamic. That runtime, self-describing quality is what lets the tool ecosystem grow without every client and server being updated in lockstep, and it is why D5's lesson on writing schemas the model can understand is the heart of the week.

## Where this fits
Get the conceptual model solid today and expose your first couple of tools so a client can `tools/list` and see them: the client-server split, the three primitives, and discovery as the mechanism that makes tools portable and dynamic. You now understand *what* MCP is; tomorrow you handle *how* the client and server actually talk, the transport, which is what determines whether your server runs as a local subprocess or a networked service.

items.title: Transport
items.body:
## How the bytes actually move
A protocol needs a transport, the channel the client and server use to exchange messages. MCP messages are JSON-RPC (a simple, standard request/response format: a method like `tools/call`, some params, and a matching response), and that JSON-RPC rides over one of two transports. The choice of transport is the first real architectural decision you make when you ship a server, because it determines where the server can run and who can reach it, so it is worth understanding both rather than copying whichever the tutorial used.

## The two transports, and when each fits
- **stdio (standard input/output):** the client launches your server as a child process and they talk over its stdin/stdout pipes. This is local and simple, no network, no ports, no auth needed because nothing is exposed, the server runs on the same machine as the client, as a subprocess. It is the right default for personal and local tools (a server over your own files, exactly this week's project): trivial to run, nothing to secure, nothing listening on a port.
- **HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE):** the server runs as a networked service the client reaches over HTTP, with SSE carrying the server-to-client stream. This is what you use when the server must be remote, shared by multiple users, or hosted separately from the client, a team tool server, a hosted service. It is more powerful and more work: now there is a network endpoint, which means you must think about who can reach it and whether they are allowed to.
The rule of thumb: stdio for local and personal, HTTP/SSE for remote and shared.

## The transport choice decides your security surface
The reason transport is not just plumbing is that it sets your entire security posture, and that hands you straight into tomorrow's lesson. A stdio server has essentially no network attack surface: it is a subprocess of a client already running on your machine, so there is nothing listening for a stranger to connect to. The moment you switch to HTTP/SSE, you have published an endpoint, and an endpoint that exposes tools over your data, search my files, read my database, is something you must now authenticate and authorise, or you have built an open door to your own systems. So the transport decision is really a decision about exposure: local-only and unexposed, or networked and therefore something you have to defend. Start your personal server on stdio precisely because it lets you learn the protocol without yet owning a security problem, then graduate to HTTP/SSE deliberately, knowing it brings auth with it.

## Where this fits
Run your server over stdio today, the client spawns it as a subprocess and they exchange JSON-RPC over the pipes, and understand exactly what would change if you moved it to HTTP/SSE for remote use. You can now actually connect a client to your server and call a tool end to end. And you have seen why the next lesson is non-optional: the instant a tool server is reachable over a network, who is allowed to call it becomes a question you must answer, which is authentication and authorisation in MCP.

items.title: Authentication and authorisation in MCP
items.body:
## A tool server is a powerful thing to leave unguarded
Your MCP server exposes tools that act over real data, read files, query a database, maybe write or send. On stdio that is fine, the only caller is a client you launched yourself. But the moment the server is reachable over a network (HTTP/SSE), those same tools are reachable by whoever can hit the endpoint, and "search my files" or "query my database" in the hands of an unauthorised caller is a breach, not a feature. So a networked tool server has to answer two questions on every call: authentication (who is making this request?) and authorisation (is this caller allowed to use this particular tool, on this particular data?). Skipping them does not make the server simpler; it makes it an open API over your private systems.

## Authentication versus authorisation, kept distinct
The two words get blurred and they are different jobs:
- **Authentication** establishes identity, who is calling. For a networked MCP server this typically means the client presents a credential (an OAuth token, an API key) that the server verifies before doing anything. No valid credential, no service.
- **Authorisation** establishes permission, what this authenticated caller may do. Identity alone is not enough: a known user might be allowed to call the read-only search tool but not the delete tool, or allowed to read their own data but not someone else's. Authorisation is the per-tool, per-resource check that runs after identity is established.
Keeping them separate matters because they fail differently and you need both: authentication without authorisation lets any logged-in caller do everything; authorisation without authentication has no trustworthy identity to base permissions on.

## Least privilege is the design principle
The discipline that ties this together is least privilege: every caller, and every tool, should have the minimum access needed and no more. Concretely, that means scoping credentials (a token that can search but not delete), gating dangerous tools behind stricter checks than read-only ones, and never exposing a tool more broadly than its job requires, your server's most destructive tool should be the hardest to reach. This is the same principle that governs good API and systems security generally, now applied to AI tooling, and it matters more here because the caller is partly an autonomous model: an agent can be talked into misusing a tool (a prompt injection that says "delete everything"), so the server, not the model's good judgement, must be the thing that enforces what is allowed. You design the server assuming the caller might try the worst tool for the wrong reason, and authorisation is what stops it.

## Where this fits
Add authentication and authorisation to your server's design, identity on every networked call, per-tool permission checks, least privilege throughout, even if you run it locally on stdio for now, so you know exactly what hardening a remote deployment requires. You have made the server safe to expose, which is the difference between a tool you can only run privately and one you could host for a team. With transport and security handled, the remaining question is the one that most determines whether your server is actually good to use: how to design the tools themselves so a model can call them correctly.

items.title: Designing tools for MCP
items.body:
## The schema is the interface the model reads
Here is the lesson that separates an MCP server that works from one that is genuinely usable: the tool's schema, its name, its description, its input schema, is the entire interface the model uses to decide whether and how to call it. The model cannot see your implementation, your comments, or your intent; it sees only what `tools/list` returns. So a tool that a human can run fine from the command line but that the model keeps calling wrong almost always has a schema problem, not a logic problem. Designing tools for MCP is therefore an exercise in writing for a model reader: every tool is only as good as the description and schema the model gets to read about it.

## What makes a tool hard for a model to call
The intro names the three usual failures, and each is a concrete design fix:
- **Too many required parameters:** a tool demanding seven inputs is one the model will routinely call with the wrong combination. Cut required params to the genuine minimum; give the rest sensible defaults.
- **Parameters that depend on implicit context:** an argument like `folder_id` that the model has no way to know is unusable, the model cannot supply a value it was never given. Tools should take inputs the model can actually produce from the conversation, not internal handles only your code knows.
- **A description that does not say *when* to use the tool:** the model picks tools by reading descriptions, so "searches files" is weaker than "search the user's personal notes by keyword; use when the user asks about something they may have written down." The description must teach the model the tool's job and its trigger, not just name its function.
Each fix is the same move: design the tool so a model with only the schema in front of it can call it correctly on the first try.

## Design for the model, not the CLI
The deeper shift is designing tools for an autonomous caller rather than a human one. A human calling a CLI can read docs, remember context, and retry after an error; a model calling over MCP has one shot per turn with only the schema as guidance. So good MCP tools are self-contained and self-explaining: clear single-purpose actions, minimal and meaningful inputs, names and descriptions that disambiguate from sibling tools (if two tools sound the same, the model coin-flips between them), and outputs that are concise and structured so they do not blow up the next agent's context, the same conciseness discipline from W13's context management, now applied to tool outputs. This is genuinely a design skill, and building your own server is what teaches it: you feel immediately when a tool is badly shaped because the model misuses it, and tightening the schema until the model calls it right is the core work of the week.

## Where this fits
Design (or redesign) your 8-10 tools for the model: minimal required parameters, no reliance on context the model cannot see, descriptions that say *when* to use each, distinct names, and concise structured outputs, then watch the model call them correctly. This is the most transferable skill in the week, because it is exactly how you design any tool an agent will use, MCP or not. One lesson remains before you ship: understanding how MCP relates to the other ways of giving models tools, so you know when to reach for it.

items.title: MCP vs OpenAI Apps SDK vs raw function-calling
items.body:
## Three ways to give a model tools
MCP is not the only way to connect tools to models, and a clear-eyed engineer knows where it sits among the alternatives:
- **Raw function-calling:** tools are functions defined directly in your agent's code, the W13 approach. The model emits a tool call, your code runs the matching function. Maximally simple and fully under your control, with zero protocol overhead, but the tools are trapped in that one codebase and reusable by nothing else.
- **MCP:** tools live in a separate server behind a standard protocol, so any compatible client can use them. You trade the simplicity of in-process functions for portability and reuse across clients.
- **OpenAI Apps SDK (and similar app/plugin frameworks):** a platform-specific way to expose tools and app experiences inside one vendor's ecosystem, deep integration with that platform, at the cost of being tied to it.
These are not ranked best-to-worst; they are points on a trade-off between simplicity, portability, and platform integration.

## The trade-off that decides which to use
The choice comes down to where the tool needs to be usable and how much you value control versus reach:
- Reach for **raw function-calling** when tools are specific to one agent and used nowhere else, no point paying protocol overhead for a tool only this agent will ever call, and in-process is simplest and fastest.
- Reach for **MCP** when tools should be reusable across multiple clients or shared, the file/data tools you want in Claude Code *and* Cursor *and* your own agent, or tools a team will share. Portability is the whole reason it exists, so use it when portability is what you need.
- Reach for a **platform app framework** when you specifically want your tools or app to live inside that platform's product surface and you accept the lock-in for the integration.
The mistake is dogma in either direction: wrapping a one-off helper in a full MCP server is over-engineering, and hard-coding tools you will obviously want to reuse everywhere is a choice you will pay for later. Match the mechanism to whether the tool needs to travel.

## Why standardisation tends to win for shared tools
There is a reason MCP is gaining ground despite being more work than raw functions: standards win wherever sharing matters. The same forces that made HTTP, SQL, and the language server protocol dominate, write once, interoperate everywhere, apply to agent tools, and a single open protocol that any client can speak beats a world where every app has its own bespoke tool format and nothing is portable. So the trajectory is that one-off, agent-specific tools stay as raw functions (and rightly so), while tools meant to be shared, across clients, across teams, across the ecosystem, converge on MCP. Knowing this lets you make the call deliberately: not "MCP for everything" and not "functions for everything," but the recognition that the value of a standard is exactly proportional to how much the thing needs to be shared, which is the judgement a senior engineer brings to the choice.

## Where this fits
Place MCP among the alternatives, raw function-calling for one-off in-codebase tools, MCP for tools that must be portable and shared, platform SDKs for deep single-platform integration, and you can now choose deliberately instead of by habit. This judgement is the capstone of the week's understanding: you have built a server and you also know when building one is the right call versus over-engineering. Tomorrow you ship the server itself.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A working MCP server exposing 8-10 well-designed tools over your personal data, that any MCP client can connect to and use. By tonight it:
- exposes a real, useful tool set over data you actually care about (notes, files, a database, a calendar), discoverable via `tools/list`.
- runs over a transport you chose deliberately (stdio for local/personal, with a clear understanding of what HTTP/SSE would add for remote use).
- is designed safely, identity and per-tool authorisation thought through, least privilege applied, even if run locally for now.
- has tools whose schemas a model can read and call correctly: minimal required params, no hidden-context inputs, descriptions that say when to use each, concise structured outputs.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is your server working from a client you did not write. Connect Claude Code (or another MCP-compatible client) to your server, not just your own agent, and watch it discover your tools via `tools/list` and call them correctly to do real work over your data: "find my notes about X," "what's on my calendar Thursday," answered by the model driving *your* tools. That cross-client moment is the entire payoff of the week and the whole point of the protocol: a tool you built is now usable by a client built by someone else, with no glue code, because you both speak MCP. If the model calls your tools correctly on the first try, your D5 schema design worked; if it fumbles, you have a precise, visible thing to fix.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the server with its tools, a README listing each tool (name, what it does, when to use it) and how to connect a client, and ideally a short recording or transcript of an external client (Claude Code) using your tools live. This is an unusually strong portfolio piece because MCP is exactly the interface real AI tooling is being built on right now: showing that you designed a clean tool server that a standard client can drive demonstrates you understand how modern agents actually get their capabilities, not just how to call an API. The schema-design discipline on display, tools a model calls correctly, is the part experienced reviewers will notice, because it is the part most people get wrong.

## Where this fits in the track
Your agents now have a loop (W13), memory (W14), and a standard, portable way to reach tools (W15). That tool-server skill feeds straight into next week: when you compose multiple agents into a system (W16), MCP servers are how they share capabilities cleanly instead of each re-implementing tools. It also lands you on the actual frontier of AI engineering, the protocol that Claude Code and other production agent tools use today, so you are no longer learning a toy version of how agents get tools; you have built the real thing. Next week is the last pillar of the phase: making many agents work together as one system.

weeks.title: Multi-Agent Systems, When One Agent Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
One agent can do a lot. A network of specialised agents, each focused on a narrow domain, can do more, and do it more reliably. Multi-agent systems exist because generalisation has limits: a single agent that is both researcher, security auditor, and style editor will be mediocre at each. Three separate agents with tight briefs will collectively outperform the generalist.

This week you build a code review agent system. Three agents work on the same submitted code: a Security agent that looks for vulnerabilities, a Quality agent that flags code smells and style issues, and a Synthesis agent that merges the findings into a coherent review. You choose the orchestration pattern and implement it.

Manager-worker is the most common pattern. A coordinator agent receives the task, decomposes it into subtasks, dispatches each to a specialist worker, collects the results, and synthesises a final output. The coordinator does not do the domain work, it manages the process. This pattern maps well to problems that can be cleanly decomposed and where the subtasks are independent.

Sequential pipeline is different: Agent A's output is the direct input to Agent B. The review does not start synthesis until security review is complete. This is appropriate when the tasks are ordered, synthesis logically requires the individual reviews to be finished. But it is slower than parallel execution and a failure at step N breaks the chain.

The shared state pattern is worth knowing even if you do not use it here: agents communicate by reading and writing to a shared data store (a database or message queue). Agents do not call each other directly. This creates looser coupling but requires careful coordination around concurrent writes.

Context window management is the main engineering challenge. The Synthesis agent must receive the outputs of the Security and Quality agents. If those outputs are long, the Synthesis agent's context fills quickly. Design each agent to produce concise, structured output that downstream agents can consume efficiently.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
This week you stop building one agent and start building a team. You build a code review agent system: three specialised agents work on the same submitted code, a Security agent hunting for vulnerabilities, a Quality agent flagging code smells and style problems, and a Synthesis agent that merges their findings into one coherent review. You choose how they are wired together and implement that orchestration. The shift from a single agent to a coordinated set of them is the last and most architectural pillar of the Agents phase: you are no longer just running a loop, you are designing how multiple loops divide work, communicate, and combine into a single trustworthy output.

## Why more than one agent at all
The instinct, after four weeks of making one agent capable, is to keep piling responsibilities onto it. Multi-agent systems exist because that instinct hits a wall: generalisation has limits. A single agent told to be security auditor, style critic, and editor all at once does each job worse than a specialist would, its attention and its prompt are split three ways, and the quality of each review suffers. Three agents with tight, narrow briefs, "you only look for security vulnerabilities," "you only flag code quality," each do their one job well, and collectively they outperform the overloaded generalist. This is the same reason organisations have specialists instead of one person doing everything: focus beats breadth on hard, distinct tasks, and a tight brief produces better work than a sprawling one.

## The two hard problems: orchestration and context
Composing agents introduces two engineering problems that a single agent never had, and the week is mostly about them:
- **Orchestration:** how are the agents wired? Does a manager dispatch them, do they run in sequence, do they communicate through shared state? Different patterns suit different problems, and choosing the wrong one makes a system slow, fragile, or incoherent. The middle of the week is a tour of the patterns so you can choose deliberately.
- **Context window management:** the Synthesis agent must read the Security and Quality agents' outputs, and if those are long, its context fills fast, the same context problem from W13, now multiplied across agents. The fix is designing every agent to emit concise, structured output that downstream agents can consume cheaply.
Get orchestration and inter-agent context right and a multi-agent system is powerful; get them wrong and it is just several agents being expensive and confusing together.

## Where this fits
This closes the Agents phase. W13 built the loop, W14 added memory, W15 standardised tools, and W16 composes agents into systems, the manager-worker idea you first met in W13's hierarchy, now grown into a full discipline with multiple patterns and real coordination. It also leans on everything before it: each agent is a W13-style loop, they may share W14-style memory, and they reach tools through W15-style servers. And, crucially, the week ends on judgement, when *not* to reach for multi-agent at all, because the most common mistake in this area is using three agents where one would have been simpler and better. Today, orient and sketch your three agents; the week teaches you how to wire them and when you should.

items.title: Manager-worker
items.body:
## The most common pattern: a manager and its workers
Manager-worker is where most multi-agent systems start, and for good reason. A coordinator (manager) agent receives the whole task, decomposes it into subtasks, dispatches each to a specialist worker, collects their results, and synthesises the final output. The crucial detail is that the manager does not do the domain work, it manages the process. For your code review, a manager receives the code, hands it to the Security worker and the Quality worker, and routes their findings to Synthesis. The manager's job is coordination: deciding who does what, gathering what comes back, and producing the combined result, while each worker stays focused on its one specialty.

## Why this maps cleanly to decomposable work
Manager-worker fits a specific shape of problem: tasks that decompose cleanly into independent subtasks. Security review and quality review are a textbook fit, they examine the same code but do not depend on each other, so they can run in parallel, and that independence is exactly what the pattern exploits. Because the subtasks do not need each other's results, the manager can dispatch them concurrently and gather the outputs as they finish, which is faster than doing them one after another. The pattern's strength is precisely this clean separation: a coordinator on top, independent specialists underneath, results flowing back up to be combined. When your problem genuinely splits into parallel, independent pieces, manager-worker is usually the right and simplest answer, which is why it is the default you reach for first.

## Where the manager earns its keep, and its cost
The manager is not free overhead, it does real work: decomposition (splitting the task sensibly), dispatch (getting each piece to the right worker), and synthesis-coordination (deciding the final shape). Done well, that coordination is what turns three independent reviews into one coherent output instead of three disconnected reports. The cost to watch is the same context problem from D1: the manager (and the synthesis step) must take in every worker's output, so if workers are verbose the manager's context balloons, which is why you design workers to return concise structured findings, not essays. The other risk is a manager that over-decomposes, spawning a worker for every trivial step, multiplying model calls for no gain, the same caution from W13's hierarchy. Used where the task has real, separable parts and workers report back tightly, manager-worker is the workhorse of multi-agent design; used to split work that did not need splitting, it is just expense.

## Where this fits
Implement your code review system as manager-worker: a coordinator that dispatches the Security and Quality agents (in parallel, since they are independent) and routes their concise findings to a Synthesis step. You have built the most common and most broadly useful multi-agent pattern, and felt both its strength (clean parallel decomposition) and its costs (coordination overhead, context pressure at the manager). Tomorrow you look at a looser pattern where agents coordinate without a manager at all.

items.title: Peer-to-peer / swarm
items.body:
## Coordination without a boss
Manager-worker has a coordinator at the top. Peer-to-peer (or swarm) patterns drop the boss: agents coordinate among themselves, communicating directly or through a shared space rather than reporting up to a single manager. No one agent owns the process; the behaviour emerges from agents reacting to each other and to a common state. In a swarm-style review, the agents might post findings to a shared workspace and pick up each other's observations, the Security agent's note about an unsanitised input prompting the Quality agent to look harder at that function, without a manager routing the traffic. The defining trait is decentralisation: control is distributed across the peers instead of concentrated in a coordinator.

## What you gain and what you pay
The appeal of peer-to-peer is looser coupling and flexibility. Without a central manager as the single point that everything routes through, the system has no single bottleneck and no single point of failure in the coordination layer, and agents can interact more fluidly, reacting to each other in ways a rigid manager-dispatch flow would not allow. The cost is exactly the flip side of that freedom: coordination becomes harder to reason about and to control. With no manager guaranteeing that every subtask is covered and results are combined, you can get gaps (no agent took responsibility for a part), duplication (two agents did the same thing), or chaos (agents reacting to each other in loops). Decentralised systems are powerful but emergent, their behaviour is harder to predict, debug, and bound, which is the recurring trade of every peer-to-peer architecture, from microservices to actual swarms in nature.

## Choosing centralised versus decentralised
The judgement between manager-worker and peer-to-peer is the classic centralised-versus-decentralised call, and it turns on how much control and predictability you need versus how much flexibility. Centralised (manager-worker) when you need a guarantee that the work gets decomposed, covered, and combined in a controlled way, most production systems, including a code review you want to be reliable and complete, want this. Decentralised (peer-to-peer/swarm) when the problem benefits from fluid, emergent collaboration and you can tolerate less predictability, more exploratory or open-ended tasks. For your code review, the centralised manager-worker is the sounder default precisely because you want a dependable, complete review, not an emergent one; understanding peer-to-peer matters so you recognise the cases where its flexibility is worth its unpredictability, and so you understand the systems you will encounter that are built that way. As a rule, prefer the centralised pattern unless you have a specific reason to want emergence, because predictability is usually worth more than flexibility in a system you have to trust.

## Where this fits
Understand peer-to-peer/swarm as the decentralised alternative to manager-worker, looser coupling and emergent flexibility, bought with harder coordination and less predictability, and see why a controlled task like code review usually wants the centralised pattern. You now hold both ends of the orchestration spectrum. Next you add a pattern that is less about who is in charge and more about quality: one agent whose entire job is to critique another's work.

items.title: Critic / reviewer
items.body:
## An agent whose job is to check the work
The critic (or reviewer) pattern adds an agent whose sole purpose is to evaluate another agent's output and push it to improve. One agent produces, a draft answer, a proposed fix, a first-pass review, and a second agent critiques it: "this misses the SQL injection in the query builder," "this style complaint is wrong, that is the project's convention." The critique feeds back into a revised output. This is the reflection idea from W13 promoted into its own agent: instead of one agent critiquing itself, a separate critic with a different brief (and often a sharper, more adversarial prompt) reviews the work. Separation helps, an agent grading its own output is prone to rubber-stamping it, whereas a dedicated critic briefed to find faults is more likely to actually find them.

## Why a separate critic raises quality
The reason this pattern earns its extra cost is that producing and critiquing are different cognitive jobs, and splitting them does each better. A producer agent is trying to generate something good; a critic agent is trying to find what is wrong, and a prompt optimised for fault-finding ("assume this review missed something, what is it?") surfaces problems that the producer, invested in its own output, glosses over. Run a draft through a critic and a revision pass and the output is consistently better, the critic catches the missed vulnerability, the weak reasoning, the overconfident claim, and the producer fixes it. This is also a natural home for your W12 eval thinking: a critic is, in effect, an LLM-as-judge wired into the workflow, evaluating output and driving a fix, the same faithfulness/correctness checks now acting as a gate rather than a report. In your code review system, a critic could review the Synthesis agent's final review for missed issues or false positives before it ships.

## The cost, and where critique is worth it
A critic doubles down on the produce-then-improve trade: every critique-and-revise cycle is more model calls, more tokens, and more latency, so you apply it where output quality matters enough to pay for it, the same tiered judgement from self-consistency and evals. High-stakes outputs (a security review someone will act on, a customer-facing answer) justify a critic; low-stakes ones do not. You also bound the cycles, a critic and producer can ping-pong indefinitely, each finding new nits, so you cap the rounds (often one or two critique passes capture most of the gain) exactly like the stopping conditions from W13. And you watch for the critic being wrong, it is a fallible model too, so a critic that invents problems can make output worse; validating the critic (does its critique actually improve results on your eval set?) is what keeps it an asset. Used deliberately, the critic pattern is one of the highest-leverage quality moves in agent design.

## Where this fits
Add a critic to your system: an agent that reviews the Synthesis agent's combined review for missed issues or false positives and drives one bounded revision pass, raising quality where it counts. You have learned the pattern that most reliably improves multi-agent output, the engineered, separated version of reflection, and connected it to your eval discipline. Next, a pattern for systems that handle varied inputs: deciding *which* agent should even handle a given task.

items.title: Routing
items.body:
## Sending each task to the right specialist
Routing is the pattern for systems that face varied inputs: a router agent (or classifier) inspects an incoming task and decides which specialist agent or path should handle it. A support system routes a billing question to the billing agent and a technical question to the technical agent; a code review system might route a Python file to a Python-specialist reviewer and a SQL migration to a database specialist. The router does not do the work, it does triage, classifying the input and dispatching it to the agent best suited to it. Where manager-worker decomposes one task across workers, routing chooses among workers for a task that only one of them should handle, it is about direction, not decomposition.

## Why routing beats one do-everything agent
Routing exists for the same specialisation reason as the whole week, applied to dispatch. A single agent that tries to handle every kind of input well is, again, a mediocre generalist; routing lets you keep a roster of sharp specialists and simply send each input to the right one, so every task is handled by an agent actually good at it. It also scales gracefully: adding a new capability means adding a specialist and teaching the router about it, rather than cramming more responsibility into one overloaded agent and its prompt. And it controls cost, the router can send a simple input to a cheap small-model agent and reserve the expensive, capable agent for the hard cases, the model-tiering idea from W7 expressed as architecture. Routing is how a system stays both specialised and broad: many narrow experts, plus a dispatcher that picks the right one.

## Getting routing right
The make-or-break of a routing system is the router's accuracy, because a misroute sends the task to the wrong specialist and the whole thing produces a bad answer confidently. So the router's classification has to be reliable, and the engineering is familiar: a clear, well-prompted classification step (often structured output, the input's category as a typed field, W6 again), sensible categories that actually map to your specialists, and a default or fallback path for inputs that fit no category cleanly rather than a wrong forced choice. You also handle ambiguity, an input that could go two ways might need both specialists (back to manager-worker) or a clarification step. And routing is exactly the kind of decision you should measure: a small eval set of inputs with known-correct destinations tells you the router's accuracy and catches the categories it confuses, the W12 discipline keeping the dispatcher honest. A well-built router is mostly invisible when it works and the source of baffling failures when it does not, which is why its accuracy is worth the same rigour as any other quality-critical step.

## Where this fits
Add routing where your system benefits from it, directing different kinds of submissions to the specialist best suited to each, with a reliable classification step, a sensible fallback, and measured accuracy. You now have the major orchestration patterns in hand, manager-worker, peer-to-peer, critic, and routing, and can compose them (a router feeding a manager-worker, a critic on the output) to fit real problems. With the patterns covered, the most important remaining lesson is the one that keeps you from misusing them: knowing when a multi-agent system is the wrong choice.

days.title: When NOT to use multi-agent

items.title: When NOT to use multi-agent
items.body:
## The pattern's biggest risk is using it when you should not
After a week of multi-agent patterns, the most valuable thing to learn is restraint: most problems do not need multiple agents, and reaching for a multi-agent system when a single agent would do is one of the most common and costly mistakes in the field. Multiple agents are not inherently better, they are more, more model calls, more latency, more cost, more orchestration code, more ways to fail, more context spent shuttling information between agents. Every one of those costs is real and paid up front, so a multi-agent system has to earn them by solving a problem a single agent genuinely could not. Often it does not, and you have built an elaborate, slow, expensive version of something one well-prompted agent handled fine, the classic over-engineering trap, dressed up as sophistication.

## When one agent is the right answer
The honest default is a single agent, and you should reach for multi-agent only when specific conditions hold. Stay single-agent when:
- the task does not cleanly decompose into independent parts, if you cannot draw clean seams, splitting just adds coordination cost without the parallelism payoff.
- a single agent already does the job well, the generalisation limit only bites when one agent is genuinely overloaded; if it is handling the task fine, more agents add nothing but expense.
- latency or cost is tight, multi-agent multiplies both, so a budget- or speed-constrained job often cannot afford it.
- the coordination overhead would exceed the benefit, if wiring the agents together costs more effort and tokens than the specialisation saves, the math is against you.
The signal that multi-agent *is* warranted is the inverse: genuinely separable subtasks, real specialisation gains (distinct domains a generalist does poorly), and a task big or varied enough that one agent's context or focus cannot hold it, exactly the code-review case, distinct domains, parallelisable, worth combining.

## Engineering judgement is choosing the simplest thing that works
The deeper lesson is the one that runs through all of senior engineering: prefer the simplest architecture that solves the problem, and add complexity only when the problem forces it. Multi-agent systems are a powerful tool, and the mark of skill is not using powerful tools at every opportunity but knowing precisely when the problem demands one. A single well-designed agent with good tools and memory handles a remarkable range of tasks; the engineer who reaches for a three-agent system by default will ship things that are slower, costlier, and more fragile than a competitor's single agent doing the same job. So you treat multi-agent as a deliberate escalation, justified by separable work, real specialisation, and a task too big for one agent, and you can always articulate why one agent would not have sufficed. That restraint is what separates engineering from architecture-astronautics, and it is the most important thing to carry out of this week.

## Where this fits
Internalise when *not* to go multi-agent: default to a single agent, and escalate only when the task genuinely decomposes, specialisation genuinely helps, and one agent genuinely cannot hold it, always able to justify the extra cost. This judgement is the capstone of the Agents phase, because it governs every pattern you learned: a tool is only as good as your discipline about when to use it. Tomorrow you ship the code review system, a case where multi-agent really is justified, and you will be able to say exactly why.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A working multi-agent code review system: submit code, and a coordinated set of specialist agents returns a single coherent review. By tonight it has:
- specialist agents with tight briefs, a Security agent for vulnerabilities, a Quality agent for code smells and style, each doing one job well.
- an orchestration pattern you chose deliberately (manager-worker as the sound default, the specialists running in parallel since they are independent) and can justify.
- a Synthesis step that merges the specialists' findings into one coherent review, with each agent emitting concise, structured output so synthesis does not drown in context.
- optionally, a critic pass on the final review, and routing if you handle varied submissions.

## The test that proves it
Submit a real piece of code with planted problems, an injection-prone query, a resource leak, a naming mess, and read the combined review. The proof is that the system catches issues across both domains and merges them coherently: the Security agent flags the injection, the Quality agent flags the leak and the naming, and Synthesis produces one review that reads as a single coherent assessment, not three stapled-together reports. Then do the comparison that justifies the whole architecture: run the same code through a single generalist agent asked to do everything, and show the multi-agent system caught more, or reviewed each domain more sharply, than the overloaded generalist. That side-by-side, specialists collectively beating the generalist, is the entire deliverable, because it is the concrete evidence for why multi-agent was the right call here and not over-engineering.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the system with its agents, the orchestration code, a README that names the pattern you chose and *why* it fit this problem, and the head-to-head example showing the specialist system outperforming a single generalist agent on the same code. That justification, articulating why this task warranted multiple agents when most do not, is what makes this a standout portfolio piece, because it shows the judgement from D6, not just the ability to wire agents together. Anyone can connect three agents; demonstrating that you chose multi-agent deliberately, for a task that genuinely earned it, and proving it beat the simpler alternative, is the senior signal reviewers actually look for.

## Where this fits in the track
This completes the Agents phase. You can now build a single agent that loops and acts (W13), give it memory across time (W14), expose its tools through a standard server (W15), and compose several agents into a coordinated system, while knowing when not to (W16). That is the full toolkit for building agents, from one loop to a team of them. Next comes the Production AI phase (W17-20), where the question shifts from "can I build it?" to "can I run it reliably, safely, and affordably for real users?", and the very first thing it asks is the one you have been circling since W12: how do you gate a deployment on whether the system actually works? You have built increasingly capable AI systems; now you learn to ship them like a professional.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You run the Security agent and Quality agent concurrently on the same code. They complete in 8 and 12 seconds respectively. The Synthesis agent starts as soon as both finish. Total time: 12 seconds. In the sequential version, total time was 8+12+6=26 seconds. What are the risks of the parallel approach that did not exist in the sequential? Race conditions are not a concern here since the agents only read the code, not write to shared state. The real risk is context: if the Security agent's output is long, it is passed verbatim to the Synthesis agent. If Quality is also long, the Synthesis agent's context grows quickly. In sequential execution, you could summarise intermediate outputs before passing them forward. In parallel, all outputs arrive simultaneously. Design both agents to produce compact structured output (under 500 tokens) to mitigate this.

weeks.title: Production Evals, Building the Confidence to Ship
weeks.context:
Shipping an AI feature without evals is like shipping code without tests, it works until it does not, and you find out from users rather than from CI. Production evals are the discipline that lets you ship with confidence: a set of golden test cases in version control, a pipeline that scores model outputs against them, and a gate that blocks deployment if quality regresses.

The difference between development evals (which you have been building) and production evals is that production evals run automatically, gate deployments, and monitor live traffic. They require infrastructure: somewhere to store results, something to trigger runs, something to alert when quality drops.

Pre-deploy evals run on every pull request. They test that a code change, a new prompt, a different model version, a modified retrieval pipeline, does not degrade quality below an acceptable threshold. The threshold is specific and numeric: if faithfulness drops below 0.80 or answer relevance drops below 0.75, the PR is blocked. These numbers are decisions you make based on what failure modes users will tolerate.

Online evals monitor production traffic. You sample a fraction of live requests (10-20%), score them with an LLM judge or deterministic metric, and store the results. Over time, you build a quality dashboard that shows how model quality changes with traffic patterns, with model updates from the provider, and with changes in the distribution of user questions. Without online evals, model degradation is invisible until it is severe.

A/B testing for AI features uses the same statistical framework as A/B testing in product development but with AI-specific gotchas: LLM responses are not binary (clicked/not clicked) but graded (quality score), which requires different statistical tests. Small sample sizes, high variance in quality scores, and provider model updates mid-experiment all complicate the analysis.

concept_check.q: You add a pre-deploy eval gate to your RAG pipeline. The eval runs on every PR and blocks merge if faithfulness drops below 0.80. A developer changes the prompt and faithfulness drops to 0.76. The PR?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You sample 15% of live production requests and score them with an LLM judge. You notice that quality scores drop every Friday afternoon. What hypotheses would you investigate? Friday afternoon traffic?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: You are A/B testing two prompts for your paper assistant. Prompt A scores 3.8 average quality (on a 1-5 scale) and Prompt B scores 4.1. You have 50 queries. Is this statistically significant? Run a tw?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
You have built development evals, the kind you run by hand to compare two pipelines. This week you turn evaluation into production infrastructure: golden test cases in version control, a pipeline that scores model outputs against them automatically, a gate that blocks a deployment if quality regresses, and online monitoring that scores a sample of live traffic so you see quality drop before your users do. The mantra to internalise on day one: shipping an AI feature without evals is like shipping code without tests, it works right up until it does not, and you find out from an angry user instead of from a failed check. This week is how you stop finding out from users.

## From running evals to evals that run themselves
The difference between what you have and what you are building is automation and gating. A development eval is something you choose to run; a production eval runs on its own, blocks bad changes, and watches live traffic, which means it needs infrastructure a one-off script does not: somewhere to store results over time, something to trigger runs (a pull request, a schedule, live traffic), and something to alert when quality drops. That infrastructure splits into two jobs that this week keeps distinct, because they answer different questions:
- **Pre-deploy evals** run on every change and ask "does this new prompt / model / pipeline degrade quality below the line?" If yes, the change is blocked before it ever reaches users.
- **Online evals** run on live traffic and ask "is quality still good *right now*, in production, on real questions?" They catch the degradation that pre-deploy evals cannot, because it comes from the world changing, not your code.
Together they cover both failure sources: changes you make, and changes that happen to you.

## The threshold is a product decision, expressed as a number
The heart of a production eval is a specific, numeric gate: if faithfulness drops below 0.80 or answer relevance below 0.75, the change is blocked. Those numbers are not arbitrary and they are not handed to you, they are decisions about what failure modes your users will tolerate, expressed in the language your eval can enforce. A medical-information feature might demand faithfulness above 0.95 because a hallucination is dangerous; a brainstorming tool might accept 0.70 because users want range over precision. Choosing the threshold forces you to articulate your quality bar concretely, which is itself valuable: "good enough" becomes "faithfulness >= 0.80," a line CI can defend on every change. This is where the W12 metrics stop being a report you read and become a contract the system enforces.

## Where this fits
This week opens the Production AI phase, and it opens it with evals on purpose, because everything else in the phase (observability, cost, deployment) assumes you can answer "is it still good?" automatically. It is the direct culmination of the W12 eval discipline: there you learned to measure RAG quality; here you wire that measurement into CI as a deployment gate and into production as live monitoring. The throughline of the whole track lands hard this week, an AI system you cannot measure is one you cannot ship responsibly, and now you make measurement automatic enough to actually gate releases on. Today, get the account and infrastructure set up and frame the two eval jobs; the week builds each.

items.title: Evals as code
items.body:
## Evals belong in version control, next to the code
"Evals as code" means your test cases live in your repository, versioned alongside the code they test, and run by your CI pipeline like any other test suite. This is the same move that made unit testing transformative: the tests are not a document someone runs occasionally, they are artifacts in the repo, reviewed in pull requests, and executed automatically on every change. Your golden test set from W12, the questions, expected answers, and source documents, becomes a checked-in fixture; your scoring pipeline becomes a CI job; and the result is that every change to a prompt, a model version, a retrieval setting, gets graded automatically before it merges. Treating evals as code is what turns evaluation from a thing you remember to do into a thing that happens whether you remember or not.

## The pre-deploy gate, concretely
The mechanism is a CI check that runs your eval and compares the score to the threshold:
```text
on every pull request:
  run pipeline over the golden set
  compute metrics (faithfulness, relevance, correctness)
  if faithfulness < 0.80 OR relevance < 0.75:
      FAIL the check  ->  block the merge
  else: PASS
```
Now a teammate who tweaks the system prompt and accidentally tanks faithfulness gets a red check on their PR, not a production incident a week later. The gate makes quality a merge requirement, exactly as a failing unit test blocks a merge today. The discipline this enforces is precious: nobody can degrade the AI's quality without CI noticing, which means you can change prompts and models freely, because the gate catches regressions instead of your users.

## Why this changes how you work
The payoff of evals-as-code is the same psychological shift that tests gave engineering: confidence to change things. Without a gate, every prompt edit is a gamble, you cannot know if it helped or quietly broke something, so you change cautiously and rarely. With a gate, you experiment freely, swap models, rewrite prompts, restructure retrieval, because the eval will tell you immediately whether quality held. That confidence is the entire point of the phase: you are building the safety net that lets you ship AI changes at speed without shipping regressions. It also makes quality a team-visible, reviewable thing, the eval score is right there in the PR, so "is this change good?" is answered by data in the review, not by argument or by waiting to see what users say.

## Where this fits
Put your golden set in version control and wire a pre-deploy eval gate into CI: every change runs the eval and is blocked if quality drops below your thresholds. You now have the regression-prevention half of production evals, the gate that stops a bad change from ever reaching users. But a change passing the gate today does not guarantee quality tomorrow, because the world shifts under a deployed model. Tomorrow you add the half that watches production itself.

items.title: Online evals
items.body:
## Pre-deploy evals cannot see the world changing
The gate from yesterday checks your changes. But an AI feature can degrade with no change from you at all: the provider silently updates the model behind the API, the mix of questions users ask drifts into territory your pipeline handles badly, a data source goes stale. None of that touches your code, so none of it trips the pre-deploy gate, and yet quality falls. Online evals close that blind spot by monitoring live production traffic: you watch the real system on real requests, continuously, so degradation that comes from the world rather than from a commit becomes visible. Without online evals, this kind of decay is invisible until it is severe enough that users complain, which is exactly the late, expensive way to find out.

## How online evals work: sample, score, store
You cannot score every production request (that would double your cost and latency), so online evals sample. The pattern:
- **Sample** a fraction of live requests, often 10-20%, enough to be representative without scoring everything.
- **Score** each sampled request with an LLM judge or a deterministic metric, the same faithfulness/relevance checks from W12, now run on live traffic instead of a fixed test set.
- **Store** the scores over time, building a history you can chart.
Out of that history comes a quality dashboard: a live view of how your AI's quality moves with traffic patterns, with provider model updates, with shifts in what users ask. The dashboard is the thing that turns "I think it's fine" into "faithfulness has held at 0.88 for three weeks, then dropped to 0.79 on Tuesday", a fact you can act on.

## The judge has no ground truth here, and that is the catch
Online evals differ from your golden-set evals in one fundamental way: there is no known-correct answer for a live user's question. On the golden set you could measure correctness against a labelled answer; in production you cannot, because nobody wrote down the right answer to a question a user just invented. So online evals lean on the metrics that need no ground truth, faithfulness (is the answer supported by the retrieved context?) and relevance (does it address the question?), which you can judge from the request and response alone, and they lean harder on the LLM-as-judge technique. This makes judge quality matter even more than in W12: a miscalibrated judge gives you a confidently wrong dashboard, so you validate it (spot-check its scores against human judgement) and you watch for trends rather than obsessing over absolute values, a drop from 0.88 to 0.79 is a reliable signal even if the exact numbers carry some judge noise. Reference-free measurement is weaker than golden-set measurement, but it is the only kind possible on live traffic, and a noisy quality signal beats none.

## Where this fits
Add online evals: sample a slice of production traffic, score it with reference-free metrics and an LLM judge, store the results, and build a quality dashboard. You can now see your AI's quality in production, not just at merge time, which means the world shifting under you becomes a visible trend instead of a silent decay. That visibility sets up tomorrow's sharper question: when the dashboard moves, how do you tell a real, sustained drop (drift) from ordinary noise?

items.title: Drift detection
items.body:
## Distinguishing real decay from noise
Your online-eval dashboard wobbles, quality scores vary request to request because language is varied and the LLM judge is itself noisy. Drift detection is the discipline of telling a meaningful, sustained decline (the model or the inputs have genuinely changed) apart from that ordinary scatter. It matters because both mistakes are costly: miss a real drift and quality rots unnoticed until users revolt; cry drift at every random dip and you drown in false alarms and learn to ignore the dashboard, which is just as bad as not having one. So drift detection is about finding the signal, a genuine shift, inside the noise of normal variation.

## What actually drifts, and why
Two distinct things change under a deployed AI, and naming them tells you where to look:
- **Model drift:** the model behind the provider's API changes, an update, a deprecation, a silently swapped version, and its behaviour on your exact prompts shifts. Your code is identical; the thing it calls is not. This is why pinning model versions and watching for provider updates matters, and why a quality drop with no deploy on your side points straight at the provider.
- **Data/distribution drift:** the inputs change. Users start asking a new kind of question your pipeline handles poorly, a new product launches and the query mix shifts, a content source goes stale. The model is unchanged; what you feed it is not.
The two have different fixes (re-tune or re-pin for model drift; expand retrieval, add coverage, or update sources for data drift), so detecting *which* drifted is half the diagnosis.

## Detecting drift without chasing noise
The practical approach is statistical and trend-based, not single-point. You compare a recent window of scores against a baseline window and ask whether the change is larger than normal variation, a sustained drop across many sampled requests, not one bad answer. You alert on trends (faithfulness has been below baseline for a day, across hundreds of samples), not on individual dips, which is what keeps the alerts trustworthy. You can watch the input side too: track the distribution of incoming questions (topics, lengths, embeddings) and flag when it shifts meaningfully from what your pipeline was built and evaluated on, catching data drift at its source before quality even drops. The throughline is the same one good alerting always follows: tune the sensitivity so that an alert means something real, because a drift detector that fires constantly gets muted, and a muted detector protects nothing. This is also where your golden-set evals re-enter, when drift fires, you re-run the rigorous offline eval to confirm and quantify it, the cheap online signal raising the alarm and the thorough offline eval diagnosing it.

## Where this fits
Add drift detection on top of online evals: compare recent quality against a baseline, alert on sustained trends rather than noise, and distinguish model drift from data drift so you know where to look. Your monitoring now does not just show quality, it tells you when quality has genuinely changed and points at the cause. Next you step back to a strategic distinction that shapes how you use all of this: the two fundamentally different jobs an eval can do.

items.title: Hill-climbing vs guard-rail evals
items.body:
## Two jobs an eval can do, and confusing them hurts
Every eval you build serves one of two purposes, and they pull in opposite directions, so naming them keeps you from misusing one as the other:
- **Hill-climbing evals** exist to make the system better. You run them while developing, read the per-case results, and use them to find weaknesses and improve, this prompt raised faithfulness, that chunking change helped recall. Their job is iteration: they are rich, detailed, and meant to be studied.
- **Guard-rail evals** exist to stop the system getting worse. They are the pre-deploy gate: a pass/fail check against a threshold that blocks regressions. Their job is protection: they are strict, fast, and meant to be enforced, not studied.
One climbs toward better; the other guards against worse. A great eval setup has both, and treating them as the same thing, or having only one, is a common and costly mistake.

## Why you need both, and why they look different
The two jobs want different evals because they answer different questions. A hill-climbing eval should be detailed and diagnostic, you want to *see* which cases fail and why, so you can improve, so it surfaces per-case breakdowns, examples, and the metric splits that point at a fix. A guard-rail eval should be a clean, reliable gate, you do not want it failing on noise or being slow on every PR, so it is a tight, stable check on the metrics that must not regress, tuned to fire only on real degradation. Use a noisy, sprawling hill-climbing eval as your merge gate and you get flaky CI that blocks good changes; use a bare pass/fail gate as your development tool and you have no idea *why* anything failed or how to improve. They are different instruments for different jobs, and good engineers keep them separate on purpose.

## How they work together over time
The two evals form a ratchet, and seeing the cycle is the payoff. You use hill-climbing evals to push quality up, experiment, measure, improve, until faithfulness reaches, say, 0.88. Then you set the guard-rail threshold below that hard-won level (0.85, say) to lock the gain in: nothing can merge that drops you back below it. Climb again with the hill-climbing eval, raise the guard-rail again, and quality moves up and stays up, improvement protected from backsliding. This is exactly how mature engineering organisations treat quality generally: tooling to get better, gates to never get worse, and the combination is what produces durable progress instead of a sawtooth of improvements and regressions. Recognising which job you are doing at any moment, climbing or guarding, tells you which eval to reach for and how to tune it.

## Where this fits
Distinguish your two eval jobs: rich, diagnostic hill-climbing evals for improving the system, and strict, stable guard-rail evals for the gate that prevents regressions, and use them as a ratchet that raises quality and locks it in. You now understand not just how to run production evals but the strategy behind them. One practical constraint remains before you ship: all of this evaluation costs money, and an eval setup you cannot afford to run is one that quietly stops protecting you.

items.title: Eval budgets
items.body:
## Evals cost money, and the bill can rival production
Running evals continuously is not free, and at production scale the cost is serious: every pre-deploy run scores your whole golden set, every online eval scores a slice of live traffic, and every LLM-judged metric is its own model call. Score a 200-case golden set with three judged metrics on every pull request, plus 15% of all production traffic continuously, and your eval spend can approach or exceed your actual feature spend. This is the trap the week has to close: an eval setup so expensive that the team turns it off, or runs it rarely, is an eval setup that no longer protects anything. So eval budgets are a first-class concern, you manage the cost of measurement deliberately, the same way you will manage the cost of the feature itself next week.

## The levers are the ones you already own
Fortunately, eval cost is just another AI cost, so the W7 and W12 toolkit applies directly:
- **Cheaper judge models:** the LLM judge rarely needs your most expensive model. A smaller, validated judge scores faithfulness and relevance well at a fraction of the price, confirm it agrees with the expensive one on a sample, then use it everywhere.
- **Batch the offline runs:** a pre-deploy or scheduled eval is a non-interactive job nobody is waiting on, so run it through the Batch API at half price.
- **Right-size the sets:** the W12 sizing lesson, do not score 500 golden cases or sample 50% of traffic when 100 cases and 15% give you the confidence you need.
- **Cache shared prefixes:** judge calls that share a long rubric prefix can prompt-cache it, paying for the rubric once.
None of this is new; it is the cost discipline you have been building, now aimed at the evaluation pipeline so it stays affordable to run continuously.

## Tier the budget to how often it runs
The strategy that resolves cost against rigour is tiered evaluation matched to frequency, the same shape as W12's tiering, now formalised as a budget:
- A **small, cheap, fast** eval runs on every pull request, a few dozen high-signal cases, cheap judge, the guard-rail gate. Cheap enough to run on every change without thinking about it.
- A **large, thorough, expensive** eval runs rarely, before a release, nightly, when drift fires, the full golden set, all metrics, the better judge. You pay for rigour exactly when a high-stakes decision warrants it.
- **Online** evals sample at a sustainable rate, tuned so continuous monitoring stays within budget.
This is the SRE instinct applied to evaluation: cheap-and-frequent for fast feedback, expensive-and-rare for the big decision, so you get a gate on every change and a deep read when it counts, without paying full-eval cost on every commit. Budgeting evals this way is what makes continuous evaluation sustainable rather than a cost the team eventually kills.

## Where this fits
Set an eval budget: estimate what your evals cost, apply the levers (cheap validated judge, batch the offline runs, right-size sets, cache rubrics), and tier the spend so cheap evals gate every change while expensive ones run only when warranted. You have made the whole production-eval system affordable enough to actually run forever, which is the difference between a safety net that protects you and one the team switches off to save money. Tomorrow you assemble it all into the deployment gate that ships this week.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A production eval system that gates deployments and monitors live quality, the safety net that lets you ship AI changes with confidence. By tonight it has:
- a golden test set in version control and a pre-deploy eval gate in CI that blocks any change dropping quality below numeric thresholds you chose deliberately.
- online evals sampling a slice of production traffic, scored with reference-free metrics and an LLM judge, feeding a quality dashboard.
- drift detection that alerts on sustained quality drops and distinguishes model drift from data drift.
- separate hill-climbing and guard-rail evals used as a ratchet, and a tiered eval budget that keeps the whole thing affordable to run continuously.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is the gate catching a regression you can point to. Take a real change that degrades quality, swap in a weaker model, or a sloppier prompt, open it as a pull request, and watch the eval gate go red and block the merge with the specific number that failed: "faithfulness 0.74 < threshold 0.80, merge blocked." That red check, a quality regression stopped automatically before it could reach a user, is the entire point of the week made concrete. Then show the other half: point at the online dashboard tracking live quality over time, and ideally a drift alert firing on a sustained drop. A gate that blocks bad changes and a dashboard that catches silent decay, both demonstrably working, is the proof that you can now ship AI like a professional rather than hoping for the best.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the eval system, the versioned golden set, the CI gate config, the online sampling and dashboard, the drift alerting, with a README explaining the two eval jobs (hill-climbing to improve, guard-rail to protect), the thresholds you chose and why, and a screenshot of the gate blocking a real regression. This is one of the most credible portfolio pieces on the entire track, because production evals are precisely where most AI engineers are weakest: plenty of people can build an AI feature, very few can demonstrate the infrastructure that ships it safely, gates regressions, and monitors live quality. Showing a working gate and a quality dashboard signals senior-level production thinking, the rare and valuable kind.

## Where this fits in the track
You have built the foundation of the Production AI phase: the ability to know, automatically and continuously, whether your AI is good enough to ship and stay shipped. Everything that follows assumes it. W18 adds observability, when an eval or a user says something is wrong, tracing lets you see *what* the system actually did and find the broken span. W19 attacks cost, making the feature (and these very evals) affordable at scale. W20 deploys the whole thing to real users behind a public URL. The phase is the answer to "can I run this reliably, safely, and affordably for real people?", and it begins, rightly, with the discipline that answers the most important question of all: how do you know it's working? You can now answer that on every change and every day, which is what it means to ship AI responsibly.

weeks.title: Observability, Seeing Inside the Black Box
weeks.context:
An AI feature that fails in production fails in ways you cannot see without instrumentation. The model returns a response, but did it use the right retrieved documents? Did the agent take the expected path? Did the tool call succeed? Did a prompt change last Tuesday cause the quality drop you see in Friday's metrics? Observability answers these questions by recording what happened inside the black box.

Tracing is the core primitive. A trace is a tree of spans, each representing a unit of work: one span for the total request, child spans for retrieval, reranking, the model call, and any tool calls. Each span has a duration, input, output, and attributes (model name, token count, cost). When something goes wrong, you look at the trace and see exactly which span is slow, which returned unexpected output, and which cost more than expected.

OpenTelemetry is the open standard for telemetry data, traces, metrics, and logs, that is increasingly adopted by AI tooling. The practical meaning: you instrument your code once with the OTel SDK, and you can send the data to any compatible backend (Langfuse, Phoenix, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo) without changing your instrumentation code. Lock-in risk is lower.

Hosted observability platforms, LangSmith, Helicone, Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, provide dashboards, query interfaces, and alerting built specifically for AI workloads. They understand the concept of a "run" that includes an LLM call, they render conversation trees, and they surface latency and cost metrics in AI-native formats. Self-hosted alternatives (Langfuse OSS, Phoenix) give you the same features without sending data to a third party, relevant when your data is sensitive.

This week you add full observability to your researcher agent from W13. Every run, every thought, every tool call, every retrieval, every model response, gets traced. By the end of the week, you can open the dashboard and see exactly what the agent did on any given run.

## Walkthrough

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Last week's evals tell you *that* quality dropped. This week you build the thing that tells you *why*. You add full observability to your W13 researcher agent: every run, every reasoning step, every tool call, every retrieval, every model response, gets recorded, so you can open a dashboard and see exactly what the agent did on any given run. When a user reports a bad answer, or an eval flags a regression, you stop guessing and start looking: which retrieval returned junk, which tool call failed, which model response went off the rails, which prompt change last Tuesday caused Friday's metric dip. Observability is how you see inside the black box, and it is the difference between debugging an AI system and shrugging at one.

## Why AI systems are especially opaque
Every production system needs observability, but AI systems need it more, because their failures are invisible without instrumentation in a way that ordinary code's are not. A normal bug throws a stack trace; an AI failure returns a fluent, confident, wrong answer with no error at all. Did the agent retrieve the right documents or irrelevant ones? Did it take the expected path through its loop or wander? Did the tool call actually succeed or silently return nothing useful? Did a prompt edit shift behaviour? None of that is visible from the final response, the system looks like it is working even when it is not. So you cannot debug an AI feature by reading its output; you have to record what happened *inside* the request and inspect that, which is exactly what observability provides.

## Tracing: the core primitive
The central tool this week is tracing, and the model is simple and powerful. A trace is a tree of spans, where each span is one unit of work with a duration, an input, an output, and attributes (model name, token count, cost). One request becomes one trace: a top-level span for the whole request, child spans for retrieval, for reranking, for the model call, for each tool call, nested to mirror what actually happened.
```text
trace: "research: GPT-4o vs Haiku cost"   2.4s  $0.011
  span: retrieve (vector search)          120ms   8 docs
  span: model call (plan)                 800ms   1.2k tok
  span: tool call: web_search             600ms   ok
  span: model call (synthesize)           900ms   2.1k tok  $0.009
```
When something goes wrong, you open the trace and see precisely which span was slow, which returned unexpected output, which cost more than expected. The tree turns an opaque request into a readable, inspectable sequence of steps.

## Where this fits
This is the second pillar of the Production AI phase, and it pairs with the first: W17 evals tell you *that* quality changed; W18 observability tells you *why*, by letting you inspect what the system did on the failing runs. It also makes everything else in the phase visible, you cannot manage cost (W19) or latency (W20) that you cannot see, and the traces you build this week are exactly where cost and latency get measured. Instrumenting the W13 agent is deliberate: a multi-step agent is the hardest thing to debug blind and the most rewarding to trace, because its whole value is the trajectory, and a trace is the trajectory made visible. Today, get the platform set up and frame what a trace is; the week instruments the agent end to end.
