items.title: Tracing primitives
items.body:
## A trace is a tree of spans
The foundational concept, worth getting exactly right, is the trace-and-span model. A **span** is a single unit of work: a retrieval, a model call, a tool call, a rerank. Each span records four things, its duration (how long it took), its input (what went in), its output (what came out), and its attributes (metadata like model name, token count, cost). A **trace** is the tree of spans for one whole request: a root span covering the entire request, with child spans nested underneath for each sub-operation, in the structure they actually executed. The nesting is the point, the tree shows not just what happened but how the operations related, which called which, what ran inside what, so reading a trace is reading the anatomy of a request.

## Why the tree structure is what makes it useful
The reason spans nest into a tree rather than sit in a flat log is that the structure is where the diagnostic power lives. A flat log tells you events happened; a trace tree tells you the total request took 2.4 seconds *and* that 1.8 of those seconds were in one model call, *and* that this call sat inside the synthesis step, not retrieval. Because every span carries its own duration, input, output, and cost, you can answer precise questions instantly: which span is the slow one (sort by duration), which returned the unexpected output (read the outputs down the tree), which cost the most (sort by the cost attribute). The same trace answers latency questions, quality questions, and cost questions, because all three are just attributes on the spans. Without the structure, you would be reading scattered log lines and guessing how they connect; with it, the request explains itself.

## Instrumenting your agent: wrap each unit of work
Adding tracing means wrapping each meaningful operation so it opens a span, records its input, runs, and records its output and attributes on close. For your researcher agent: a root span per research request, a child span around each retrieval (input: the query; output: the docs; attribute: how many), a child span around each model call (input: the messages; output: the response; attributes: model, tokens, cost), a child span around each tool call (input: the args; output: the result; attribute: success or failure). The agent's loop naturally produces a tree, each iteration's reasoning, tool call, and observation become nested spans, so the trace ends up being a faithful recording of the agent's trajectory, the exact thing you wished you could see when an agent went wrong in W13. The discipline is to instrument at the right granularity: a span per real unit of work (retrieval, model call, tool call), not so fine that the tree is noise, not so coarse that a slow step hides inside a giant span.

## Where this fits
Instrument your researcher agent with traces and spans: a span per retrieval, model call, and tool call, each recording duration, input, output, and attributes, nesting into one trace per request. You can now reconstruct any single run from its trace, which is the raw capability all of observability builds on. Raw spans in your own code are the primitive; tomorrow you send them to a platform built to store, render, and query them, so a trace tree becomes a dashboard you can actually live in.

items.title: Hosted observability
items.body:
## Why not just build the dashboard yourself
You could store spans in your own database and build your own viewer, and for one agent you might. But observability has a lot of surface, storing traces at volume, rendering conversation trees, querying across runs, alerting on patterns, and rebuilding all of that is rebuilding a category of tooling that already exists and is good. Hosted observability platforms, LangSmith, Helicone, Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, give you that surface out of the box, and crucially they are built specifically for AI workloads, which generic logging tools are not. So the practical move is to send your spans to one of these rather than hand-roll the dashboard, and spend your effort on instrumenting well rather than on building a trace viewer.

## What "AI-native" actually buys you
The reason an AI-specific platform beats a generic one is that it understands the shape of AI work. It knows what a "run" is, an LLM call with its prompt, response, tokens, and cost, and renders it as such, not as an opaque HTTP request. It draws conversation and agent trees, so a multi-step agent run shows up as the readable trajectory you instrumented, not a flat log. And it surfaces the metrics that matter for AI in native formats, latency per call, tokens, cost per run, quality scores, right next to the trace, so you are not reverse-engineering cost from raw logs. This AI-native rendering is the difference between a dashboard you actually use to debug and a pile of JSON you technically have, the platform speaks the language of LLM calls, agents, and retrievals, which is exactly the language your problems are in.

## OpenTelemetry and the self-hosting choice
Two decisions shape how you adopt a platform, and both are about avoiding traps. First, **OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is the open standard for telemetry, traces, metrics, and logs, increasingly adopted by AI tooling, and the practical payoff is portability: instrument your code once with the OTel SDK and you can send the data to any compatible backend (Langfuse, Phoenix, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo) without rewriting your instrumentation. That lowers lock-in, you can switch platforms without re-instrumenting, so prefer OTel-compatible instrumentation where you can. Second, **hosted versus self-hosted**: the hosted platforms are easiest, but they mean sending your traces, which include prompts and responses, real user data, to a third party. When that data is sensitive, self-hosted alternatives (Langfuse OSS, Phoenix) give you the same AI-native features without the data leaving your control. The choice is the standard build-versus-buy-versus-host trade, weighed against how sensitive your traffic is, and it previews exactly the privacy concern you will handle on D6.

## Where this fits
Send your agent's traces to a hosted (or self-hosted) AI-native observability platform, using OTel-compatible instrumentation to keep your options open, and explore the rendered conversation trees, latency, and cost views. You now have a real dashboard where any run is inspectable, not just spans buried in your own logs. With traces flowing to a platform that understands them, the next two days turn the trace into a management tool: first for cost, then for latency.

items.title: Cost tracking integrated with traces
items.body:
## Cost lives in the trace
You learned cost discipline back in W7, estimating and reducing spend. Observability makes it continuous and precise by attaching cost to the trace. Every model-call span already records its model, input tokens, and output tokens, so the platform can compute the dollar cost of that span and roll it up the tree to a total cost per request. Now cost is not a monthly surprise on a provider bill, it is an attribute you can see on every run, broken down by exactly which step spent it. Cost tracking integrated with traces means you can answer, for any request, "what did this cost, and where did the money go?", the question that, at scale, decides whether a feature is sustainable.

## Why per-span cost is the unlock
A single total-cost number tells you the feature is expensive; per-span cost tells you *what to fix*, and that difference is the whole value. With cost on every span, you can see that a research request costs eleven cents and that nine of those cents are in one synthesis call that stuffs all retrieved documents into the context, that is an actionable finding, a fat span you can target, not a vague "it's pricey." You can find the expensive runs (sort traces by total cost) and the expensive steps within them (sort spans by cost), and you almost always discover the spend is concentrated: a few steps, a few request types, a handful of users or queries dominate the bill. That concentration is good news, because it means a targeted fix to the costly span (a cheaper model there, trimming what goes into that call, caching it) moves the total far more than diffuse optimisation. You cannot do that targeting without per-span cost, which is why integrating cost into traces is what makes W19's optimisation possible.

## From visibility to control
Cost-in-traces turns spend from something you discover after the fact into something you manage in real time. Because every run's cost is recorded, you can build a cost dashboard (spend over time, cost per request, cost per feature, cost per user), set alerts when cost per request creeps up (a sign a prompt grew or retrieval is pulling too much), and attribute spend to the parts of the system responsible, the same way you attribute latency or errors. This is the data foundation for everything in W19: you cannot cut a cost by 50% if you cannot see where the 100% goes, and the trace is where it goes. It also catches cost regressions the way evals catch quality regressions, a change that doubles tokens per request shows up immediately as a cost spike per run, not a month later on the bill.

## Where this fits
Integrate cost tracking into your traces: compute per-span cost from model and token attributes, roll it up to per-request totals, and build a cost view that shows where the money goes. You can now see spend at the resolution of individual steps, which is the exact visibility next week's cost optimisation depends on. The same trace that carries cost also carries duration, so tomorrow you turn it on the other production constraint users feel directly: latency.

items.title: Latency budgets
items.body:
## Latency is a feature, and the trace already measures it
Users feel latency directly, an AI feature that takes eight seconds to respond feels broken even if the answer is perfect, so response time is a feature you must manage, not an afterthought. And you already have the instrument: every span records its duration, so the trace tree is also a latency breakdown. The root span is the total time the user waited; the child spans show where that time went, retrieval, each model call, each tool call. A latency budget is the practice of setting a target for total response time and using the trace to see whether you are within it and, when you are not, exactly which span blew it. Latency stops being a vague "it feels slow" and becomes "the second model call takes 1.8 of our 2.5-second budget."

## Reading the trace for the bottleneck
The diagnostic power is the same as for cost, because it is the same tree: sort spans by duration and the slow step is obvious. In AI systems the culprit is usually a model call (large generations are the dominant cost in time as well as money), but the trace keeps you honest about *which* one, and sometimes surprises you, a retrieval hitting a cold index, a tool call waiting on a slow external API, a rerank you forgot was expensive. Without the trace you would optimise by guesswork and often "fix" the wrong thing; with it, you target the actual bottleneck. The trace also reveals structure you can exploit: steps that run sequentially but did not need to (two independent retrievals, two specialist agents from W16) are visible as back-to-back spans that could be parallel, turning a sum of durations into a max of durations, often the single biggest latency win available.

## The levers, and the tension with quality and cost
Once the trace shows where the time goes, the levers are concrete: **parallelise** independent steps so they overlap instead of stacking; **stream** the response so the user sees tokens immediately and perceived latency drops even if total time is unchanged (the W7 streaming idea, now a latency tool, and the thing you will deploy in W20); **use faster models** on the latency-critical path (the smaller model is quicker as well as cheaper); and **cache** so a repeated step returns instantly (W19). The judgement is that these levers trade against quality and cost, a faster smaller model may be less capable, parallelism adds complexity, so you spend your latency budget where users feel it most and accept slower steps where they do not (a background enrichment can be slow; the first visible token cannot). Setting an explicit budget forces that prioritisation: you decide the target, the trace tells you who is over it, and you fix the spans that matter to the experience rather than chasing milliseconds everywhere.

## Where this fits
Set a latency budget for your agent and use the trace's per-span durations to find and fix the bottleneck, parallelising independent steps, streaming output, routing the hot path to a faster model where it pays. You can now manage response time with the same precision as cost, both read off the same traces, which is what production AI systems demand. One critical concern remains before you ship observability: those traces contain real prompts and responses, which means real user data, and recording everything has a privacy cost.

items.title: Privacy and PII redaction
items.body:
## Observability records user data, and that is a liability
Everything good about tracing, that it records every input and output, is also a risk: those inputs and outputs are real user data, and they may contain personal or sensitive information, names, emails, account numbers, health details, whatever users typed into your AI. The moment you trace, you are storing that, possibly on a third-party platform, possibly retained for a long time, possibly visible to your whole team on a dashboard. So observability is not just an engineering feature, it is a data-handling responsibility: you have created a detailed record of what users said, and you are now accountable for protecting it. Privacy and PII redaction is the discipline of getting observability's benefits without turning your trace store into a sensitive-data breach waiting to happen.

## Redact at the boundary, and collect less
The core technique is PII redaction: detect and scrub personal data from spans before they are stored, so the trace keeps its diagnostic shape (this step retrieved 8 docs, that call cost nine cents, the answer had this structure) while the sensitive specifics are masked. You redact at the instrumentation boundary, scrubbing as the span is recorded, so the raw PII never reaches the trace backend in the first place, rather than trying to clean it after it has already been stored and possibly synced to a vendor. Detection ranges from pattern matching (emails, card numbers, phone numbers have recognisable shapes) to model-based PII detection for the harder cases (names, free-text identifiers). And the cheapest privacy win is collecting less: you do not have to store the full prompt and response verbatim, often the metadata, durations, token counts, costs, retrieval counts, success flags, is enough to debug performance and cost without retaining the literal user text, so capture the structure and redact or omit the content where you can.

## Privacy as an engineering constraint, not an afterthought
Handling this well means treating privacy as a design constraint on your observability, the same way auth was a design constraint on your MCP server. Concretely: redact PII before storage; set retention limits so traces expire rather than accumulating sensitive data forever; control access so the dashboard of user conversations is not open to everyone; and let the data sensitivity drive the build-versus-host choice from D3, the more sensitive the traffic, the stronger the case for self-hosting your observability so the data never leaves your control. This is also increasingly a legal requirement, not just good practice, regulations govern how you store and retain personal data, and "we logged everything to a third party with no redaction" is a real liability. The mature stance is that you want maximum insight into your system's behaviour with minimum exposure of your users' data, and good redaction is how you get both: you keep the engineering signal and drop the personal content. An observability setup that ignores this is one incident away from being the problem instead of the tool that finds problems.

## Where this fits
Add privacy to your observability: redact PII at the instrumentation boundary before storage, prefer collecting metadata over raw content, set retention limits and access controls, and let sensitivity inform whether you self-host. Your tracing is now something you can responsibly run on real user traffic, not just on your own test queries, which is what makes it usable in actual production. Tomorrow you assemble the fully observable agent and ship it.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A fully observable version of your researcher agent: open the dashboard, pick any run, and see exactly what happened, every reasoning step, retrieval, tool call, and model response, with its duration and cost. By tonight it has:
- complete tracing: a trace per request, spans for every retrieval, model call, and tool call, each with input, output, duration, and attributes, nesting into a faithful tree of the agent's trajectory.
- those traces flowing to an AI-native observability platform (hosted or self-hosted) that renders the agent's runs as readable trees.
- cost integrated into traces (per-span and per-request) and a latency budget you manage from span durations.
- PII redaction at the instrumentation boundary, retention limits, and access control, so it is safe to run on real traffic.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is debugging a real failure from the trace, not the output. Find (or plant) a run where the agent gave a bad answer, then, without rerunning anything, open its trace and diagnose the cause: "the answer was wrong because the retrieval span returned three irrelevant documents, so the model synthesised from bad context, you can see the junk docs right there in the retrieval span's output." That, pinpointing *why* a run failed by reading its trace instead of guessing, is the entire payoff of observability and the proof it works. Show the cost and latency views too: this run cost eleven cents, mostly in the synthesis span; it took 2.4 seconds, mostly in one model call. Being able to look inside any run and explain exactly what it did, what it cost, and how long it took is the deliverable, because it is precisely the capability that makes a production AI system debuggable instead of a black box.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the instrumented agent, the platform configuration, and the redaction layer, with a README showing an annotated trace of a real run and a worked example of diagnosing a failure from its trace. Include the cost and latency views. This is a strong portfolio piece because observability is invisible until something breaks and then it is everything: demonstrating that you instrument AI systems properly, trace every step, track cost and latency per span, and handle user-data privacy responsibly, signals exactly the production maturity that separates someone who can build an AI demo from someone who can operate an AI system in production.

## Where this fits in the track
The Production AI phase is building the operational backbone, and you now have its two core senses: evals (W17) that tell you *that* something is wrong, and observability (W18) that tells you *why* by letting you see inside any run. Together they are how you run an AI system rather than just launch it. They feed directly into what is next: the cost data in your traces is the map for W19's optimisation (you cannot cut spend you cannot see), and the latency and streaming work previews W20's deployment, where you put the whole thing behind a public URL for real users. The lesson is the one every operator learns: a system you cannot see inside is a system you cannot run, and you have just made your agent fully visible, which is what it takes to ship it for real.

weeks.title: Caching, Batching, and Cost Optimisation, Spending Cents Instead of Dollars
weeks.context:
AI API costs scale with usage. A feature that costs $0.02 per request is sustainable at 100 requests/day and painful at 100,000. The engineers who ship AI features that are both good and affordable are the ones who understand exactly where the money goes and have applied the right tools to reduce it. This week you take one of your four major projects and cut its cost by 50% without measurable quality loss.

Exact-match caching is the simplest and most effective optimisation. If the same prompt is sent twice, return the cached response. Hash the complete prompt (model, messages, temperature, and any other parameters that affect output) as the cache key. Cache responses in Redis or a SQLite table with a TTL. Hit rate depends on your workload, systems with common system prompts and repeated query patterns can achieve 30-50% cache hit rates.

Semantic caching extends this: cache by meaning, not exact text. Embed the user's query, check the cache for a semantically similar query (cosine similarity above 0.95), and return the cached response if found. This catches paraphrases of the same question. The risk: two questions can be semantically similar but require different answers. Set the threshold conservatively (0.95, not 0.85) and add a fallback to fetch fresh if the cached response does not seem to fit.

Prompt caching at the provider level discounts the input tokens in a stable, repeated prefix. If your system prompt is 2000 tokens and never changes, prompt caching means you pay cache-read rates (roughly 10% of input rates on Anthropic, similar on OpenAI) for those 2000 tokens after the first call. At scale, this is substantial.

Batch APIs are underused. If you are running evaluations, generating reports, or processing documents overnight, the batch API offers 50% cost reduction for accepting 24-hour latency. Evals, batch document processing, and asynchronous enrichment pipelines are all good candidates.

Model routing, using a smaller model for simpler queries, is the highest-leverage optimisation but requires the most care. You need a reliable classifier, and you need to measure quality on the routed requests to ensure the cheaper model is actually good enough.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
This week has a hard, measurable goal: take one of your four major projects and cut its cost by 50% without measurable quality loss. Not "make it a bit cheaper", a specific 50% reduction you prove with the cost data from last week's traces, while your W17 evals confirm quality did not drop. You will apply a stack of optimisations, exact-match caching, prompt caching, model routing, batching, distillation, and measure the savings from each, ending with a feature that does the same job for half the money. This is the week cost stops being a worry at the back of your mind and becomes a number you drive down deliberately.

## Why cost is an engineering skill, not an accident
AI API costs scale with usage, and that scaling is unforgiving: a feature that costs two cents per request is fine at a hundred requests a day and a serious problem at a hundred thousand. The same code that is delightful in a demo can be financially ruinous at scale, and nothing about it changed except how many people use it. So affordability is not luck, it is engineering: the people who ship AI features that are both good and sustainable are the ones who understand exactly where the money goes and have applied the right tool to each cost. Two engineers can build the same feature and one costs ten times the other, and the difference is entirely this week's skills. Cost optimisation is what makes the difference between a feature that survives success and one that gets killed the moment it gets popular.

## See it before you cut it
The reason this week follows observability is that you cannot optimise what you cannot measure, and the traces from W18 already show you where the money goes, per span, per request, per feature. Before applying a single optimisation, you read that data to find the concentration: cost is almost never spread evenly, a few request types, a few steps, a handful of expensive calls dominate the bill. That concentration is the opportunity, because a targeted fix to the fat span moves the total far more than diffuse tinkering everywhere. So the week's method is measure, target, optimise, re-measure: find the biggest cost from the traces, apply the right lever, confirm the saving and that quality held, repeat, until you have hit 50%. Optimising by guesswork wastes effort on cheap things; optimising from the trace data spends effort where the money actually is.

## Where this fits
This is the third pillar of the Production AI phase, and it depends on the first two: observability (W18) gives you the cost map, and evals (W17) let you cut cost safely, because every optimisation must be checked against the eval to prove quality survived, the whole point is cheaper *without* measurable quality loss, and the eval is what measures it. It also fulfils the cost thread that has run through the track since W7, where you first learned the levers; now you apply them systematically against a real target. Today, pick the project to optimise and read its trace data to find where its money goes; the week works down that list, lever by lever.

items.title: Exact-match caching
items.body:
## The cheapest token is the one you do not spend
The simplest and often most effective optimisation is exact-match caching: if the same prompt is sent twice, return the stored response instead of calling the model again. The cost of a cache hit is essentially zero, no model call, no tokens, so every hit is a request you got for free. It is first because it is both the easiest to implement and frequently the highest-impact, many real workloads repeat themselves far more than you would expect, common questions, retried requests, shared system prompts, and every one of those repeats is a full-price call you can replace with a lookup. Before any cleverer technique, you check whether you are paying repeatedly for answers you already have.

## Getting the cache key right is the whole game
The subtlety in exact-match caching is the key, and getting it wrong breaks correctness. The cache key must be a hash of *everything that affects the output*: the model, the full messages, the temperature, and any other parameter that changes the response. Miss one, hash only the user's text but ignore that the model or system prompt differs, and you will serve a response generated under different conditions, a subtle, nasty bug where the cache returns a plausible-but-wrong answer. So you hash the complete request. You store the responses somewhere fast with a time-to-live: Redis or even a SQLite table, with a TTL so stale answers expire (important when the underlying data or correct answer can change over time, you do not want to cache last week's stock price forever). The TTL is a correctness-versus-savings dial: longer TTL means more hits and more savings but more risk of serving stale content, so you tune it to how fast the right answer changes.

## Knowing what hit rate to expect
The value of exact-match caching depends entirely on your hit rate, the fraction of requests that find a cached answer, and that varies by workload. Systems with common system prompts and repeated query patterns, FAQs, popular queries, retried requests, can hit 30-50%, which is a third to half your calls eliminated outright, an enormous saving for trivial effort. Systems where every request is genuinely unique get little from exact matching, which is precisely the case D3's semantic caching is built for. So you measure your hit rate rather than assuming, and you read it as a diagnostic: a high hit rate means caching alone is a huge win; a low one tells you your requests are too varied for exact matching and points you toward caching by meaning instead. Either way, exact-match caching is the right first move because it is cheap to add, it never harms quality (a hit returns the identical response the model would have given), and it tells you how repetitive your workload really is.

## Where this fits
Add exact-match caching to your target project: hash the complete request (model, messages, all output-affecting params), store responses in Redis or SQLite with a tuned TTL, and measure your hit rate. You have eliminated the cost of every exact repeat for almost no effort and learned how repetitive your workload is. Exact matching only catches identical requests, though; tomorrow you extend caching to catch paraphrases of the same question, and then move to the provider-level caching that discounts even your unique requests.

items.title: Prompt caching (Anthropic/OpenAI)
items.body:
## Provider-level caching: a discount on the prefix you always send
Exact-match caching skips repeated whole requests; prompt caching attacks a cost inside *every* request. Most of your prompts share a large, stable prefix, a long system prompt, a fixed set of instructions, few-shot examples, a retrieved document set, that you send on every single call. Prompt caching at the provider level lets you pay a steep discount on that repeated prefix: after the first call, the provider charges cache-read rates, roughly 10% of normal input rates on Anthropic, similar on OpenAI, for the cached prefix tokens, instead of full price. If your system prompt is 2000 tokens and never changes, you pay full price for it once and a tenth of the price for it on every subsequent call. At scale, where that prefix ships on millions of requests, the saving is substantial and requires no change to what your feature does.

## Structure your prompt so the cache can work
The catch is that prompt caching only discounts a *stable prefix*, the cache matches from the start of the prompt up to the first point where anything differs, so the order of your prompt determines how much gets cached. The discipline is to put everything stable first and everything variable last: the unchanging system prompt, instructions, and examples at the top (cached), the user's specific question at the bottom (not cached, and it does not need to be). Put a variable token early, a timestamp, a per-request id, the user's name in the system prompt, and you break the cacheable prefix at that point, losing the discount on everything after it. On the Anthropic API you mark the cache boundary explicitly with `cache_control` on the stable portion (the source-of-truth detail from the claude-api skill: an ephemeral `cache_control` breakpoint tells the provider where the reusable prefix ends). So prompt caching is partly a prompt-engineering task: arrange the prompt stable-to-variable so the largest possible prefix is reused.

## When prompt caching pays, and when it does not
Prompt caching shines under a specific shape of workload: a large stable prefix relative to the variable part, sent frequently. A RAG or agent system with a long instruction block and retrieved context, hit constantly, is the ideal case, you amortise that big prefix across every call. It pays less when the prefix is small (little to discount) or when calls are so infrequent that the cache entry expires between them (prompt caches have a short lifetime, so the savings come from sustained, repeated traffic, not occasional calls). It also composes with exact-match caching rather than competing: exact-match skips fully repeated requests entirely, prompt caching discounts the shared prefix of the requests that *do* run because their variable part differs. The judgement is to recognise your prompt's shape, a big fixed prefix plus a small variable tail, mark the boundary correctly, and confirm the saving in your trace data, because a misplaced cache boundary silently gives you none of the discount you think you are getting.

## Where this fits
Add prompt caching to your target project: identify the large stable prefix, order the prompt stable-to-variable, mark the cache boundary (`cache_control` on Anthropic), and confirm the input-cost drop in your traces. Combined with yesterday's exact-match caching, you are now paying full price neither for repeated requests nor for repeated prefixes. Caching reduces what you pay per call; tomorrow you reduce cost a different way, by sending cheaper requests to a cheaper model in the first place.

items.title: Model routing
items.body:
## The highest-leverage lever: do not use the big model for easy work
Model routing is using a smaller, cheaper model for simpler queries and reserving the expensive, capable model for the hard ones. It is the highest-leverage cost optimisation available, because the price gap between model tiers is large (a small model can be five to twenty times cheaper than a flagship), and a great deal of real traffic is simple enough that the cheap model handles it perfectly well. If half your requests are easy classifications or short factual answers, routing those to the small model can cut your bill dramatically while the hard requests still get the capable model they need. The insight is that using your most expensive model for *every* request means overpaying for all the easy ones, and routing is how you stop.

## Routing well requires a reliable classifier and real measurement
Routing is the highest-leverage lever and it requires the most care, because its whole premise is a judgement that can be wrong: deciding which requests are "simple enough" for the cheap model. That decision needs a reliable classifier, a fast, cheap step (often a small model or a heuristic) that inspects each request and routes it, and a misrouting has a real cost: send a hard request to the weak model and you get a bad answer at a bargain price, which is no bargain. So the non-negotiable discipline is to measure quality on the routed requests, not just overall: your W17 evals must confirm that the cheap model is actually good enough on the slice you sent it, because a cost win that quietly tanks quality on a third of traffic is a loss. You tune the routing boundary against the evals, push more traffic to the cheap model as long as quality holds on it, and pull back when it does not. Routing without that measurement is gambling with quality to save money; routing with it is engineering.

## Routing as architecture, with a fallback
Done well, routing becomes part of your system's architecture, not a hack. A router classifies each request by difficulty (or by type) and dispatches it: trivial requests to the cheap model, hard ones to the capable model, and ambiguous ones can default to the capable model (fail safe toward quality, since the cost of a wrong cheap answer usually exceeds the saving). You can route on more than difficulty, length, task type, required capability, even the user tier, the same routing pattern you met in W16's multi-agent systems, now serving cost. And it composes with everything else this week: a routed request can still hit the cache and still use prompt caching, so the levers stack. The mature version is a system that spends model capability like a budget, lavishing the expensive model only where the task demands it and defaulting to cheap everywhere else, which is exactly how cost-efficient production AI is built. The discipline that keeps it honest is always the eval: more traffic to the cheap model is only a win while the measured quality on that traffic stays above your bar.

## Where this fits
Add model routing to your target project: a classifier that sends simple requests to a cheap model and hard ones to the capable model, with a safe default and, critically, eval coverage on the routed slice to prove the cheap model is good enough. This is usually the single biggest line-item reduction available, which is why it sits at the centre of the week. Routing picks an existing cheaper model per request; tomorrow you go further and consider *creating* a cheap specialised model that matches the expensive one on your specific task.

items.title: Distillation
items.body:
## When a small model can replace a big one for your task
Routing chooses among existing models. Distillation creates a cheaper one: you take a large, capable "teacher" model and use it to train a smaller "student" model that reproduces the teacher's behaviour on your specific task. The student is far cheaper and faster to run, and because it is specialised to your narrow use case, it can match the teacher's quality *on that task* despite being a fraction of the size. The classic recipe is to run the expensive model over many examples of your task, collect its outputs, and fine-tune the small model on those input-output pairs, the small model learns to imitate the big one where it counts. Distillation is the step beyond routing: instead of paying the big model for the hard cases, you teach a small model to handle them cheaply.

## Why specialisation makes a small model competitive
The reason distillation works is the same generalisation limit from the agents phase, turned to your advantage. A large model is expensive partly because it is a generalist, capable across an enormous range of tasks. Most production features do not need that range, they need to do one narrow thing extremely well. A small model cannot be a great generalist, but it *can* be a great specialist, and on a single well-defined task with good training data from the teacher, it can close most or all of the quality gap at a tiny fraction of the cost and latency. So distillation trades breadth you are not using for cost you are paying: you give up the big model's general capability (which your feature did not need) and keep its quality on your task (which is all your feature uses). When a feature is high-volume and narrow, classification, extraction, a specific kind of generation, distillation can be the difference between affordable and not.

## The cost-to-build versus cost-to-run trade
Distillation is more involved than the other levers, and that shapes when to reach for it. Caching and routing are cheap to add and pay off immediately; distillation requires building a training set (running the teacher over many examples), fine-tuning the student, and rigorously evaluating that the student actually matches the teacher on your task, real upfront work and real ML engineering. So it pays off when run-time volume is high enough that the per-request savings dwarf the one-time build cost: a feature serving millions of requests justifies the effort to distill; one serving hundreds does not, the build cost would never amortise. It also carries an ongoing cost, a distilled model is frozen, so when your task shifts or the teacher improves, you must re-distill to keep up, which is maintenance the API models do not require. The judgement is volume and stability: distill a high-volume, stable, narrow task where the run-time saving is large and lasting; stick to routing and caching for everything else. Reaching for distillation on a low-volume feature is over-engineering; ignoring it on a million-request classifier is leaving the biggest saving on the table.

## Where this fits
Understand distillation as the heaviest cost lever: train a cheap specialised student model to match an expensive teacher on your narrow task, justified when volume is high and the task is stable, validated by evals proving the student matches the teacher. You now hold the full ladder of cost optimisation, from a one-line cache to a custom distilled model. The techniques are only durable if you keep watching the bill, so tomorrow's lesson is the discipline that makes all of this stick: treating cost as something you monitor continuously, not optimise once.

items.title: Cost dashboards as a discipline
items.body:
## Optimisation decays without a discipline to hold it
You can cut a feature's cost by 50% this week and watch it creep back up over the next three months, a prompt grows, retrieval starts pulling more documents, a new feature ships without caching, traffic shifts toward expensive request types. Cost optimisation is not a one-time project you finish; it is a property you maintain, and the thing that maintains it is a cost dashboard treated as an ongoing discipline. The point of this lesson is the mindset shift: cost is not a number you fix once and forget, it is a metric you watch continuously, the same way you watch quality and latency, so that regressions show up as a visible spike the day they happen instead of a nasty surprise on next quarter's bill.

## What the dashboard tracks, and why each cut matters
A cost dashboard, built from the W18 trace data, makes spend continuously visible along the dimensions that let you act:
- **Cost over time:** the trend line. A sudden step up means something changed (a deploy, a traffic shift); a slow climb means gradual bloat. Either is a signal to investigate.
- **Cost per request:** the efficiency metric. Total cost rising because you have more users is success; cost *per request* rising means the feature got less efficient, a regression to hunt down.
- **Cost per feature and per user:** attribution. These reveal where the money concentrates, which feature dominates the bill, whether a handful of heavy users drive most of the spend, so you target optimisation where it pays.
Slicing cost these ways turns a single scary total into a map of where to act, exactly as per-span cost did for a single request, now at the level of the whole system over time.

## Cost as a first-class production metric
Treating cost as a discipline means giving it the same machinery as quality and reliability. You set alerts on cost per request so that a change which doubles token usage pages you immediately, a cost regression caught like an eval regression, not discovered on the invoice. You make cost part of code review and deployment, a change that raises per-request cost should be as visible and as questioned as one that drops quality, ideally surfaced right in the pull request alongside the eval score. And you keep the optimisation work going: the dashboard continuously shows the new biggest cost, so optimisation becomes a routine of measure-target-cut-re-measure rather than a one-off heroic effort. This is the production-engineering stance applied to money: what you do not measure, you cannot control, and a feature whose cost no one watches will drift expensive, because every individual change that adds a little cost looks harmless until they accumulate. The dashboard is what makes the 50% you cut this week stay cut.

## Where this fits
Build a cost dashboard from your trace data, cost over time, per request, per feature, per user, with alerts on per-request cost, and adopt the discipline of watching it like any production metric. Your optimisation is now durable, not a one-time win that quietly erodes, because regressions become visible the day they happen. Tomorrow you assemble the optimised, monitored project and ship the 50% reduction as the week's deliverable.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A real project whose cost you have cut by 50% without measurable quality loss, with the dashboard to keep it cut. By tonight you have:
- exact-match caching (full requests) and prompt caching (stable prefixes) eliminating repeated spend.
- model routing sending simple requests to a cheap model, with eval coverage proving the cheap model is good enough on the routed slice.
- batching applied to any non-interactive work (evals, bulk processing) for the 50% batch discount, and distillation considered or applied where volume justifies it.
- a cost dashboard tracking spend over time and per request, with alerts, so the saving is maintained, not just achieved.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a number with a guarantee attached: this project now costs roughly half what it did, and quality did not drop. You prove both halves from data, the cost dashboard shows the before-and-after per-request cost (eleven cents to five, say), and your W17 evals show faithfulness and relevance held within noise across the change. That pairing is the whole point and the whole difficulty: cutting cost is easy if you do not care about quality (just use the cheapest model for everything), and the engineering is cutting it *while proving quality survived*. A 50% reduction backed by an eval that confirms no measurable quality loss is the deliverable, because it demonstrates the exact discipline that makes AI features sustainable at scale, spending cents instead of dollars, deliberately, without breaking what users rely on.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the optimised project with its caching, routing, and cost dashboard, and a README that lays out the optimisation as a story: here was the cost, here is the trace data showing where it went, here is each lever I applied and what it saved, here is the eval confirming quality held, here is the 50% result. Show the before-and-after cost chart and the eval numbers side by side. This is a genuinely impressive portfolio piece because cost optimisation is where AI features live or die at scale and where most engineers are weakest, so demonstrating that you found the cost from traces, applied the right lever to each, and proved quality survived with evals signals exactly the production judgement that lets a company actually afford to run what you build.

## Where this fits in the track
You now have the third operational pillar: an AI feature that is not just good and observable but *affordable*, cut to half its cost and monitored to stay there. Combined with evals (W17) and observability (W18), you can build AI that is correct, debuggable, and economically sustainable, the three things that separate a feature that survives success from one that gets shut off when it gets popular. One pillar of the Production AI phase remains: actually deploying the thing. Next week you take your strongest project from the whole track, put it behind a public URL, and make it work reliably for real users, the final step that turns everything you have built from code on your laptop into a product in the world.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You implement exact-match caching and measure a 20% cache hit rate. Your cost drops by 20%. You expected more. Why might the hit rate be lower than expected and how do you investigate? Generate a cache key frequency histogram: count how many times each unique cache key was requested. If most keys are seen only once, your workload is highly non-repetitive and exact-match caching is not the right tool. Investigate semantic caching instead. Also check: are you including the full prompt in the hash (including the system prompt)? If the system prompt varies per user or per session, keys that look similar are different. Consider hashing only the user message for lookup and using the full key only for storage.

weeks.title: Deployment, Shipping AI Features to Real Users
weeks.context:
Code that works locally but is not deployed is not a product. Deploying AI features involves every challenge of deploying regular web features, servers, containers, environment variables, scaling, plus AI-specific challenges: streaming responses through your hosting layer, managing API key rotation, handling the latency characteristics of large model calls, and keeping long-running agent tasks alive when HTTP connections time out.

Platform choices matter. Vercel and Railway are excellent for Next.js and Python FastAPI apps respectively, with one-click GitHub integration and automatic deploys. Fly.io gives you more control and is cheaper at modest scale. Cloudflare Workers run at the edge globally with ultra-low cold starts but have execution time limits that may affect long model calls. AWS Lambda is flexible but cold starts add latency for the first request after idle. Matching the platform to your app's characteristics is the first deployment decision.

Streaming through a hosting layer is not always transparent. Vercel functions have a 30-second timeout on the Hobby tier that breaks long streaming responses. Netlify has similar constraints. Cloudflare Workers have a different streaming model than Node.js. When you deploy a streaming AI endpoint, test the actual streaming behaviour on the target platform, do not assume it works the same way it did locally.

Long-running requests are the hardest case. An agent that researches a topic for 3-5 minutes cannot use a synchronous HTTP endpoint. The architecture for long-running tasks: the HTTP endpoint accepts the request and returns a job ID immediately. A background worker executes the task. The client polls for results or receives a webhook when complete. This is standard async job queue architecture applied to AI tasks.

This week you deploy your strongest project from the last 19 weeks. It must have a public URL, work reliably under repeated use, and handle errors gracefully.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Code that works on your laptop is not a product. This week you take your strongest project from the last nineteen weeks and deploy it: a public URL anyone can hit, working reliably under repeated use, handling errors gracefully instead of crashing. By Sunday someone who is not you can open a link, use your AI feature, and have it just work, which is the moment a project stops being something you built and becomes something that exists in the world. Deployment is the step that turns nineteen weeks of capability into an actual thing people can use, and it has its own set of challenges that have nothing to do with how good your model or your prompts are.

## Deploying AI is web deployment plus AI-specific hazards
Shipping an AI feature involves every challenge of deploying any web feature, servers, containers, environment variables, scaling, secrets, plus a set of hazards specific to AI that catch people who assume it is just another web app:
- **Streaming through the hosting layer:** AI responses stream token by token, and your hosting platform may not pass that stream through the way it did locally, timeouts and buffering can break streaming in ways a normal request never reveals.
- **Long-running requests:** an agent that researches for three to five minutes cannot live on a normal HTTP request that times out in thirty seconds, so long tasks need a different architecture entirely.
- **API key management:** your provider keys are now secrets in a deployed system, to be stored, rotated, and protected, not hard-coded.
- **Latency characteristics:** large model calls are slow and variable, and your deployment has to stay responsive and reliable around that.
The week is mostly about these AI-specific hazards, because the generic web-deployment parts you can lean on platforms for, but the AI parts will surprise you if you assume they work the same in production as on localhost.

## Deployment is where the whole phase becomes real
This week is where everything in the Production AI phase comes together on a live system. The evals from W17 become a real deployment gate on the thing you are shipping; the observability from W18 becomes production monitoring of real traffic; the cost work from W19 keeps the deployed feature affordable under actual load. Deployment is not a separate concern bolted on at the end, it is the context that makes the rest of the phase matter, evals, observability, and cost optimisation are all things you do *because* the system is serving real users, and now it is. The reason this is the last week before the advanced and capstone phases is that it closes the loop: you have learned to build AI systems, measure them, see inside them, and afford them, and deployment is what puts them in front of the people they were built for.

## Where this fits
This closes the Production AI phase. W17 gave you confidence the system is good, W18 gave you sight into what it does, W19 made it affordable, and W20 puts it live for real users behind a public URL. It is also the bridge to the rest of the track: the advanced phase (W21-23) hardens what you have shipped, and the capstone (W24) builds one real product end to end, which is this week's deploy skill applied to a project you take all the way. Today, pick your strongest project, the one worth showing the world, and frame its deployment; the week handles the platform, the streaming, the auth, the limits, and the operations that make it reliable.

items.title: Deployment platforms
items.body:
## The platform is your first real deployment decision
Where you deploy shapes everything that follows, and the platforms are not interchangeable, each suits a different kind of app:
- **Vercel** is excellent for Next.js front-ends and serverless functions, with one-click GitHub integration and automatic deploys, the smoothest path for a web app with an AI backend, but with serverless timeout limits that matter for streaming and long calls.
- **Railway** is similarly easy for Python services (FastAPI), good when your AI logic lives in a Python backend.
- **Fly.io** gives you more control and is cheaper at modest scale, running real containers close to users, more setup, more flexibility.
- **Cloudflare Workers** run at the edge globally with ultra-low cold starts, superb latency, but with execution-time limits that can cut off long model calls.
- **AWS Lambda** is flexible and scales, but cold starts add latency to the first request after idle, felt sharply when that request also waits on a slow model.
Matching the platform to your app's characteristics, web app versus Python service, short calls versus long agent runs, latency-critical versus not, is the first deployment decision, and getting it wrong means fighting your platform all week.

## Choose against your app's actual shape
The right platform falls out of two questions about your specific project. First, what is it, a Next.js app (Vercel), a Python backend (Railway, Fly), an edge-latency-critical endpoint (Cloudflare)? Second, and this is the AI-specific part, how long do its requests run? A quick chat completion is fine on serverless; a three-minute agent run will hit a serverless timeout and fail, which immediately rules some platforms out or forces the async architecture from D3. Cold starts matter too: if your feature is hit sporadically, a platform with slow cold starts adds seconds to the first request, on top of the model latency, for a bad first impression. So you match deliberately: the platform's strengths (ease, control, edge latency, scale) and its constraints (timeouts, cold starts, execution limits) against your app's type and its latency profile. This is the same fit-the-tool-to-the-job judgement from the model and architecture choices earlier in the track, now applied to infrastructure, and the constraint that bites hardest in AI is almost always the timeout, because model calls are slow.

## Where this fits
Pick your deployment platform by matching its strengths and constraints to your project's type and its request-length profile, paying special attention to timeout and cold-start limits, because those are what AI workloads strain. You have made the foundational deployment decision the rest of the week builds on. The first place your platform choice gets tested is streaming: AI responses stream, and whether your chosen platform passes that stream through cleanly is the next thing to verify, not assume.

items.title: Streaming responses through your hosting layer
items.body:
## Streaming is the AI deployment hazard people miss
AI responses stream, tokens appear one at a time, and that streaming is what makes a chat feel alive instead of frozen for ten seconds. But streaming through a hosting layer is not always transparent: the platform sits between your code and the user, and it may buffer, time out, or simply not support streaming the way your local server did. The trap is that it works perfectly on localhost and breaks in production, because localhost has no serverless timeout, no edge proxy, no platform-imposed limits. So the rule is non-negotiable: when you deploy a streaming endpoint, test the actual streaming behaviour on the target platform, do not assume it works because it worked locally. This is the single most common way a deployed AI feature ships broken.

## The concrete ways platforms break streaming
The hazards are specific and platform-shaped, which is exactly why D2's platform choice and this lesson are linked:
- **Function timeouts cut the stream.** Vercel's Hobby tier has a 30-second function timeout that will kill a long streaming response mid-output; Netlify has similar constraints. A response that streams for forty seconds simply gets severed, and the user sees it stop partway with no error.
- **Edge runtimes stream differently.** Cloudflare Workers have a different streaming model than Node.js, so code that streams correctly in a Node server may need rewriting for the edge, and behaviour you relied on may not exist.
- **Proxies buffer.** Some hosting layers buffer the response and deliver it all at once, defeating the entire point of streaming, the user waits the full duration and then gets everything in a lump, exactly the frozen experience streaming was meant to avoid.
Each of these is invisible locally and obvious in production, which is why you test on the real platform.

## Streaming as architecture, and the limit it exposes
Getting streaming right in production means treating it as part of your deployment architecture, not just a client feature. You verify the whole path, model to your server to the hosting layer to the browser, actually streams end to end on the deployed platform, and you confirm nothing along the way buffers or times out before a realistic response finishes. Streaming is also your best tool against the latency you cannot remove: model calls are slow, but a streaming response makes the user feel a fast system because tokens start arriving immediately, so perceived latency drops even though total time is unchanged, the W7/W18 idea now shipped to real users. But streaming also surfaces a hard boundary: it keeps the user engaged for responses of seconds, but it cannot save a task that runs for *minutes*, because the underlying HTTP connection (and the platform's timeout) will give out long before a three-minute agent finishes. That boundary is exactly the problem tomorrow solves: when a request is too long to hold a connection open at all, streaming is not enough and you need a different architecture entirely.

## Where this fits
Deploy your streaming endpoint and test the real streaming behaviour on your target platform, watching specifically for timeout cutoffs, edge-runtime differences, and buffering proxies that silently break what worked locally. Your interactive AI responses now stream correctly in production, which is what makes the feature feel alive. Streaming controls who can perceive the system as fast; the next thing a public URL forces you to control is who can reach it at all, which is authentication.

items.title: Auth
items.body:
## Deployed means reachable by anyone, so identity comes first
On localhost your AI feature had no users but you. Deployed behind a public URL, it is reachable by anyone on the internet, which makes authentication, knowing who is making each request, the first thing you add, not the last. Without it, your endpoint is an open door: anyone can call your AI feature, which means anyone can spend your API budget, access whatever data it can reach, and use the expensive model calls you are paying for, with no idea who they are. Auth is what turns a public URL from "anyone can do anything" into "known users can do what they are allowed," and for an AI feature that fronts real model spend and real data, that boundary is not optional.

## Why auth matters more for AI endpoints specifically
Authentication is standard web practice, but an AI endpoint raises the stakes in a way a static page does not, because every unauthenticated request can cost you real money. A normal open endpoint that gets abused serves some extra traffic; an open *AI* endpoint that gets abused runs up a provider bill, each anonymous call is a model call you pay for, so an unprotected AI URL is not just a security hole, it is a financial one, and a discovered, unauthenticated AI endpoint can be drained by a script in an afternoon. Auth is the gate that ties every request to an identity you can hold accountable: a known user you can rate-limit (tomorrow), bill, or cut off. It is also the foundation for everything user-specific, per-user history, per-user data access, per-user limits, none of which is possible until you know who is calling. So auth comes early in the deployment week because almost every other protection depends on having an identity to attach it to.

## Doing auth without reinventing it
The practical guidance is to use established authentication rather than building your own, identity is a solved problem with sharp edges, and rolling your own is how breaches happen. Use a proven provider or library (the kind of managed auth your other projects already lean on) to handle the hard parts, sessions, tokens, password storage, OAuth flows, correctly. Then protect the AI endpoint itself: every request to it must carry a valid credential, verified before any model call runs, so an unauthenticated request is rejected before it can cost you anything. Manage your *provider* secrets with the same seriousness, your OpenAI and Anthropic API keys are now secrets in a deployed system, stored in environment variables or a secrets manager (never in code or the client bundle), and rotated periodically, because a leaked provider key is someone else spending your money. The discipline is least privilege again, from W15: known identities, verified on every call, with the powerful and expensive operations gated behind that identity, so the system is safe to expose to the open internet.

## Where this fits
Add authentication to your deployed feature: established auth verifying identity on every request before any model call, with provider API keys stored as managed secrets and rotated. Your public URL is now a controlled door, known users only, which protects both your data and your budget. Auth tells you *who* is calling; it does not yet stop a known user (or a leaked credential) from calling a thousand times a minute and running up your bill, so tomorrow you add the limit that does.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.body:
## Even known users need a ceiling
Authentication tells you who is calling, but a known caller can still overwhelm you, accidentally with a runaway loop, or deliberately by hammering the endpoint, and on an AI feature every excess call is real money and real load. Rate limiting caps how many requests a given caller can make in a window, protecting your system and your budget from being drained by any single user, whether malicious, buggy, or just enthusiastic. It is the natural partner to auth: auth identifies the caller, rate limiting bounds what that caller can do, and together they turn an open-ended liability (anyone can call as much as they want) into a controlled one (each identity gets a defined, affordable allowance).

## Why rate limiting is doubly important for AI
Every web service benefits from rate limiting, but for an AI feature it guards two things at once, and that double duty is what makes it essential rather than nice-to-have:
- **It caps cost.** Each request triggers paid model calls, so unbounded requests mean an unbounded bill. A leaked credential or an abusive user without rate limiting can run up enormous provider charges fast, the financial attack auth alone does not stop. Rate limiting puts a hard ceiling on how much any one caller can spend of your money.
- **It protects capacity and fairness.** Model calls are slow and resource-heavy, so a flood from one caller can starve everyone else and degrade the service for legitimate users. Limiting per caller keeps one heavy user from ruining the experience for the rest, and keeps your own backend and provider rate limits from being blown.
For a normal API, rate limiting is mostly about capacity; for an AI API it is also a direct, necessary cost control, which is why it is a required part of shipping AI to real users, not an optimisation.

## Designing limits that fit the feature
Good rate limiting is tuned, not just present. You set limits per identity (the auth from D4 is what makes "per user" possible) and at a level that fits real usage, generous enough that legitimate users never feel it, tight enough that abuse and runaway costs are capped, and you can tier them (a free user gets a small allowance, a paid user more), turning rate limiting into part of your product model rather than only a defence. You decide the window (requests per minute, per hour, per day) to match how the feature is used, and you fail gracefully when a limit is hit: return a clear "rate limit exceeded, try again shortly" with the standard signals, not a crash or a silent hang, so a user who bumps the limit understands what happened. You also respect the *provider's* rate limits, your own limiting helps you stay under the caps OpenAI and Anthropic impose, so you degrade politely instead of getting throttled or cut off upstream. The judgement is to bound the worst case (cost, abuse, capacity) without taxing the normal case, the same balance that runs through all of production engineering.

## Where this fits
Add rate limiting to your deployed feature: per-identity caps tuned generous-for-real-users and tight-for-abuse, optionally tiered, failing gracefully on exceed, and keeping you within provider limits. Combined with auth, your AI endpoint is now safe to expose, controlled access and bounded usage, so neither your data nor your budget can be drained by a single caller. Your feature is deployed, streaming, authenticated, and limited; the last thing before you ship is the operations that keep it running reliably once real users depend on it.

items.title: Health checks, dashboards, on-call
items.body:
## Shipping is the start of running, not the end
A deployed feature is not a finished feature, it is a running one, and running things need operating. The day after you ship, real users depend on your AI endpoint, and something will eventually go wrong, the provider has an outage, latency spikes, an error rate climbs, a deploy breaks streaming, and the question is whether you find out from your monitoring or from an angry user. Operational readiness is the set of practices that let you know your system's health and respond when it degrades: health checks, dashboards, and an on-call plan. This is the production-engineering mindset that the whole phase has been building toward, the recognition that the launch is the beginning of the system's life, and keeping it alive and healthy is its own ongoing discipline.

## The three operational primitives
Three things turn a deployed feature into an operable one:
- **Health checks:** a simple endpoint (and dependency checks) that report whether the service is up and its critical dependencies, the model provider, the database, the vector store, are reachable. Your platform and uptime monitors poll it, so an outage is detected automatically and immediately, not when a user complains. A health check is the difference between "we knew within a minute" and "we found out an hour later."
- **Dashboards:** the live view of the system's vital signs, built on the W18 observability, request rate, error rate, latency, cost, quality. This is where you *see* health, the trends that say the system is fine or that something is drifting wrong, and it is the same trace data from W18 now serving live operations.
- **On-call:** a plan for who responds when something breaks and how they are alerted. Alerts fire on the conditions that matter (error rate up, latency over budget, the provider down, quality dropped via W17's online evals), and someone is responsible for acting. Without this, a 3am outage runs until morning.
Together they answer the operator's core questions: is it up, is it healthy, and who fixes it when it is not.

## Reliability is engineered, and alerts must mean something
The deeper lesson is that reliability is built, not hoped for, and the production phase has handed you every piece: evals (W17) tell you if quality breaks, observability (W18) shows you what the system is doing, cost monitoring (W19) catches spend regressions, and this week's health checks and dashboards tie them into live operations with someone accountable. The discipline that makes it work is the same one from drift detection: alerts must mean something. An alerting setup that fires constantly gets muted, and a muted alert protects nothing, so you tune alerts to fire on real, actionable degradation, not on every transient blip, so that an alert reliably means "a human needs to look now." You also plan for graceful failure, when the provider is down or a limit is hit, the feature should degrade with a clear message rather than crash, because in a system that depends on an external model, the provider *will* have a bad day, and how you handle it is the difference between a brief blip and an outage. This is what separates a feature that launches from one that *stays* reliably available, and it is the operational maturity that makes everything else you built worth deploying.

## Where this fits
Add operational readiness to your deployed feature: health checks so outages are detected automatically, dashboards (on your W18 traces) showing live vitals, and an on-call plan with alerts tuned to fire only on real, actionable problems, plus graceful degradation when the provider fails. Your feature is now not just deployed but *operable*, you will know when it is unhealthy and have a plan to respond, which is what reliability actually requires. Tomorrow you bring it all together and ship the public, reliable product that closes the phase.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Your strongest project from the whole track, deployed: a public URL, working reliably under repeated use, handling failure gracefully. By tonight it has:
- a deployment platform chosen to fit its type and request-length profile, with streaming verified end to end on that platform (not assumed from localhost).
- authentication on every request and provider keys managed as rotated secrets, so the endpoint is controlled and your budget is protected.
- rate limiting per identity, capping cost and protecting capacity, failing gracefully on exceed.
- operational readiness: health checks, a live dashboard on your W18 traces, alerts tuned to real problems, and graceful degradation when the provider has a bad day.
- the W17 eval gate guarding deploys and W19's cost work keeping it affordable under real load.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is the simplest and hardest test there is: send the link to someone who is not you, on a device that is not yours, and have them use it successfully. It works, it streams responsively, it requires them to sign in, it does not fall over when they use it repeatedly, and when something goes wrong (they hit a limit, the provider hiccups) it tells them clearly instead of freezing or crashing. That, a stranger using your AI feature over the public internet and having it just work, reliably, is the entire deliverable, because it is the precise moment the project stops being code you wrote and becomes a product that exists. Everything else in the phase, the evals, the traces, the cost work, was preparation for this: a real AI feature, live, that real people can use and rely on.

## Ship the artifact
This is the artifact, the live URL, plus the repo with its deployment configuration, auth, rate limiting, and operational setup, and a README that documents how it is deployed: the platform and why, how streaming is handled, how auth and rate limiting protect it, how it is monitored and what happens when the provider fails. A deployed, working, public AI product is the strongest single thing you can put in a portfolio, far stronger than any amount of code that only runs locally, because it proves you can take an AI feature all the way from idea to something real users can actually use. The production maturity on display, streaming that works in production, controlled access, bounded cost, real monitoring, is exactly what an employer means when they ask whether you can ship.

## Where this fits in the track
This completes the Production AI phase, and with it the core of the entire track. You can now build AI systems (the building and RAG and agents phases), and you can run them in production, measured (W17), observable (W18), affordable (W19), and deployed for real users (W20). That combination, building capable AI *and* operating it responsibly at scale, is what an AI engineer is, and it is rare, because most people can do one half and not the other. What remains is sharpening and proof: the advanced phase (W21-23) hardens what you have built against the harder realities of production AI, and the capstone (W24) has you take one real product all the way through everything you have learned, the building, the evaluating, and the shipping you just did this week. You have crossed the line from someone who experiments with AI to someone who ships it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You deploy a streaming FastAPI endpoint to Railway. Locally, responses stream word by word. On Railway, the entire response appears at once after a delay. What is likely happening? The hosting layer is buffering the streaming response. Common cause: Railway (or a reverse proxy in front of it) is waiting for the response to complete before forwarding it to the client. Fix: set the correct headers to disable buffering: `X-Accel-Buffering: no` (for nginx reverse proxies), ensure your FastAPI endpoint returns a `StreamingResponse` not a `Response`, and verify the ASGI server (uvicorn) is configured for streaming. Test with curl and the --no-buffer flag to confirm streaming is working before browser testing.

weeks.title: Fine-Tuning, When Prompting Stops Being Enough
weeks.context:
Prompting gets you far. Fine-tuning takes you further, on the specific tasks where prompting has hit its ceiling. The ceiling appears when: the task has a narrow, consistent format that the model should always follow but prompting cannot enforce reliably, the domain uses vocabulary or notation the base model handles poorly, or you need the model to embody a specific style or persona consistently across thousands of interactions.

Fine-tuning works by continuing the model's training on your specific examples. After fine-tuning, the model has internalized your examples as learned weights, not as in-context instructions. The practical effect: you can use a shorter prompt (saving tokens), the model follows your format more consistently, and performance on your specific task improves, sometimes dramatically.

Dataset preparation is where most fine-tuning projects fail. The JSONL format is simple: each line is a JSON object with a messages array, identical to the chat completions format. The hard part is the data quality: diverse examples, clean expected outputs, and a train/test split that tests for generalisation rather than memorisation. If your test set comes from the same narrow distribution as your training set, your eval scores are optimistic.

When not to fine-tune: when you have fewer than a few hundred examples, when your failure mode is hallucination (fine-tuning can amplify rather than reduce hallucination), when prompting plus RAG can solve the problem, or when the task distribution changes frequently (retraining is expensive). Fine-tuning is a commitment, not a quick fix.

Open-source fine-tuning with Axolotl, Unsloth, or HuggingFace TRL gives you control and privacy, your data stays on your hardware. But it requires a GPU, careful hyperparameter selection, and understanding of the training process. Hosted fine-tuning (OpenAI, Mistral, Together AI) is operationally simpler but more expensive and your data goes to a third party.
