items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
For twenty weeks you have shaped model behaviour with prompts. This week you learn the tool for when prompting hits its ceiling: fine-tuning, continuing a model's training on your own examples so the behaviour you want is baked into its weights instead of begged for in the prompt. You will prepare a real dataset, fine-tune a model on a task where prompting genuinely falls short, and, just as importantly, learn to judge when fine-tuning is the right call and when it is an expensive mistake. The headline lesson of the week is restraint as much as technique: fine-tuning is a commitment, not a quick fix, and knowing precisely when to reach for it is the senior skill, more than knowing how to run the training.

## Where prompting actually hits its ceiling
Prompting gets you remarkably far, so the first thing to learn is the narrow set of cases where it genuinely runs out. The ceiling appears when:
- the task has a **strict, consistent format** the model should always follow, but prompting cannot enforce it reliably, it mostly complies and occasionally drifts, and "occasionally wrong" is unacceptable.
- the domain uses **vocabulary or notation the base model handles poorly**, specialised legal, medical, or scientific notation it was not well trained on.
- you need a **specific style or persona held consistently** across thousands of interactions, which a prompt approximates but does not lock in.
What these share is that you need behaviour to be *reliable and intrinsic*, not merely *usually present when instructed*. Fine-tuning addresses exactly that: it moves the behaviour from fragile in-context instruction to learned weights. Recognising these signatures, format you cannot enforce, domain the base model fumbles, style you need consistent at scale, is how you tell a real fine-tuning case from one a better prompt would have solved.

## What fine-tuning actually changes
Fine-tuning works by continuing the model's training on your specific input-output examples, so afterward the model has *internalised* your examples as adjusted weights rather than reading them as in-context instructions each time. That mechanism produces three practical effects worth being precise about: you can use a **shorter prompt** (the behaviour is in the weights, so you stop spending tokens re-explaining it every call, a real cost saving at scale), the model follows your **format more consistently** (it learned the pattern rather than being asked to follow it), and **performance on your specific task improves**, sometimes dramatically, because the model is now specialised toward it. The trade is generality for reliability-on-your-task: you give up nothing you were using and gain consistency the base model could not provide through prompting alone. Understanding that fine-tuning changes the weights, not the prompt, is what makes the rest of the week, datasets, methods, costs, make sense.

## Where this fits
This opens the Advanced phase, the weeks that harden and extend what you have built. Fine-tuning is the natural first advanced topic because it is the most common "what's beyond prompting?" question and the one most often answered wrong, people fine-tune when they should prompt, or prompt when they should fine-tune. It builds directly on your eval discipline: you cannot honestly tell whether fine-tuning helped without the W12/W17 evals, and dataset quality is itself an eval-shaped problem. Today, get the account set up and frame the central question the week keeps returning to, not "how do I fine-tune?" but "should I, for this task?", because the technique is only valuable when aimed at the right problem.

items.title: When to fine-tune
items.body:
## The decision is the skill
Most of fine-tuning's value, and most of its waste, is in the decision of whether to do it at all, so this lesson is the heart of the week. Fine-tuning is a commitment: it costs effort to build the dataset, money to train, and ongoing work to maintain, and it is genuinely hard to reverse course once you have built a feature around a custom model. So you reach for it deliberately, when prompting has provably hit its ceiling, not reflexively because it sounds more advanced. The discipline is to treat fine-tuning as the heavier tool it is, justified by a real, measured failure of the lighter tools, and to know the cases where it actively makes things worse.

## When NOT to fine-tune
The clearest way to learn the decision is the list of cases where fine-tuning is the wrong answer, because each is a trap people fall into:
- **You have fewer than a few hundred examples.** Fine-tuning needs a substantial, diverse dataset; with too little data you teach the model your handful of examples by rote and get a model that is worse, not better, on anything slightly different.
- **Your failure mode is hallucination.** Fine-tuning does not reliably reduce hallucination and can *amplify* it, training the model to produce confident outputs in your format makes it confidently wrong more fluently. Hallucination is a grounding problem, which RAG addresses, not a weights problem.
- **Prompting plus RAG can solve it.** If better instructions and retrieved context get you there, do that, it is cheaper, faster to change, and does not commit you to a custom model. Fine-tuning is for when these are genuinely insufficient.
- **The task distribution changes frequently.** A fine-tuned model is frozen at training time, so if your task shifts often, you are signing up to retrain repeatedly, expensive and slow. Prompts adapt instantly; weights do not.
Each "don't" maps to a property of fine-tuning: it needs lots of data, it bakes in behaviour (including bad behaviour), it is a commitment, and it is static. Internalise these and you will avoid the most common and costly fine-tuning mistakes.

## When fine-tuning is genuinely the right tool
The positive case is the mirror image: fine-tune when you have a few hundred-plus diverse, clean examples; when the problem is **consistency of format, style, or domain behaviour** rather than factual grounding; when prompting plus RAG has been tried and genuinely falls short; and when the task is **stable** enough that a frozen model stays valid long enough to amortise the cost. A classic good fit is a narrow, high-volume, stable task with a strict output format the base model *almost* nails but not reliably, fine-tuning closes that last gap and, as a bonus, shortens the prompt. The right mental order is a ladder you climb only as far as you must: prompt first, add RAG if you need knowledge, and fine-tune only when a consistency or domain-fit problem survives both. Reaching the top of that ladder when a lower rung would have done is the over-engineering this lesson exists to prevent; refusing to climb it when a real format problem demands it is the opposite mistake. The skill is reading which rung your problem is actually on.

## Where this fits
Make the fine-tune-or-not decision explicitly for a candidate task: check it against the "don't" list (enough data? not a hallucination problem? not solvable by prompt+RAG? stable enough?) and the positive case (a consistency/format/domain problem prompting cannot fix). You now hold the most important judgement in the week, the one that decides whether the rest of it is well spent. With a task that genuinely warrants it, tomorrow you do the actual fine-tuning the simplest way, through a hosted provider, and meet the place most fine-tuning projects actually fail: the data.

items.title: Hosted fine-tuning
items.body:
## The simplest path: let a provider do the training
Hosted fine-tuning, OpenAI, Mistral, Together AI, is the operationally simplest way to fine-tune: you upload a dataset, the provider trains the model on their hardware, and you get back a fine-tuned model you call through the same API as the base model. There is no GPU to manage, no training loop to write, no hyperparameter expertise required to get started, which makes it the right place to learn and often the right choice in production when the data is not sensitive. The trade-offs are real, it is more expensive than running training yourself and your data goes to a third party, but for getting a working fine-tune without first becoming an ML-infrastructure engineer, hosted is where you start, and where this lesson lives.

## The format is easy; the data quality is everything
The format hosted fine-tuning expects is deliberately simple: JSONL, one JSON object per line, each a `messages` array identical to the chat-completions format you already use, the input messages and the expected assistant response. That is the easy part, and it lulls people. The hard part, and where most fine-tuning projects actually fail, is the *quality* of what goes in those lines:
- **Diverse examples:** the training set must span the real range of inputs the model will see, not a narrow slice, or the model only learns the slice.
- **Clean expected outputs:** every example's target is teaching the model what "correct" looks like, so a sloppy or inconsistent target teaches sloppy, inconsistent behaviour, garbage targets produce a garbage model, faithfully.
- **A proper train/test split:** you hold out test examples to measure whether the model *generalises*, and the split has to be honest.
The model becomes its data. Spend your effort here, not on the training mechanics, because a perfect training run on a bad dataset gives you a bad model, reliably.

## The trap that makes evals lie: an optimistic test set
The subtlest and most damaging dataset mistake is a test set drawn from the same narrow distribution as the training set, because it makes your eval scores optimistic and hides the model's real weakness. If your test examples look just like your training examples, a model that merely *memorised* the training distribution scores beautifully, and you ship believing it is great, then it falls apart on the genuinely varied inputs of production. The fix is to build the test set to probe *generalisation*: examples from a different source, different phrasings, edge cases the training set did not contain, so a high score actually means "handles new inputs," not "memorised the old ones." This is your W12 eval discipline applied to fine-tuning, and it is non-negotiable here, because fine-tuning's whole risk is overfitting to your examples, and an honest, distinct test set is the only thing that catches it. A fine-tune you cannot trust the eval on is a fine-tune you cannot trust at all.

## Where this fits
Run a hosted fine-tune end to end: prepare a JSONL dataset with diverse inputs and clean targets, split it so the test set genuinely probes generalisation (not memorisation), train through the provider, and evaluate honestly. You now have a working fine-tuned model and, more importantly, have met the real difficulty, data quality and honest evaluation, rather than the easy mechanics. Hosted training sends your data away and costs more; tomorrow you look at the open-source path that keeps data private, and the efficient methods (LoRA/QLoRA) that make it feasible without a server farm.

items.title: LoRA and QLoRA
items.body:
## Training without rewriting the whole model: LoRA
Full fine-tuning adjusts all of a model's weights, which for a large model means enormous memory and compute, far more than most people have. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is the technique that makes fine-tuning practical: instead of updating every weight, it freezes the original model and trains a small set of additional low-rank "adapter" weights alongside it. You end up with a tiny adapter (megabytes, not gigabytes) that, applied on top of the frozen base, produces the fine-tuned behaviour. The result is nearly the quality of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and cost, which is why LoRA, and not full fine-tuning, is how most open-source fine-tuning is actually done today.

## QLoRA: fine-tuning on hardware you might own
QLoRA pushes LoRA further by quantizing the frozen base model, storing its weights at lower precision (4-bit instead of 16-bit), which slashes the memory needed to hold the model during training. The combination is what brings fine-tuning down to a single consumer or modest cloud GPU: LoRA means you train only small adapters, and quantization means the big frozen model fits in far less memory while you do. The practical effect is dramatic, fine-tuning that would have required a cluster becomes something you can run on one GPU, with a small, manageable quality trade from the quantization that is usually well worth the access it buys. QLoRA is why "fine-tune your own model on your own hardware" went from a big-lab capability to something an individual engineer can do.

## Why the open-source path, and what it costs you
The reason to run LoRA/QLoRA yourself with tools like Axolotl, Unsloth, or HuggingFace TRL, rather than hosted fine-tuning, comes down to control and privacy: your data never leaves your hardware, which matters when the data is sensitive (proprietary, regulated, personal) and you cannot send it to a third party, and you get full control over the training process. The cost of that control is real and is the flip side of hosted's simplicity: you need a GPU, you must select hyperparameters carefully (tomorrow's lesson), and you have to actually understand the training process rather than handing it off. So the choice mirrors the build-versus-buy theme that runs through the whole production phase: hosted fine-tuning is operationally simple, costs more, and sends your data away; open-source LoRA/QLoRA keeps data private and gives control, at the price of needing a GPU and real training expertise. You pick based on data sensitivity and how much training control you need, the same way you chose self-hosted observability in W18.

## Where this fits
Understand LoRA and QLoRA as the techniques that make fine-tuning feasible without a server farm, train small adapters, quantize the frozen base, and keep your data on your own hardware, and weigh the open-source path (private, controllable, GPU-required) against hosted (simple, costly, third-party). You now know both routes to a fine-tuned model and when each fits. Running training yourself means owning the knobs, so tomorrow you learn the handful of hyperparameters that actually decide whether a fine-tune succeeds or fails.

items.title: Hyperparameters that matter
items.body:
## A few knobs decide success; most do not matter
When you run fine-tuning yourself, you face a long list of hyperparameters, and the practical truth is that a small handful do most of the work while the rest rarely need touching. Knowing which few matter saves you from both paralysis (tuning everything) and disaster (ignoring the ones that count). The ones that actually decide whether a fine-tune succeeds are about how much the model changes and how many times it sees your data:
- **Learning rate:** how big a step each update takes. Too high and the model changes violently, overfitting your examples or destabilising (catastrophic forgetting, where it loses general ability); too low and it barely learns your task at all. This is the single most important knob, and the most common cause of a bad fine-tune.
- **Number of epochs:** how many times the model passes over your dataset. Too few and it underfits (has not learned your task); too many and it overfits (memorises your examples and generalises poorly). There is a sweet spot, and it is usually small.
- **LoRA rank (for LoRA/QLoRA):** the size of the adapter, its capacity to learn. Higher rank can capture more but risks overfitting and costs more; lower rank is leaner. Moderate is usually right.
Get these three sensible and you are most of the way; obsessing over the rest is wasted effort.

## The failure you are tuning against is overfitting
Almost every hyperparameter on that list is really a control on the same underlying risk: overfitting, the model learning your specific training examples too well and failing to generalise to new inputs. A learning rate too high, too many epochs, an adapter with too much capacity, all push the model toward memorising rather than learning, and the symptom is the same: great scores on data that looks like training, poor performance on anything genuinely new. This is why D3's honest, distinct test set is not separate from hyperparameter tuning but the very instrument you tune *with*: you watch performance on the held-out, generalisation-probing test set and adjust the knobs to maximise *that*, not the training score. A model that scores 0.98 on training and 0.70 on a distinct test set is overfit, and the fix is in these hyperparameters (lower the learning rate, fewer epochs, smaller rank). Tuning fine-tuning is, in practice, the disciplined search for the settings that learn your task without memorising your data.

## Tune empirically, against your eval
The right way to set these is not to guess clever values but to run small experiments and let your eval decide, the hill-climbing eval discipline from W17 applied to training. Start from the provider's or tool's sensible defaults (they are tuned to be reasonable), change one knob at a time, and measure the effect on your held-out test set, keeping what improves generalisation. This empirical loop matters because the right values depend on your specific dataset and model, there is no universal magic number, only the setting that works for *your* data, found by measuring. It also keeps you honest about diminishing returns: often the defaults are close, a small learning-rate or epoch adjustment gets you the rest, and further tuning buys nothing, so you stop. The skill is the same engineering judgement as everywhere else in the track, change deliberately, measure the effect, keep what the data says is better, rather than turning knobs by superstition.

## Where this fits
Focus your tuning on the few hyperparameters that matter, learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank, understand that they are all really controls on overfitting, and set them empirically against a held-out test set that probes generalisation. You can now run a fine-tune that learns your task without memorising your data, the difference between a model that works in production and one that only looked good on training scores. With the technique in hand, the week closes its judgement arc tomorrow: weighing whether all of this was, for your task, actually worth it.

items.title: Cost-benefit analysis
items.body:
## Fine-tuning has to earn its cost
You now know how to fine-tune; this lesson asks whether you should have, in full accounting. Fine-tuning carries costs that a prompt-based solution does not, and a clear-eyed cost-benefit analysis is what separates fine-tuning as a sound engineering decision from fine-tuning as a resume-driven one. The costs are not just the training run:
- **Dataset cost:** building and cleaning a few hundred-plus quality examples is real, often substantial, human effort, usually the biggest hidden cost.
- **Training cost:** the compute to train (and re-train), whether you pay a provider or run your own GPU.
- **Maintenance cost:** a fine-tuned model is frozen, so when your task shifts or a better base model arrives, you must re-do the work to keep up, an ongoing tax prompting does not charge.
- **Operational cost:** managing, versioning, and serving a custom model is more complex than calling a base model with a prompt.
Against those you weigh the benefits, more consistent behaviour, better task performance, shorter prompts (token savings at scale), and the analysis is whether the benefits, multiplied by your volume, exceed the full cost over the time the model stays valid.

## Where the numbers actually favour fine-tuning
The cost-benefit math has a characteristic shape, and reading it tells you when fine-tuning pays. The big upfront costs (dataset, training) are largely fixed, while the main benefit, cheaper per call via shorter prompts plus better, more reliable output, scales with volume. So fine-tuning pays off at **high volume on a stable task**: a feature serving millions of requests amortises the fixed cost easily and reaps the per-call savings and consistency across all of them, while a low-volume feature can never recover the dataset-and-training investment, the prompt-based version is simply cheaper all-in. Stability matters just as much: a stable task lets a frozen model stay valid long enough to earn out, while a fast-changing task forces repeated retraining that destroys the economics. This is the same volume-and-stability logic as distillation in W19, because they are cousins, both trade upfront specialisation work for ongoing per-call savings, and both only pay when volume is high and the task holds still. When you see high volume plus stability plus a real consistency problem, fine-tuning's numbers work; miss any of the three and they usually do not.

## The honest comparison includes the alternative
A real cost-benefit analysis does not evaluate fine-tuning in isolation, it compares it head-to-head against the best non-fine-tuned solution, because the right question is never "is the fine-tuned model good?" but "is it enough better than prompt-plus-RAG to justify everything it costs?" Often a well-built prompt-and-RAG system gets close enough that the marginal gain from fine-tuning does not justify the dataset, training, and maintenance burden, in which case the senior decision is *not* to fine-tune, even though you could. Your evals are what make this comparison honest: measure the fine-tuned model and the prompt+RAG baseline on the same test set, put real numbers on the quality gap, and weigh that gap against the real cost. Sometimes the numbers clearly favour fine-tuning and you commit with confidence; sometimes they do not and you save yourself a costly commitment, and being able to tell those apart with data, rather than reaching for the fancier tool by default, is exactly the engineering maturity this week is teaching. The aphorism to carry out of the week: fine-tuning is a commitment, not a quick fix, so make it only when the numbers say the commitment pays.

## Where this fits
Do the full cost-benefit analysis for your task: total the dataset, training, maintenance, and operational costs, weigh them against the volume-scaled benefits, and compare honestly against the prompt+RAG baseline on the same eval. You can now make the fine-tune-or-not call as a real engineering decision backed by numbers, which is the whole point of the week. Tomorrow you ship the result, whether that is a fine-tuned model that earned its place or a documented decision that prompting was the right answer after all.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
Either a fine-tuned model that demonstrably beat the prompt-based baseline, or a documented, evidence-backed decision that fine-tuning was not worth it, both are valid, senior deliverables. By tonight you have:
- a clear analysis of whether the task warranted fine-tuning (checked against the "don't" list and the positive case).
- if you fine-tuned: a quality dataset (diverse inputs, clean targets), a train/test split that genuinely probes generalisation, a trained model (hosted, or LoRA/QLoRA on your own hardware with sensibly tuned learning rate, epochs, and rank).
- an honest eval comparing the fine-tuned model against the prompt+RAG baseline on the same held-out test set.
- a cost-benefit analysis accounting for dataset, training, maintenance, and operational costs against volume-scaled benefits.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is a decision defended with numbers, not a model for its own sake. If you fine-tuned, the proof is the head-to-head: "on a held-out test set that probes generalisation, the fine-tuned model hit 0.94 format-consistency versus 0.81 for the best prompt+RAG version, with a shorter prompt, and at our volume the dataset-and-training cost pays back in N weeks." If you decided *not* to fine-tune, the proof is equally rigorous: "prompt+RAG reached 0.90, fine-tuning would have added an estimated few points for a dataset-and-training cost that our volume never amortises, so prompting is the right call." Either way, the thing you are demonstrating is the judgement, a fine-tuning decision made with evals and a cost model, not vibes, which is precisely the skill that is rare and valuable. A defended "no" is as strong as a successful "yes."

## Ship the artifact
Commit the work, the dataset and trained model if you fine-tuned, plus a README that tells the decision as a story: the task and why prompting hit (or did not hit) its ceiling, the dataset and how you ensured an honest test split, the training approach and key hyperparameters, the head-to-head eval against the baseline, and the cost-benefit analysis with its conclusion. That decision narrative is what makes this a standout portfolio piece, because fine-tuning is widely misunderstood, most people either fear it or over-reach for it, so demonstrating that you can fine-tune competently *and* judge when not to, with data behind the call, signals a depth of understanding that pure "I fine-tuned a model" projects do not.

## Where this fits in the track
You have added the most important tool beyond prompting and, more valuably, the judgement to wield it sparingly, fine-tuning when a real consistency or domain problem and the volume-and-stability economics justify it, prompting plus RAG when they do not. That is the Advanced phase doing its job: not piling on techniques, but deepening your judgement about which technique a problem actually needs. Next week you extend your systems past text entirely, into vision and audio, as the modality boundary dissolves and capable models start handling tasks that used to need specialised pipelines. The throughline holds: a powerful tool is only as good as your discipline about when to use it, and you have just practised that discipline on the most over- and under-used tool in the field.

items.body: You fine-tune on 100 examples and your test set score improves from 0.72 to 0.89. You declare success. What is the validity threat to this conclusion? Overfitting to the test set. If your 100 examples and your 20 test examples came from the same source with similar distribution, the model may have memorised the training patterns rather than learning to generalise. weeks.title: Multimodal, Vision, Audio, and Beyond Text
weeks.context:
Language models started as text-in, text-out systems. They are now text-in-anything-out and anything-in-text-out systems. Vision models read images. Audio models transcribe and generate speech. Video models are arriving. The unifying trend is that the modality boundary is dissolving, tasks that required specialised computer vision or speech processing pipelines can now often be handled by a capable multimodal model.

This week you build a meeting assistant. Audio in, structured notes and action items out. You record or use a mocked meeting audio, transcribe it with Whisper, optionally process it with speaker diarization, then extract the structured content with a language model. The end-to-end pipeline demonstrates the architecture that underpins most real-world AI audio processing.

Vision is the more developed multimodal capability. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet both accept images as part of the messages array. The images can be base64-encoded or referenced by URL. Document parsing, chart understanding, screenshot analysis, and form extraction all become possible without specialised OCR or computer vision pipelines. The limitation: each image consumes significant tokens (512-2048 depending on resolution and the model's processing), which affects cost and context window usage.

Audio in/out is the next frontier in production AI applications. Whisper and its distilled variants provide offline transcription. AssemblyAI and Deepgram provide managed transcription APIs with speaker labelling, punctuation, and sentiment. For audio output, OpenAI TTS and ElevenLabs provide high-quality speech synthesis. Cartesia provides real-time, low-latency synthesis suited for conversational applications.

The architecture decisions matter: do you transcribe locally (private but requires GPU or CPU time) or via API (easier but costs money and sends audio to a third party)? Do you diarize (who spoke when) and does the structured output improve when you know the speaker?

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Until now everything you have built has been text in, text out. This week you cross the modality boundary. You build a meeting assistant: audio goes in, structured notes and action items come out. You take meeting audio (recorded or mocked), transcribe it with Whisper, optionally figure out who spoke when, and then hand the transcript to a language model to extract the structured content, decisions, action items, owners. That end-to-end pipeline, raw audio to structured insight, is the architecture under most real-world AI audio processing, and building it teaches the general shape of multimodal systems: convert the non-text modality into something a language model can reason over, then let the language model do what it is best at.

## The modality boundary is dissolving
The big shift to internalise is that language models started as text-in, text-out systems and have become text-in-anything-out and anything-in-text-out systems. Vision models read images; audio models transcribe and generate speech; video understanding is arriving. The unifying trend is that the boundary between modalities is dissolving, and the practical consequence is enormous: tasks that used to require specialised computer-vision or speech-processing pipelines, OCR engines, custom CV models, bespoke audio analysis, can now often be handled by a single capable multimodal model or a simple pipeline around one. Work that was a whole engineering discipline a few years ago is now a few API calls. This week is about learning to wield that, and to judge when a multimodal model is the right tool versus when a specialised pipeline still wins.

## The pattern: convert, then reason
The meeting assistant reveals the architecture that recurs across multimodal work: you rarely ask one model to do everything, you build a pipeline where each stage handles what it is best at. Audio is hard for a language model to reason over directly, so you first **convert** it to text with a transcription model (Whisper), optionally enriching it with **diarization** (labelling who spoke when), and only then do you ask the **language model to reason** over the clean transcript to extract structured notes and action items, which is exactly the structured-output skill from W6 applied to a new input source. This convert-then-reason shape, transform the non-text modality into text (or into the model's native multimodal input), then apply the language reasoning you already know, is the backbone of most production multimodal systems, and seeing it in the meeting assistant lets you build any of them.

## Where this fits
This is the second week of the Advanced phase, extending your reach past text into the modalities real products increasingly demand. It builds squarely on what you have: the extraction step is W6 structured outputs, the pipeline thinking is the same composition you used for agents and RAG, and the cost and architecture judgements are the ones the whole track has trained. It also sets up the harder, real-time and video frontiers later in the week, and the cost awareness that multimodal especially requires (images and audio are token-hungry). Today, get the vision and audio SDKs set up and frame the convert-then-reason architecture; the week builds out each modality, vision, audio, real-time, video, and the cost discipline that keeps multimodal affordable.

items.title: Vision inputs
items.body:
## Images as just another message part
Vision is the most developed multimodal capability, and the most striking thing about using it is how little new there is to learn: capable models like GPT-4o and the current Claude vision models accept images as part of the same `messages` array you already send text in. You add an image to the message, base64-encoded inline or referenced by URL, alongside your text prompt, and the model reasons over both together: "here is a photo of a receipt, extract the line items," "here is a chart, summarise the trend." The image is just another part of the message, so all of your existing skills, structured outputs, prompting, the whole API, carry straight over. Vision is not a separate system you learn; it is your existing model calls with pictures added.

## What vision replaces
The reason vision matters so much is the pile of specialised pipelines it makes unnecessary. Tasks that used to require dedicated OCR engines or custom computer-vision models, document parsing, chart and graph understanding, screenshot analysis, form and table extraction, now often work with a single vision-model call and a good prompt. You can hand the model a scanned invoice and get structured fields back, show it a dashboard screenshot and ask what is wrong, give it a photo of a form and extract the data, all without training a vision model or wiring up OCR. For the meeting assistant this means a photo of a whiteboard or a shared slide can become structured content the same way the audio does. This is the modality boundary dissolving in the most useful possible way: a capability that was a specialist engineering project becomes a prompt, which is why "do I still need a CV pipeline for this?" is now a real and often-no question.

## The catch: images are expensive in tokens
Vision's one significant limitation is cost, and it is a real constraint you design around: each image consumes a significant number of tokens, roughly 512 to 2048 depending on the image's resolution and how the model processes it, which affects both your bill and your context-window budget. An image is not a cheap add-on; it can cost as much as a substantial block of text, and several high-resolution images in one request can eat a large share of the context window before the model has read your prompt. So you design with image-cost in mind: send images at the resolution the task actually needs rather than the maximum (a form does not need 4K), avoid stuffing many images into one call when a few would do, and remember that the W18/W19 cost discipline now has a new and hungry line item. Vision is powerful and easy to use, and precisely because it is so easy to drop an image into a message, the cost discipline matters, because an image-heavy feature can get expensive fast if you are not deliberate about resolution and count.

## Where this fits
Use vision by adding images to the messages array, base64 or URL, and apply your existing structured-output skills to extract data from documents, charts, and screenshots, while respecting that each image is a real token cost you size deliberately. You can now handle the visual modality with the tools you already have, no specialised CV pipeline required. Vision is image-in; tomorrow you build the audio-in half that the meeting assistant is centred on, where the convert-then-reason pipeline really comes into its own.

items.title: Audio in
items.body:
## Audio becomes tractable by becoming text
The meeting assistant's core is audio in, and the key move is that you do not ask a language model to reason over raw audio, you first transcribe it to text, then reason over the text. Transcription is a solved, high-quality capability: **Whisper** (and its faster distilled variants) gives you offline transcription you run yourself, and managed APIs like **AssemblyAI** and **Deepgram** give you transcription as a service with extras built in, speaker labelling, punctuation, even sentiment. Once the audio is a clean transcript, the rest is the text work you already know: hand it to a language model with a structured-output prompt and extract the decisions, action items, and owners. Convert-then-reason: the transcription model turns sound into text, and the language model turns text into structure.

## Diarization: knowing who said what
A meeting is not just words, it is words *by people*, and that is where diarization comes in: labelling who spoke when, so the transcript reads as a conversation ("Alice: let's ship Friday. Bob: I'll own the deploy.") rather than an undifferentiated wall of text. This matters because speaker identity often changes the meaning and the structure you want to extract: an action item belongs to whoever committed to it, a decision matters more when the decision-maker made it, and "I'll handle that" is useless without knowing who "I" is. So a real engineering question for the meeting assistant is whether to diarize, and whether the structured output actually improves when the model knows the speaker. Often it does, owners get attached to action items correctly, but diarization adds cost and complexity, so you test whether it earns its place rather than adding it reflexively, the same measure-don't-assume discipline from the rest of the track.

## The architecture decision: local versus API
Audio forces a concrete build-versus-buy decision that captures the whole week's architecture thinking. Do you transcribe **locally** (Whisper on your own CPU/GPU) or via **API** (AssemblyAI, Deepgram)? The trade is sharp:
- **Local (Whisper):** private, the audio never leaves your machine, and there is no per-minute API cost, but it requires GPU or meaningful CPU time and you manage the processing yourself.
- **API:** far easier, often higher quality with diarization and punctuation included, but it costs money per minute and sends the audio, potentially sensitive meeting recordings, to a third party.
This is the same privacy-versus-convenience axis you met with self-hosted observability and open-source fine-tuning, and it resolves the same way: sensitive audio and high volume push you toward local processing, while convenience and quality push you toward an API, and you choose based on how private the audio is and how much you have. Naming the trade explicitly is what keeps it a deliberate decision rather than a default.

## Where this fits
Build the audio-in pipeline: transcribe with Whisper (or a managed API), optionally diarize to attach speakers, then apply structured-output extraction to produce notes and action items, choosing local-versus-API transcription deliberately on privacy and cost. The meeting assistant's core now works end to end, raw audio to structured insight. So far the pipeline is batch, record then process; tomorrow you look at the harder real-time case, where audio and response have to happen live, with no time to wait.

items.title: Realtime APIs
items.body:
## When the pipeline has to run live
The meeting assistant so far is batch: you have the whole recording, you process it, you get notes. Real-time APIs handle the much harder case where there is no "whole recording", audio streams in and the system must respond *as it happens*: live transcription as someone speaks, a voice assistant that listens and replies in conversation, real-time translation. The defining constraint is latency: in a live, conversational setting, even a second of delay is jarring, because humans expect conversational turn-taking to feel immediate. Batch processing can take its time; real-time cannot, and that single difference, the response must arrive while the interaction is still happening, reshapes the entire architecture.

## Why real-time is a different engineering problem
Real-time multimodal is not just batch done faster; it is a different problem with different tools, and the differences are worth naming:
- **Streaming both ways:** audio streams *in* continuously (you cannot wait for the speaker to finish) and the response streams *out* as it is produced, so the whole pipeline is built around streams, not request-response, the streaming skills from W7 and W20 now load-bearing on both ends.
- **Latency-optimised components:** ordinary TTS that takes a second to start is too slow, so real-time uses low-latency synthesis built for it, **Cartesia**, for example, provides real-time, low-latency speech synthesis suited to conversational applications, where OpenAI TTS and ElevenLabs are excellent for high-quality batch output but not necessarily for instant conversational turns.
- **Purpose-built realtime APIs:** providers offer dedicated realtime endpoints that handle the streaming audio-in, processing, and audio-out loop as one low-latency pipeline, rather than you stitching transcribe-then-think-then-speak stages that would each add delay.
The architecture shifts from "process a file" to "maintain a live, low-latency conversation loop," which is a genuinely harder system to build and reason about.

## The latency budget is brutal, and you spend it carefully
Real-time makes the latency budget from W23's preview unforgiving: the *total* round trip, hear the audio, transcribe it, have the model think, synthesise the reply, must feel instant, and that budget is split across every stage, so each one has to be fast. This forces hard trade-offs you did not face in batch: you may use a faster, slightly less capable model because a smarter-but-slower one breaks the conversational feel; you may start responding before fully processing the input; you choose low-latency synthesis over the highest-fidelity voice. Every component is chosen and tuned for speed because the experience lives or dies on it, where in batch you could afford the slow, high-quality option at every stage. This is the latency-versus-quality trade at its most acute, and it is why real-time is the frontier: it demands the full streaming and latency toolkit working together under a hard, human-perceptible deadline. The judgement is knowing when a feature genuinely needs real-time (live conversation, live captioning) versus when batch is fine (meeting notes after the fact), because real-time's complexity and latency constraints are a steep price you pay only when the interaction must be live.

## Where this fits
Understand real-time multimodal as a distinct architecture, bidirectional streaming, latency-optimised components like Cartesia for synthesis, purpose-built realtime APIs, and a brutal end-to-end latency budget that forces speed-over-quality choices at every stage. You now know both modes, batch (your meeting assistant) and real-time (live conversation), and when each is warranted. The modalities so far have been image and audio; tomorrow you look at the arriving frontier of video, and then close the week on the cost discipline multimodal especially demands.

items.title: Video understanding
items.body:
## Video: the modality still taking shape
Video is the arriving frontier, the modality where capabilities are advancing fast but are less settled than vision or audio. The conceptual key is that video is not a wholly new thing to learn but a *combination* of modalities you already have: a video is a sequence of images (frames) plus an audio track, and most video understanding today is built by decomposing it into exactly those parts you can already handle. So rather than waiting for one model to magically "understand video," you apply the convert-then-reason pattern again, break the video into frames and audio, process each with the vision and audio skills from this week, and let a language model reason over the combined result. Video understanding is, for now, largely an orchestration of vision and audio, which means you are closer to handling it than it first appears.

## How video understanding is built today
The practical architecture follows from that decomposition, and it is the same pipeline thinking the whole week has used:
- **Sample frames** from the video (you rarely need every frame, often a frame every few seconds captures the content) and process them with a **vision** model, what is happening, what is on screen, what changed.
- **Transcribe the audio track** with the **audio** skills from D3, what is being said, by whom.
- **Reason over the combination** with a language model: the visual events plus the spoken content together, extracted into whatever structure you need (a summary, a highlight reel, searchable moments).
The dominant constraint shouts immediately: a video is a *lot* of frames, and each frame is an image with the token cost from D2, so naive "send every frame" is ruinously expensive and slow. The central engineering problem of video is therefore sampling, choosing which frames actually carry information, because processing all of them is rarely affordable or necessary. Smart frame selection, skip near-duplicates, sample more densely where things change, is what makes video understanding tractable.

## Treat the frontier with appropriate caution
The honest framing of video is that it is genuinely useful today *and* still maturing, so you approach it differently from the settled capabilities. The decompose-into-frames-and-audio approach works now and is how most production video features are built, so it is worth knowing. But native end-to-end video models are advancing quickly, which means the best architecture is a moving target, and a heavy system you build around today's frame-sampling approach may be superseded, so you stay lighter and more adaptable here than you would on stable ground. The cost and latency are also at their most extreme, video multiplies the image-cost problem by frame count, making the W19 cost discipline and the D6 multimodal-cost lesson absolutely central, not optional. The mature stance toward an advancing frontier is to use what works now (frame sampling plus audio plus language reasoning), keep the design adaptable because better tools are coming, and respect that video is the most cost- and latency-intensive modality by a wide margin, so you reach for it only when the use case truly needs moving pictures rather than a few key frames or the audio alone.

## Where this fits
Understand video as a composition of the vision and audio modalities you already have, sample frames, transcribe audio, reason over the combination, with frame sampling as the central technique that keeps the enormous cost tractable, and treat it as an advancing frontier you build for adaptably. You have now covered the full modality range, image, audio, real-time, video, all through the same convert-then-reason pattern. Every one of these modalities is more token-hungry than text, so the week closes tomorrow on the cost discipline that multimodal makes essential.

items.title: Think it through
items.body: Cost out a multimodal pipeline (audio in, vision in, text reasoning, audio out) for 1000 users / month. Where's the dominant cost?

items.title: Cost of multimodal
items.body:
## Multimodal is expensive in a way text is not
Across this whole week, one constraint has kept recurring: multimodal inputs are far more token-hungry than text. An image is hundreds to thousands of tokens; audio means transcription cost (per minute, if via API) plus the tokens of the resulting transcript; video multiplies image cost by frame count into the most expensive case by far. So a multimodal feature can cost many times what an equivalent text feature costs, and the gap is large enough that ignoring it turns a sustainable feature into an unaffordable one at scale. This closing lesson makes multimodal cost a first-class design concern, because the very ease of dropping in an image or a video, it is just another message part, hides how much each one actually costs, and that is exactly how multimodal bills get out of control.

## The levers specific to multimodal
The W19 cost toolkit all applies, and multimodal adds its own levers that come straight from understanding where the tokens go:
- **Right-size the resolution:** image token cost scales with resolution, so send images at the resolution the task needs, not the maximum, a form or a chart rarely needs full resolution to be read correctly, and dropping resolution can cut the image's token cost substantially with no quality loss on the task.
- **Sample, don't stream, frames:** for video, the frame-sampling from D5 *is* the primary cost control, processing one informative frame every few seconds instead of all of them is often a 10x-plus saving.
- **Choose local vs API on cost as well as privacy:** local Whisper has no per-minute fee (just your compute), which at high audio volume can dramatically undercut a per-minute transcription API, so volume can flip the D3 decision toward local on cost grounds alone.
- **Convert once, reason many times:** transcribe or caption a piece of media once, then run all your text reasoning over the cheap transcript, never re-process the expensive raw media for each question.
Each lever follows directly from knowing that the expensive part is the media-to-tokens conversion, so you do it minimally and at the right fidelity.

## Cost discipline is what makes multimodal shippable
The larger point is that multimodal does not get a pass on the production discipline you built in W17-20, it needs it *more*, because its costs are higher and easier to incur accidentally. You track multimodal cost in your traces (W18) just like text cost, watching the per-request cost of image- and audio-heavy calls, you set the same cost dashboards and alerts (W19) so a feature that starts sending full-resolution images or over-sampling frames shows up as a spike, and you make the convert-then-reason architecture itself a cost decision, do the expensive media conversion once, cache it, and run cheap text reasoning thereafter. The architecture you have used all week, convert the modality to text, then reason, is not only a capability pattern but a cost pattern: it isolates the expensive step (conversion) so you pay for it once and keep the rest in cheap text. Multimodal features are genuinely powerful and genuinely pricey, and the engineers who ship ones that survive at scale are the ones who treat the cost with the same seriousness as the capability, sizing resolution, sampling frames, choosing local versus API on the numbers, and watching the bill.

## Where this fits
Apply cost discipline to multimodal: right-size image resolution, sample video frames, weigh local-versus-API transcription on cost as well as privacy, convert-once-reason-many, and track multimodal cost in your traces and dashboards like any other production metric. You can now build multimodal features that are affordable as well as capable, which is what makes them shippable rather than just demoable. Tomorrow you assemble the meeting assistant and ship the full multimodal pipeline.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A working meeting assistant: audio in, structured notes and action items out, demonstrating the convert-then-reason pipeline that underpins real multimodal AI. By tonight it:
- takes meeting audio and transcribes it (Whisper locally, or a managed API), with diarization if it improves the result.
- extracts structured content, decisions, action items with owners, by applying structured-output reasoning to the transcript.
- handles the architecture decisions deliberately: local versus API transcription chosen on privacy and cost, diarization included only if it earns its place.
- is cost-aware, sized resolution where vision is involved, convert-once-reason-many, multimodal cost tracked like any other.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is the full pipeline turning raw audio into useful structure. Feed it a real (or realistically mocked) meeting recording and get back clean, correct notes: the decisions that were made, the action items, and who owns each, accurate enough that someone who missed the meeting could act from your assistant's output alone. That, raw audio in, structured and correctly-attributed insight out, end to end, is the entire deliverable, because it proves you can build the convert-then-reason architecture that nearly all production multimodal systems use: transform the non-text modality into something a language model can reason over, then apply the language reasoning you already mastered. If the action items are correctly attributed to speakers, your diarization decision paid off; if the structure is clean, your W6 extraction skills transferred intact to a new input modality.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the meeting assistant with its pipeline, a README explaining the convert-then-reason architecture and the decisions you made (local vs API transcription and why, whether diarization helped, how you controlled cost), and an example run, a sample audio in, the structured notes out. This is a compelling portfolio piece because it is visibly *useful*, everyone has sat in a meeting wishing for exactly this, and because it demonstrates multimodal competence built on solid architecture rather than a flashy one-off: a clean pipeline, deliberate build-versus-buy and privacy choices, and cost awareness. Showing that you can extend AI past text into audio (and the vision and real-time and video understanding around it) signals that you can build the multimodal features real products increasingly demand.

## Where this fits in the track
You have crossed the modality boundary, your AI engineering now reaches past text into vision, audio, real-time, and video, all through the same convert-then-reason pattern, and you understand the cost discipline that multimodal especially requires. That is the Advanced phase widening your range. One advanced week remains before the capstone: W23 takes a production project and makes it measurably faster and meaningfully safer, the hard edges of safety, latency, and adversarial inputs that every real AI product eventually has to face. Then the capstone has you take one project all the way through everything you have learned. The modality boundary dissolving is one of the biggest shifts in the field, and you can now build on the right side of it.

weeks.title: Safety, Latency Engineering, and the Hard Edges
weeks.context:
AI features have a unique failure surface compared to regular software. The inputs are unbounded natural language. The outputs are probabilistic. The system can be manipulated through the very mechanism it uses to function. This week you take a production project and make it measurably faster and meaningfully safer.

Latency engineering starts with measurement. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is the user-perceived latency, how long until something appears on screen. Total completion time matters for throughput but streaming makes TTFT the UX metric that matters. Break your request path into stages: DNS lookup, TLS handshake, server startup, input processing, first token generation, completion. Measure each stage separately. The fix for a DNS latency problem is different from the fix for a slow prompt processing step.

Content moderation is a layer that most AI applications need and most developers add too late. The OpenAI moderation API is free and fast, classify your inputs before sending them to the expensive model. Anthropic's Claude has built-in moderation that you can configure via the system prompt. For domain-specific moderation (finance, healthcare, legal), a custom classifier trained on examples from your domain outperforms generic moderation APIs.

Prompt injection in real products is not a theoretical concern. Users will try to override your system prompt, extract your instructions, or use your AI as a proxy for requests you did not intend. The defence-in-depth approach: wrap user content in delimiters, validate output format, apply content moderation on both input and output, and limit what the model can do (tool use with restricted scope, no access to sensitive data).

The latency-safety tradeoff is real. Adding a moderation check adds 100-300ms per request. Adding output validation adds more. Users notice. The engineering question is not "should we have safety measures" but "how do we implement them with minimal latency impact and maximum coverage."

concept_check.q: You measure that your p95 TTFT is 2.4 seconds. You want to get it below 1 second. You instrument the request path and find: DNS 5ms, TLS 40ms, request serialisation 15ms, server processing 200ms, mode?

concept_check.q: You add content moderation as a synchronous step before the main model call. Your average latency increases by 180ms. Users complain about slowness. How do you redesign the moderation step to reduce l?

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
This week you take a production project, your deployed feature from W20 is the natural choice, and make it two things at once: measurably faster and meaningfully safer. Not "feels snappier" and "probably fine", measurably faster (you will profile the request path and cut a real bottleneck) and meaningfully safer (you will add the moderation, validation, and adversarial defences a public AI feature actually needs). These two goals, latency and safety, are the hard edges of production AI: the unglamorous engineering that separates a feature that survives contact with real users and bad actors from one that is fast in the demo and falls over (or gets abused) in the wild.

## Why AI has a failure surface ordinary software does not
AI features fail in ways regular software does not, and naming why frames the whole week. Three properties make the failure surface unique:
- **The inputs are unbounded natural language.** A traditional form takes constrained input; an AI feature takes anything a human can type, including things you never imagined and things designed to break it. You cannot enumerate the inputs, so you cannot test them all.
- **The outputs are probabilistic.** The same input can produce different outputs, and the model can produce something wrong, unsafe, or off-format without any error firing, so "it worked when I tried it" guarantees little.
- **The system can be manipulated through the very mechanism it uses to function.** The model reads instructions in natural language to do its job, which means an attacker can *also* give it instructions in natural language, the input channel and the attack channel are the same. This is prompt injection, and it has no equivalent in ordinary software.
These three properties are why an AI feature needs safety engineering that a normal web feature does not, and why this week exists.

## Two hard edges, one real tension
The week pursues speed and safety together on purpose, because they are in genuine tension and a good engineer holds both. Every safety layer you add, a moderation check, output validation, costs latency, often 100 to 300 milliseconds each, and users notice slowness. So the question is never the naive "should we have safety measures?", of course you should, but the real engineering question: "how do we get maximum safety coverage with minimum latency impact?" That framing, safety and speed as a trade you optimise rather than a choice you make, is the mindset of the week. You will measure latency precisely enough to know exactly what each safety layer costs, and you will design those layers to be as cheap and as well-placed as possible, so the feature ends up both fast *and* safe, not one at the expense of the other.

## Where this fits
This is the last week of the Advanced phase, and it hardens what the Production AI phase shipped: W20 put a feature live, and W23 makes it fast enough and safe enough to *stay* live in front of real, unpredictable, sometimes hostile users. It draws together threads from across the track, the latency and streaming work from W7/W18/W20, the cost discipline, the structured-output validation from W6, into the specific disciplines of latency engineering and safety. And it is the last skill-building week before the capstone, where you will need exactly this production-hardening to ship something real. Today, frame the two goals and the tension between them; the week measures and fixes latency, then builds the layered safety a public AI feature requires.

items.title: Latency engineering
items.body:
## You cannot speed up what you have not measured
Latency engineering starts with measurement, not optimisation, because the slow part is rarely where you guess. The first move is to break your request path into its distinct stages and time each one separately: DNS lookup, TLS handshake, server startup (cold start), input processing, first-token generation, completion. Each stage is a different problem with a different fix, the cure for a slow DNS lookup has nothing in common with the cure for slow prompt processing, so a single "the request takes 3 seconds" number is useless; you need to know *which* of those three seconds is the problem. This is the W18 observability discipline turned specifically on latency: instrument the path, measure the stages, and let the data point at the bottleneck instead of optimising by superstition.

## The metric that actually matters: time-to-first-token
For a streaming AI feature, the latency metric that matters to users is **time-to-first-token (TTFT)**, how long until *something* appears on screen, not total completion time. This is a crucial reframe. Total completion time matters for throughput and cost, but because you stream (W20), the user's experience of speed is dominated by how quickly the first token arrives: a response that starts in 400ms and streams for 6 seconds *feels* fast, while one that shows nothing for 3 seconds and then dumps everything *feels* slow, even if the second finishes sooner. Streaming makes TTFT the UX metric, so it is the number you optimise for the user-perceived experience, while watching total time for your cost and capacity. Knowing which metric maps to which concern, TTFT for felt speed, completion time for throughput, keeps you optimising the thing the user actually feels rather than a number that looks good but does not change their experience.

## Different stages, different fixes
Once measurement localises the bottleneck, the fix follows from *which* stage is slow, and the value of stage-by-stage profiling is that it routes you to the right one:
- **DNS/TLS/connection slow:** a networking and infrastructure problem, fixed with connection reuse, keep-alive, edge placement, regional deployment closer to users, nothing to do with the model.
- **Cold start slow:** a deployment problem (the W20 platform choice), fixed with warm instances or a platform with faster cold starts, the first-request-after-idle penalty you met in deployment.
- **Input processing slow:** your own pipeline, retrieval, pre-processing, fixed by parallelising or trimming the work before the model call.
- **First-token generation slow:** the model itself, fixed with a faster model on the hot path, a shorter prompt, or prompt caching so the model is not re-reading a huge prefix.
- **Completion slow:** addressed by streaming (so the user does not wait for it) and by not generating more tokens than needed.
The discipline is the same as cost optimisation in W19: measure to find where the time actually goes, apply the fix specific to that stage, re-measure to confirm, rather than guessing and "optimising" a stage that was never the problem.

## Where this fits
Profile your project's request path stage by stage, identify the real bottleneck from the data, optimise for TTFT as the user-perceived metric, and apply the fix specific to the slow stage. Your feature is now measurably faster, and you know *why*, which is the first half of the week. The other half is safety, and it comes with a latency cost you now have the tools to measure precisely, so tomorrow you start adding protection while watching exactly what each layer costs.

items.title: Content moderation
items.body:
## The cheap safety layer most people add too late
Content moderation is a layer most AI applications need and most developers bolt on far too late, after an incident rather than before. The idea is simple: classify inputs (and outputs) for harmful or disallowed content *before* they reach, or after they leave, the expensive model, and block or handle the bad ones. The good news is that the basic layer is nearly free: the **OpenAI moderation API is free and fast**, so you can classify every input before sending it to your main model at negligible cost and latency, and Anthropic's Claude has built-in moderation you can configure via the system prompt. There is little excuse to skip it, and the reason to add it early is that the cost of *not* having it, a harmful input reaching your model, a harmful output reaching a user, is far higher than the tiny cost of the check.

## Where generic moderation ends and custom begins
Generic moderation APIs catch broadly harmful content, violence, hate, self-harm, the universal categories, and for most applications that baseline is the right and sufficient first layer. But moderation is domain-specific at the edges, and this is where judgement comes in: a finance app needs to catch things a generic moderator does not (market manipulation, fraudulent requests), a healthcare app has its own line, a legal app another. For these, **a custom classifier trained on examples from your domain outperforms generic moderation APIs**, because it knows what "harmful" means in *your* context, which a general-purpose model cannot. So the pattern is layered: the free generic moderation as the always-on baseline, plus a domain-specific classifier where your application has risks the generic layer misses. You start with the cheap universal layer because it is free and catches the obvious, and you add custom moderation only where your domain genuinely needs it, the same don't-over-engineer judgement applied to safety.

## Moderation on both ends, and the latency it costs
Two refinements make moderation real. First, you moderate **both input and output**: input moderation stops a harmful request before it costs you a model call and before it can manipulate the model, and output moderation catches the cases where the model produces something harmful anyway (remember outputs are probabilistic, so a clean input can still yield a bad output). Defence on both ends, because either can be the failure point. Second, moderation has a latency cost you now measure precisely: each check adds time, the generic API is fast but not free of latency, and a custom classifier or an output check adds more. This is the week's central tension made concrete, every safety layer costs milliseconds, so you place them deliberately: the free, fast input check is almost always worth it; heavier checks you weigh against their latency, run in parallel with other work where possible, and apply where the risk justifies the delay. The engineering is maximum coverage for minimum latency, which means cheap-and-broad first, expensive-and-targeted only where needed.

## Where this fits
Add content moderation to your project: free generic moderation on inputs as the baseline, output moderation for the probabilistic failures, and a domain-specific classifier where your application has risks the generic layer misses, measuring the latency each layer costs. Your feature now refuses obviously harmful content coming in and going out. Moderation handles harmful *content*; the next threat is structural, an attacker manipulating the model through the input channel itself, which moderation alone does not stop, so tomorrow you handle output sanitisation and then prompt injection.

items.title: Output sanitisation
items.body:
## Probabilistic output is untrusted output
The model's output is probabilistic, which means you can never fully trust its shape or content, and output sanitisation is the discipline of treating model output as untrusted until you have checked it, exactly as you would treat user input. The model might return malformed JSON when you needed valid JSON, include content that should have been filtered, produce a format your downstream code cannot handle, or, most dangerously, emit output that becomes harmful when something else *executes* it. So before model output flows into the rest of your system, into your UI, your database, another tool, you validate and sanitise it, because "the model usually returns what I asked for" is not a guarantee you can build a reliable or safe system on.

## The two jobs: validate the format, neutralise the danger
Output sanitisation does two distinct things, and both matter:
- **Validate the format.** When you expect structured output, you check it actually conforms, valid JSON, the required fields present, values in range, the W6 structured-output skill now used as a safety gate, and you handle the failure (retry, fall back, error cleanly) rather than letting malformed output crash a downstream step. This catches the probabilistic format failures that "it worked in testing" misses.
- **Neutralise dangerous content.** This is the security half, and it is critical wherever model output gets *used* by another system. Model output rendered into a web page can carry a cross-site-scripting payload; model output used to build a database query or a shell command can carry an injection; model output passed to a tool can carry instructions. So you escape, encode, or strip output according to where it is going, treating it with the same suspicion as any untrusted data, because in security terms that is exactly what it is.
The unifying principle is that the boundary between the model and the rest of your system is a trust boundary, and output crossing it gets validated and sanitised, never passed through blindly.

## Why this is a security issue, not just a quality one
The reason output sanitisation belongs in a safety week and not just a "handle errors" lesson is that unsanitised model output is a genuine attack vector, especially in combination with the prompt injection you will study tomorrow. Consider the chain: an attacker injects a prompt that makes your model emit a malicious script, and your app renders that output straight into a page, now the attacker has run code in your users' browsers, using your model as the delivery mechanism. The model became a weapon precisely because its output was trusted and executed without sanitisation. This is why output handling is defence-in-depth: even if moderation misses something and even if an injection succeeds in steering the model, sanitising the output before it is rendered or executed can stop the harm from landing. You assume the layers before this one might fail, and you make the output boundary a place where danger is caught regardless, which is the layered-defence mindset that the next lesson, on adversarial inputs, makes central. Treating model output as untrusted is not paranoia; it is the recognition that a probabilistic system fronted by unbounded input will eventually produce something you did not want, and the only safe assumption is that it will.

## Where this fits
Add output sanitisation: validate that structured output conforms and handle the failures, and escape or neutralise output according to where it flows (page, query, tool) so model output cannot become an execution vector. Your feature now treats the model-to-system boundary as the trust boundary it is. You have defended content (moderation) and output (sanitisation); the remaining threat is the attacker actively trying to subvert the model through its own instruction channel, prompt injection, which the next lesson confronts directly.

items.title: Adversarial inputs
items.body:
## Prompt injection is real, not theoretical
In a real product, users *will* try to subvert your AI: override your system prompt ("ignore your instructions and..."), extract your hidden instructions to see how you work, or use your AI as a free proxy for requests you never intended it to serve. This is prompt injection, and the lesson opens by insisting it is not a theoretical concern but something that happens to deployed AI features as a matter of course, the moment they are public, people probe them. It is the unique-to-AI attack from D1: because the model functions by following natural-language instructions, an attacker who can put natural language into the model's context can *also* give it instructions, and the model has no built-in way to tell your instructions from theirs. There is no single patch that closes it, so you defend in depth.

## Defence in depth, because there is no silver bullet
The defining feature of prompt-injection defence is that no single measure stops it, so you layer several, each catching what others miss:
- **Wrap user content in delimiters.** Clearly mark where user input begins and ends in the prompt, and instruct the model to treat everything inside as data to be processed, not instructions to be obeyed. This does not fully solve injection, but it raises the bar and helps the model distinguish your instructions from the user's content.
- **Apply moderation on both input and output.** D3's layer catches some injection attempts coming in and some harmful results going out, one reason it runs on both ends.
- **Validate output format.** D4's sanitisation catches when an injection succeeded in making the model produce something unexpected or dangerous, stopping the harm even when the steering worked.
- **Limit what the model can do.** The most important and most reliable defence: restrict the model's actual capabilities so that *even a fully successful injection* cannot cause serious harm, tools with tightly restricted scope, no access to sensitive data, least privilege from W15 applied as a safety control.
Each layer is imperfect alone; together they make a successful, *harmful* injection much harder, which is the whole philosophy of defence in depth.

## The decisive principle: limit the blast radius
Among those layers, one is the most important and worth stating as the core principle: assume the injection might succeed, and make sure that success cannot hurt you. You cannot perfectly prevent a model from being steered by clever input, the attack surface is unbounded natural language, so the robust strategy is to limit the blast radius, constrain what the model is *able* to do so that the worst-case outcome of a successful injection is acceptable. If the model has no tool that can delete data, an injection that says "delete everything" does nothing; if it has no access to other users' records, an injection cannot exfiltrate them; if its tools are scoped to read-only and low-stakes actions, the damage ceiling is low no matter what an attacker convinces it to attempt. This is exactly the least-privilege design from MCP (W15) reframed as injection defence: the model's *capabilities*, not its *compliance*, are what you control, because you can enforce capabilities absolutely and you cannot enforce compliance at all. An attacker can talk the model into wanting to do anything; they cannot give it a power you never granted. So you design assuming the prompt defences will sometimes fail, and you make that failure survivable by ensuring the model simply cannot reach anything catastrophic.

## Where this fits
Defend against prompt injection in depth: delimit user content, moderate input and output, validate output, and, most importantly, restrict the model's capabilities so a successful injection has a small blast radius, the least-privilege principle from W15 as your strongest safety control. Your feature is now hardened against the AI-specific attack that every public AI product faces. Defences sometimes fail despite all this, so the last safety lesson is about what you do when something gets through: knowing it happened, and responding, through audit logs and incident response.

items.title: Audit logs and incident response
items.body:
## Assume something will get through
You have layered moderation, sanitisation, and injection defences, and they will still, eventually, fail, because the input surface is unbounded and attackers are creative. The mature stance is not to assume your defences are perfect but to assume something will eventually get past them and to be *ready*: to know when it happened and to be able to respond. Audit logs and incident response are that readiness layer. Audit logs record what the system did, who asked what, what the model returned, which tools it called, what was flagged, so that when something goes wrong you can reconstruct it, and incident response is the plan for what you actually do when an audit log (or a user, or an alert) reveals a problem. This is the safety equivalent of the W18 observability and W20 on-call disciplines: you cannot respond to what you cannot see, and you cannot respond well without a plan.

## What to log, and the privacy tension
Audit logs for an AI feature record the security-relevant trail: the inputs (especially flagged or suspicious ones), the outputs, the tool calls the model made, the moderation decisions, enough to answer, after an incident, "what did the attacker send, what did the model do, what did it touch, and how far did it get?" Without that trail, an incident is a mystery you cannot investigate or learn from; with it, you can see exactly what happened and close the gap. But this collides directly with the W18 privacy lesson: audit logs, by recording inputs and outputs, contain user data, possibly sensitive, so you face the same tension and resolve it the same way, log what you genuinely need for security and accountability, redact PII where you can, set retention limits, and control access to the logs, because an audit log that becomes a sensitive-data trove is its own liability. The discipline is to capture enough to investigate incidents without turning the safety log into a privacy problem, the same balanced judgement, security visibility versus data exposure, that observability required.

## Incident response: the plan you make before you need it
The other half is having a plan *before* an incident, because the middle of one is the worst time to invent it. Incident response for an AI feature answers, in advance: how do we detect that something bad happened (alerts on spikes in flagged content, anomalous tool use, user reports)? Who responds and how are they reached (the on-call from W20)? How do we contain it quickly, can we disable the affected capability, block an abuser, roll back a bad change, without taking the whole product down? And, crucially, how do we *learn* from it, the blameless retrospective that turns an incident into a fix so the same gap does not reopen, the same post-mortem discipline that closes the capstone next week. This readiness is what separates a team that handles a security event in an hour from one that is still scrambling a day later, and it embodies the week's underlying truth: safety is not a state you reach and hold but a posture you maintain, layered defences to prevent harm, plus logging and a response plan for when prevention inevitably falls short. You build the defences hoping they hold and the response plan knowing they sometimes will not.

## Where this fits
Add audit logging and an incident-response plan to your project: a security trail of inputs, outputs, and tool calls (redacted and retention-limited like your observability), detection and alerting, a fast containment path, and a blameless retrospective process, so that when a defence fails you know and can respond. Your feature is now not just defended but *operable under attack*, which is the final piece of production safety. Tomorrow you assemble the faster, safer project and ship it as the week's, and the Advanced phase's, deliverable.
