items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A production project made measurably faster and meaningfully safer, hardened for the real world. By tonight it has:
- a profiled request path with a real bottleneck fixed, optimised for time-to-first-token as the user-perceived metric, with each stage measured.
- content moderation on input and output (free generic baseline, plus domain-specific where needed).
- output sanitisation treating model output as untrusted, format validated, dangerous content neutralised before it is rendered or executed.
- defence-in-depth against prompt injection, delimited input, moderation, output validation, and above all restricted model capabilities so a successful injection has a small blast radius.
- audit logging and an incident-response plan for when a defence fails.

## The test that proves it
The deliverable is proof on both axes, with the trade between them made explicit. On speed: before-and-after numbers from your profiling, "TTFT dropped from 1.9s to 0.6s by fixing the cold-start and prompt-caching the system prefix," a measured improvement, not a vibe. On safety: try to break your own feature and show it holds, feed it a prompt-injection attempt and watch it refuse or contain it, send harmful content and watch moderation block it, and confirm that even a steering attempt that gets through cannot reach anything dangerous because the model's capabilities are restricted. The most senior part of the proof is quantifying the tension: "the safety layers add 180ms total; here is how I kept that minimal by running moderation in parallel and using the free fast checks on the hot path." Showing a feature that is *both* faster and safer, with the cost of safety measured rather than hand-waved, is the deliverable, because it demonstrates you can engineer the hard edges instead of choosing between speed and safety.

## Ship the artifact
Commit the hardened project with its latency profiling, moderation, sanitisation, injection defences, and audit/incident setup, plus a README that documents both: the latency analysis with before-and-after TTFT and which stage you fixed, and the safety architecture as defence-in-depth with the latency cost of each layer and how you minimised it. Include your own break-it attempts and how the system held. This is a portfolio piece that signals genuine production maturity, because latency and safety are exactly the unglamorous hard edges that separate engineers who can build an AI demo from those who can run an AI product in front of real, unpredictable, sometimes hostile users. Demonstrating that you measure latency to the stage, defend in depth, and limit the blast radius shows the security and performance thinking that most AI portfolios completely lack.

## Where this fits in the track
This completes the Advanced phase, and with it all the skill-building of the track. You can now build AI systems (building, RAG, agents), run them in production (evals, observability, cost, deployment), and extend and harden them (fine-tuning, multimodal, and now safety and latency, the hard edges). That is the full range of an AI engineer, capability plus production maturity plus the judgement that ties them together. Everything now points at the capstone: next week you take one real product all the way through everything you have learned, scoped tightly, researched with real users, built, evaluated, observed, cost-modelled, deployed, and hardened, and ship it as the proof of the whole journey. You have built the skills; the capstone is where you show you can put them together to make something real.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You measure that your p95 TTFT is 2.4 seconds. You want to get it below 1 second. You instrument the request path and find: DNS 5ms, TLS 40ms, request serialisation 15ms, server processing 200ms, model queue time 1800ms, first token 340ms. Where do you focus? The bottleneck is model queue time: 1800ms waiting before the model starts processing. This is a provider-side issue during peak load. Solutions: switch to a provider or model with lower queue time at your usage tier, implement request scheduling to avoid peak hours for batch operations, or add a cheap fast cache to serve common queries without queuing for the model. The first token generation (340ms) is the model's actual processing time and is much harder to reduce.

weeks.title: Capstone, Ship Something Real, End to End
weeks.context:
Twenty-three weeks of skill building leads here: building one real AI product, end to end, and shipping it. Not a demo. Not a tutorial follow-along. A product that solves a specific problem for a specific user, with a public URL, an eval suite, observability, and a cost model that makes sense.

The scoping decision is the hardest part of a capstone. The instinct is to build something impressive, multi-agent, multimodal, RAG plus fine-tuning plus streaming. The correct instinct is to build something that solves one problem well. A translator with domain-specific fine-tuning and excellent evals is a better portfolio piece than a sprawling agent system that half-works. Ruthless scope reduction is a senior engineering skill.

User research before code means talking to three people who would realistically use the product you are imagining, before you write a line of code. What problem do they actually have? Is the problem you are solving the one they care about? What would they be willing to use, even if it is rough? This is not optional for a capstone, it is the step that determines whether you build something real or something imaginary.

Defining success metrics before starting means you have a standard against which to evaluate your capstone when it is done. "Good" is not a metric. "85% answer faithfulness on my golden eval set, under 1.5 seconds TTFT on median queries, positive user feedback from 5 test users" is a metric. If you cannot define what success looks like before you start, you will never know if you succeeded.

The capstone deliverables are concrete: a working app at a public URL, a README that a stranger can follow to understand the product, an eval report showing quality metrics, a cost breakdown showing the cost per user, and a retrospective document that honestly assesses what worked and what did not.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## What you're building this week
Twenty-three weeks of skill-building lead here: one real AI product, built end to end and shipped. Not a demo, not a tutorial follow-along, a product that solves a specific problem for a specific person, with a public URL, an eval suite, observability, and a cost model that makes sense. This is where everything converges, the building skills, the RAG, the agents, the evals, the observability, the cost discipline, the deployment, the safety, applied together to make one thing that actually works and that someone other than you would actually use. The capstone is not a new lesson; it is the proof that you can put the whole track together to ship something real, which is the entire point of having learned it.

## The hardest part is scope, not code
The instinct walking into a capstone is to build something *impressive*, multi-agent and multimodal and RAG plus fine-tuning plus streaming, everything you learned, all at once. That instinct is wrong, and resisting it is the single most important thing this week teaches. The correct instinct is to build something that solves *one problem well*: a translator with domain-specific tuning and excellent evals is a far better portfolio piece than a sprawling agent system that half-works, because a thing that does one job reliably demonstrates engineering, and a thing that does five jobs badly demonstrates the opposite. Ruthless scope reduction is itself a senior engineering skill, arguably *the* senior skill, and the capstone is partly a test of whether you have it. The whole week is built to enforce it: pick small, validate with real users, define done, build the slice, ship it working.

## Ship something real means real on every axis
"Real" is concrete and the capstone makes it measurable. A real product here means all of these, not some: a working app at a **public URL** anyone can use; a **README** a stranger can follow to understand and run it; an **eval report** showing actual quality metrics on a real test set; a **cost breakdown** showing cost per user that makes business sense; and an honest **retrospective** assessing what worked and what did not. Each of those is a discipline from the track, deployment (W20), the documentation and clarity of thought a good README forces, evaluation (W12/W17), cost (W19), and the reflective practice that turns a project into learning. A capstone that is missing any of them is missing a part of what it means to ship professionally, so the deliverables are not a checklist bolted on, they are the definition of "real" expressed as artifacts.

## Where this fits
This is the capstone, the culmination of the entire track and the bridge from "I learned AI engineering" to "I shipped an AI product." It uses everything: the convergence is the point. It is structured as a real product cycle, scope, user research, design, build, ship, reflect, because that cycle, not any single technique, is what professional engineering actually is, and doing it once end to end is what makes you able to do it again. Today, orient and internalise the one rule that governs the whole week: build something small that works completely, not something large that works partially. The rest of the week is the disciplined process that gets you there.

items.title: Picking a project you can ship in 7-10 days
items.body:
## The scoping decision determines everything
The hardest and most consequential decision of the capstone happens before you write any code: choosing a project you can actually ship, completely, in seven to ten days. Get this right and the week is hard but achievable; get it wrong, pick something too big, and you will reach Sunday with an impressive half-built thing that does not work, which is worth far less than a small thing that does. Scoping is the decision the whole week's success rests on, and it runs against every instinct, because ambition pulls toward "more" and good engineering pulls toward "enough." This lesson is about developing the judgement to pick a scope that fits the time, which is the same judgement you will use sizing every real project for the rest of your career.

## Ruthless scope reduction is the senior skill
The reframe that makes scoping possible is to treat *cutting* scope as the skill, not a compromise. Junior engineers measure a project by how much it does; senior engineers measure it by whether it does its one thing reliably and shipped. A translator that does domain-specific translation with excellent evals beats a sprawling agent system that half-works, every time, as a product and as a portfolio piece, because the first proves you can finish and the second proves you cannot. So you practise ruthless reduction: take your project idea and strip it to the single core thing it must do to be valuable, then cut everything else, the nice-to-haves, the second feature, the impressive-but-inessential, until what remains is small enough to build completely in the time you have. This is genuinely hard, it feels like giving up on the vision, but a small complete product *is* the vision delivered, and a big incomplete one is the vision failed. The mark of the skill is being a little uncomfortable with how small your scope is, that discomfort usually means it is right.

## Fit the scope to the time, with a margin
Practically, you scope by working backwards from seven to ten days and being honest about how long things actually take. Define the smallest version that genuinely solves the problem, the minimum that a real user would find useful, and check it fits the time with room to spare, because shipping (deployment, the README, the eval, fixing what breaks) always takes longer than building, and the last 20% takes the most time. Leave margin: a scope that *just barely* fits if everything goes perfectly does not fit, because nothing goes perfectly. It is far better to scope small, finish with time to polish and evaluate and write up, and have a complete working product, than to scope ambitiously and be debugging a broken core on the final day. Pick the project you are confident you can finish *and* make good, not the one you could finish if you got lucky, because a shipped small thing demonstrates everything the capstone is meant to demonstrate, and an unshipped big thing demonstrates none of it.

## Where this fits
Make the scoping decision: pick a project, reduce it ruthlessly to the one core thing that makes it valuable, and confirm that minimal version fits seven to ten days with margin to spare. This decision, more than any technical choice, determines whether your capstone succeeds, which is why it comes first. But "valuable" assumes you know what a user actually needs, and the surest way to scope the wrong thing is to imagine the user instead of asking them, so tomorrow, before any code, you talk to real people.

items.title: User research before code
items.body:
## Talk to three real people before you write a line
Before you write any code, you talk to three people who would realistically use the product you are imagining. Not three friends who will be nice about it, three people who actually have the problem you think you are solving. This is not optional padding for the capstone; it is the step that determines whether you build something *real* or something *imaginary*, and it is the difference between a product and a project. The reason it comes before code is brutal and simple: code written to solve a problem nobody has is wasted no matter how good the code is, and the only way to know whether the problem is real is to ask the people who would have it. An hour of conversation before you build can save a week of building the wrong thing.

## The questions that separate real from imaginary
The conversations have a purpose, to validate (or kill) your assumptions, so you ask questions that can actually disconfirm your idea:
- **What problem do they actually have?** Not whether they like your solution, what genuinely frustrates them in this area. You are listening for the real pain, which is often adjacent to, or different from, the one you assumed.
- **Is the problem you are solving the one they care about?** You may have a clever solution to a problem that ranks tenth on their list. If it is not a problem they actually feel, the cleverest solution finds no users.
- **What would they actually use, even if it is rough?** This reveals the true minimum, the smallest thing that would earn real usage, which is exactly the scope you are trying to find. People will tell you what they would put up with, and that is your MVP.
The goal is to come out knowing whether your imagined product addresses a real, felt, cared-about problem, and what the smallest version that earns use looks like, before you have spent any building time discovering it the expensive way.

## User research feeds the scope, and the honesty it requires
User research and yesterday's scoping are a loop: the conversations tell you what the core valuable thing actually is, which is what you ruthlessly scope *toward*, so doing the research first means you cut toward the real need rather than your guess at it. It also frequently reshapes the idea, the problem people actually care about is often narrower, or different, than the one you walked in with, and discovering that *now*, before code, is a gift, not a setback. The discipline this demands is intellectual honesty: you have to be willing to hear that your idea is not quite right and to change it, which is hard when you are attached to a vision. But a capstone built on a validated real need, even a humbler one than you imagined, is worth infinitely more than a polished solution to a problem you invented at your desk. This is the same measure-don't-assume principle that runs through the whole track, evals over vibes, traces over guesses, applied at the very start to the most important question of all: are you building something anyone wants? Asking real users is how you replace your assumption with evidence before it is expensive to be wrong.

## Where this fits
Do user research before code: talk to three real potential users, find out what problem they actually have, whether it is the one you are solving, and what they would use even rough, then let that reshape your idea and sharpen your scope toward the validated need. You now know you are building something real, the foundation everything else rests on. With a validated problem and a tight scope, tomorrow you turn that clarity into a concrete plan in the most clarifying way possible, by writing the README before the code.

items.title: Writing the README first
items.body:
## Write the README first
Before you build, you write the README, the documentation of the finished product, as if it already exists. What it does, who it is for, how to use it, what problem it solves, what it does not do. This feels backwards, documentation is supposed to come last, but writing it first is one of the most clarifying tools in engineering, because to write a clear README you have to *think clearly* about exactly what you are building, and any vagueness or confusion in your plan shows up immediately as a README you cannot write. README-first is forcing-function design: it makes you specify the product concretely, in plain language, before you have spent a single hour building the wrong version of it.

## Why writing it first clarifies the build
The power of README-first comes from what it exposes. When you try to describe the product to a stranger and find yourself unable to explain in one sentence what it does or who it is for, you have just discovered that your idea is not yet clear enough to build, far cheaper to discover in a paragraph than in a week of code. When listing the features makes the scope feel too big to write up cleanly, that is your scoping (D2) telling you to cut more. When you cannot describe how a user would use it step by step, you have found a hole in your design before it became a hole in your code. The README becomes a specification and a scope contract in one: it pins down precisely what you are committing to build, and, just as importantly, what you are *not* (the "what it does not do" section is where ruthless scope reduction gets written down and made real). You build *to* the README, so the clearer it is, the straighter the build.

## A README a stranger can follow
The standard to write to is concrete: a README a stranger can follow to understand the product and run it, which is also exactly one of the capstone's required deliverables, so writing it first means the deliverable is done early and *guides* the build rather than being scrambled together at the end. Writing for a stranger forces the right discipline, you cannot lean on context only you have, so you must state plainly what the thing is, the problem it solves, who it is for, how to set it up and use it, which is precisely the clarity that makes the product itself coherent. And because you wrote it before building, you get to *build to spec*: when you are deep in implementation and tempted to add a feature or wander from the plan, the README is the agreement you made with yourself about what this product is, keeping you scoped and on-target through the messy middle of the build. A capstone guided by a clear README written first tends to come out focused and complete; one where the README is an afterthought tends to sprawl, because nothing was holding the scope.

## Where this fits
Write the README first: describe the finished product clearly enough that a stranger could understand and run it, use the act of writing it to expose any vagueness in your plan, and let it serve as both your specification and your scope contract through the build. You now have a concrete, written target, and one capstone deliverable already in hand. The README says *what* you are building; tomorrow you sketch *how*, the architecture, on paper, before committing it to code.

items.title: Architecture diagram on paper
items.body:
## Design the architecture on paper first
With the README defining what you are building, you sketch *how* before you build it: the architecture, on paper (or a whiteboard, or a simple diagram), not in code. The components, how data flows between them, where the model calls happen, where retrieval or tools or storage sit, what talks to what. The "on paper" part is deliberate and matters: drawing the architecture is fast and cheap to change, where discovering an architectural problem after you have built it is slow and expensive to fix. A few minutes with a pen can surface a design flaw that would cost you two days of rework if you only found it mid-build, which is the entire economic case for designing before coding.

## Why a diagram catches what code hides
Sketching the architecture forces you to see the whole system at once, and that wide view catches problems that are invisible when you are heads-down in one file. Drawing the data flow reveals the bottleneck (everything routes through one slow step), the expensive path (this user action triggers four model calls), the fragile dependency (the whole thing breaks if this external API is down), and the over-complication (you drew five components where two would do), all *before* you have written code that bakes those problems in. It also right-sizes your design against your scope: if the diagram is sprawling and complex for a seven-day capstone, that is a signal to simplify the architecture or cut scope further, the diagram makes over-engineering visible as a tangle of boxes. And it connects every component to a decision you can now make deliberately, which model goes here, do I need a vector DB or is this small enough for in-memory, is this synchronous or does it need the async job pattern from W20, so you make the architectural calls thoughtfully on paper rather than by accident in code. The diagram is cheap thinking that prevents expensive building.

## A simple architecture is the goal, not a limitation
The most valuable thing the paper diagram usually tells you is to make the architecture *simpler*, and you should listen, because for a capstone, a clean simple architecture that you can build completely and that works reliably beats a sophisticated one that you cannot finish or cannot debug. The whole track has pushed this judgement, the right number of agents is often one (W16), the right answer is often prompt+RAG not fine-tuning (W21), the simplest thing that solves the problem wins, and the capstone is where you apply it to your own system end to end. So as you sketch, actively prefer the simpler design: fewer components, fewer model calls, fewer moving parts, as long as it still solves the validated problem from your user research. A simple architecture is not a lesser capstone, it is a sign you understood the problem well enough to solve it without excess, which is exactly the senior judgement the capstone is meant to show. Complexity you can justify from the requirements is fine; complexity for its own sake is the thing the paper diagram is there to catch and cut.

## Where this fits
Sketch your architecture on paper before coding: lay out the components and data flow, use the wide view to catch bottlenecks, expense, fragility, and over-complication early, right-size the design against your scope, and actively prefer the simplest architecture that solves the validated problem. You now have a clear what (the README) and a clear, simple how (the diagram), which is everything you need to build with confidence. You will build over the coming days; before you ship, one practice ensures the capstone produces *learning* and not just a product, the post-mortem, which you set up next.

items.title: The post-mortem
items.body:
## The post-mortem turns a project into learning
The capstone produces a product, but its more durable output is what you *learn* from building it, and the post-mortem (retrospective) is the practice that captures that learning instead of letting it evaporate. It is an honest written assessment, after the build, of what worked and what did not: where your estimates were wrong, what broke and why, which decisions you would make differently, what you would tell yourself at the start. It is a required capstone deliverable precisely because reflection is what converts experience into skill, ship a product and move on and you have a product; ship it and reflect honestly and you have a product *and* a clearly better engineer for the next one. The post-mortem is how a single capstone keeps paying off long after it ships.

## Honesty is the whole value
A post-mortem is only worth writing if it is honest, and honesty about your own work is genuinely hard, which is exactly why it is valuable and why most people do it badly. A retrospective that says "it went well, I learned a lot" is worthless; one that says "I underestimated the eval work by three days, my first architecture had a bottleneck I had to rip out on day five, and the user research showed my original idea was solving the wrong problem" is gold, because each honest admission is a specific, transferable lesson you carry into every future project. The discipline is the *blameless* honesty from W23's incident response, turned inward: you are not beating yourself up, you are examining what happened clearly so you can do better, treating your own mistakes as data rather than as failures to hide. The willingness to write down "here is what I got wrong and what I now understand because of it" is a hallmark of engineers who keep improving, and its absence is a hallmark of those who plateau, the same mistakes, unexamined, repeated.

## Reflection is a professional discipline, and a portfolio signal
Beyond your own growth, the post-mortem signals something to anyone reviewing your capstone, which makes it disproportionately valuable as a portfolio artifact. A polished product with a thoughtful, honest retrospective demonstrates self-awareness and engineering maturity that the product alone cannot: it shows you can assess your own work critically, that you understand *why* your decisions worked or did not, and that you learn deliberately rather than by accident, exactly the qualities that distinguish an engineer who will keep growing from one who has hit their ceiling. Anyone can show you something that works; showing that you understand its weaknesses, what you would change, and what the building taught you is a rarer and stronger signal. So you set up the post-mortem now, before the final build days, noting decisions and surprises as they happen while they are fresh, so that when you write it after shipping it is grounded in what actually occurred rather than a vague reconstruction. The habit of reflecting honestly on your work is one of the most valuable things to carry out of the entire track, because it is the engine that keeps every future project making you better.

## Where this fits
Set up your post-mortem: commit to an honest written retrospective of what worked and what did not, capture decisions and surprises as they happen so it is grounded in reality, and treat blameless self-honesty as the source of its value, for your own growth and as a maturity signal in your portfolio. With scope set, users consulted, README and architecture drawn, and reflection ready to capture the lessons, everything is in place. Tomorrow you ship, the product and all its deliverables, and complete the capstone and the track.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## What you ship this week
A real AI product, built end to end and shipped, with every deliverable that makes it real. By the end you have:
- a working app at a **public URL** that a stranger can use, solving one validated problem well (ruthlessly scoped, grounded in real user research).
- a **README** (written first) that a stranger can follow to understand and run it.
- an **eval report** showing real quality metrics on a real test set (W12/W17), and **observability** so you can see what it does in production (W18).
- a **cost breakdown** showing a sensible cost per user (W19), and the deployment, auth, and safety hardening to run it for real (W20/W23).
- an honest **post-mortem** assessing what worked and what did not.

## The test that proves it: define success before you start
The capstone's defining discipline is that you define what success looks like *before* you start, because "good" is not a metric and a goal you cannot measure is one you can never know you hit. Vague "make it good" becomes concrete and checkable: "85% answer faithfulness on my golden eval set, under 1.5 seconds TTFT on median queries, and positive feedback from 5 test users." Those are the standards you set at the start and measure against at the end, and the proof of your capstone is meeting the ones you defined, the eval report hits the quality bar you set, the latency meets the TTFT target you named, the test users you researched with confirm it solves their problem. The deliverable is not "a thing exists" but "a thing meets the specific, measurable success criteria I committed to before building it," which is exactly how professional work is judged: against a defined bar, with evidence, not against a feeling. If you defined success up front, you will know precisely whether you succeeded, and you can show anyone the numbers that prove it.

## Ship the artifact, and what it represents
Ship all of it, the live URL, the repo, the README, the eval report, the cost breakdown, the post-mortem, as one coherent capstone, a complete, real, measured AI product. This is the single strongest thing you can put in front of an employer or a collaborator, because it is end-to-end proof: not that you can follow a tutorial or call an API, but that you can take a problem from "three people actually have this" all the way to "a working, evaluated, observable, affordable, deployed product that meets the bar I set," which is precisely what doing the job requires. Every individual skill on the track matters, but this is the artifact that shows you can *integrate* them into something real, and that integration, more than any single technique, is what makes you an AI engineer rather than someone who knows about AI.

## Where this fits in the track
This is the end, and the beginning. The capstone completes a journey from the building phase through RAG, agents, production, and the advanced hard edges, and it proves the thing the whole track was for: that you can ship real AI products, not just understand the pieces. What you carry out is not a list of techniques but a way of working, scope ruthlessly, validate with real users, define success measurably, build the simplest thing that works, evaluate honestly, observe what you ship, manage the cost, harden it for the world, and reflect to keep improving, which is exactly how AI engineering is done in practice and exactly what the rest of your career will ask of you. You started as someone learning AI engineering; you finish as someone who has shipped a real, measured AI product end to end. The next one is yours to choose, and you now have everything you need to build it.

cards.prompt: The fastest way to learn a new tool is to read the docs end-to-end before writing any code.
cards.whenRight: Right - building a tiny example first beats reading every page.
cards.whenWrong: Docs are a reference, not a tutorial. Code first, read second.

cards.prompt: Committing small checkpoints helps you debug regressions and review your own progress.
cards.whenRight: Exactly - tiny commits are a superpower.
cards.whenWrong: They really do help; `git revert` is one command away.

cards.prompt: Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow without understanding is a sustainable long-term strategy.
cards.whenRight: Correct - understanding the why is what makes you employable.
cards.whenWrong: Short-term it works; long-term it stalls you.

items.title: Finish and ship the week's project
items.body:
[CODE] The capstone. Build and ship ONE AI product to a public URL. It must use: at least one major model (GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, Llama), at least one of (RAG, agents, fine-tuning), real auth, real eval suite, real observability, real cost dashboard, a real domain. It should solve a real problem for a real audience (you count as your own user, but not exclusively). Public launch on day 7. Share it somewhere, Twitter, your blog, Hacker News, Reddit. Get feedback. Iterate.

Ship checklist:
 - It runs from a clean clone / fresh open, no "works on my machine" steps missing.
 - Commit it to your repo with a short README saying what it does and how to run it.
 - Tag or note this as your Week 24 deliverable so you can look back on it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have two capstone ideas: (A) a multi-agent research assistant that searches the web, reads papers, and synthesises reports, and (B) a focused code review tool that checks Python code for common security vulnerabilities and suggests fixes. Which is more likely to produce a strong portfolio project in 10 days? B, almost certainly. Idea A requires getting the agent loop right, getting web search to work reliably, getting quality retrieval, and getting the synthesis to be coherent, four hard problems in sequence. Idea B has one core problem (extraction of security vulnerabilities with accurate recommendations) and a clear evaluation criterion (is the finding real? Is the recommendation correct?). A focused project executed well demonstrates more engineering judgment than an ambitious project executed poorly.

items.body:

```bash
git add . && git commit -m 'Capstone, Ship Something Real, End to End'
git tag v24.0 && git push --tags
```
